Contributions to Finance and Accounting

The book series ‘Contributions to Finance and Accounting’ features the latest
research from research areas like financial management, investment, capital mar-
kets, financial institutions, FinTech and financial innovation, accounting methods
and standards, reporting, and corporate governance, among others. Books published
in this series are primarily monographs and edited volumes that present new research
results, both theoretical and empirical, on a clearly defined topic. All books are
published in print and digital formats and disseminated globally. This book series is
indexed in Scopus.

Part I
Foundations and Market Evolution

The Rise of Robo-Advisory in FinTech
Alex Zarifis , Narmin Nahidi , and Larisa Yarovaya
Abstract This chapter explores the transformative rise of robo-advisory within the
broader FinTech revolution, tracing its evolution from traditional human advisors
to AI-driven platforms that democratise financial services. The chapter begins
by situating robo-advisory within the rapidly evolving financial landscape shaped
by digitalisation, disintermediation, and changing client expectations. It examines
the drivers behind this shift, including advancements in AI and data analytics,
evolving investor demands for personalisation and accessibility, as well as the
cost and scalability pressures facing financial institutions. The chapter differ-
entiates between rule-based and AI-powered systems, highlighting how modern
robo-advisors increasingly leverage machine learning, behavioural insights, and
alternative data to offer dynamic and adaptive services. Emerging trends, such
as hybrid advisory models, behavioural nudges, ethical challenges surrounding
algorithmic transparency, and inclusivity concerns, are also addressed. Moreover,
the chapter maps out key players and market trends, emphasising regional variations,
consolidation patterns, and niche market opportunities. A novel framework of
six AI-driven business models is introduced to explain how robo-advisory is
strategically deployed across incumbent and disruptive financial organisations. The
chapter concludes by underscoring that success in robo-advisory is not solely a

1 Introduction
1.1 The FinTech Landscape and the Rise of Robo-Advisory
The financial landscape is undergoing a fundamental transformation driven by
technological innovation, societal shifts, and evolving stakeholder expectations.
At the heart of this transformation lies financial technology (FinTech), which is
challenging traditional models and reshaping how financial services are delivered,
consumed, and regulated. Among the many FinTech innovations, robo-advisors
offering algorithm-based financial planning and investment services are rapidly
rising to prominence. Their emergence signals a shift not only in how financial
advice is delivered but also in the broader relationship between finance, technology,
and society.
The integration of AI into financial services is occurring alongside a soci-
etal movement towards personalisation, accessibility, and digital empowerment.
Consumers now expect real-time, tailored services delivered with the speed and
convenience characteristic of digital platforms. Financial services are no longer
the exclusive domain of affluent clients or institutional investors; rather, a new
generation of retail investors is gaining access to sophisticated tools once reserved
for wealth management elites. This democratisation of finance is a key hallmark
of the FinTech era. At the same time, this empowerment is not entirely organic; it
reflects both a “push” by providers keen to scale and automate services, and a “pull”
from users demanding more control, transparency, and value.
Stakeholders in this ecosystem include individual investors, financial institutions,
FinTech startups, regulators, and AI developers. Each group plays a different role
and experiences unique challenges. Financial institutions face the dual pressure
of integrating new technologies while preserving trust and compliance. For them,
robo-advisory offers both opportunity and threat: a means to scale operations and
reach new markets, but also a potential disruption to traditional advisory models.
Startups, on the other hand, often position themselves as agile disruptors, leveraging
automation to enter markets with lower overheads and more streamlined offerings.
Regulators must balance the need for innovation with the imperatives of investor
protection, fairness, and systemic stability. AI developers are tasked with creating

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 5
systems that are not only technically robust but also ethically sound, interpretable,
and aligned with human financial goals.
Robo-advisors exemplify how digital innovation is blurring the boundaries
between finance and technology. At a basic level, these platforms use algorithms
to assess an investor’s profile based on factors such as risk tolerance, financial
goals, and investment horizon and then propose and manage portfolios accordingly.
Many also provide supplementary services like retirement planning, ESG investing,
and debt management. Although the sophistication of these platforms varies, some
incorporate advanced AI techniques, including natural language processing and
machine learning, to offer more dynamic, conversational, and predictive services.
This revolution goes beyond digitising traditional services; it introduces entirely
new ways of interacting with, accessing, and delivering financial products. FinTech
lowers barriers to entry, expands financial inclusion, and enables the rise of
automation-driven platforms like robo-advisors. These platforms exemplify how
financial services are evolving from static, manual systems into dynamic, data-
intensive ecosystems. The robo-advisor may use generative AI in both the frontend
and the backend, both in the interaction and the analysis. This is not, however,
necessarily the case, and there are robo-advisors that do not use advanced AI in
either the frontend or the backend and are as effective. The varying use of AI
highlights a key insight: success in robo-advisory does not always require the
latest technological sophistication. Some effective robo-advisors use simple rule-
based systems, prioritising user trust and clarity over complexity. Others push
the frontier with real-time natural language processing, predictive analytics, and
adaptive learning. This divergence reflects the broader diversity of strategies in
FinTech, where innovation can take the form of both cutting-edge tech and user-
friendly minimalism.
Robo-advisors are digital platforms that offer investment advice and typically
create customised portfolios for individuals based on their preferences. These
automated investment advisors are guiding an increasing volume of people and
resources. They are growing in their ability and influence. The AI used can draw
on a huge breadth of data and identify patterns that a human would miss and that
may even defy a rational explanation. In practice, however, customisation is often
limited, and the investors are simply put in a number of categories based on their
dispositions to risk and their goals. The state of the art of what generative AI can do
in this context and what is offered can be quite different, with some simpler services
riding the wave of popularity of AI.
While neither the service nor the technology underpinning it is completely new,
the scale at which it is being used now is very different from even a few years ago.
The recent explosive growth of this innovation has clearly moved forward to the
next stage of its diffusion to far wider audiences.
Despite their limitations, from the consumer’s perspective they are liberating
finance, making financial services available to far more people. Retail and novice
investors can act in a more informed way even if they have limited money and time.
From the perspective of the financial organisations, this will be their decisive battle,
which will either enable them to scale dramatically or fall victim to the consolidation
that typically comes with disruptive technologies like this. In an age where little

6 A.Zarifisetal.
is certain, there is one certainty for financial robo-advisors: Competitions will
be fierce. Robo-advisors are not only easier to adopt, but they are also easier to
evaluate and compare with each other. Along with Fintech, comparison websites
are disrupting finance making the competition fiercer, and this applies to automated
advisors. People are willing to give their money to a machine to manage, but they
want to know from other people which is the best machine to give it to.
Those that are left standing in the end may or may not closely resemble the
financial institutions of today. This is therefore one of the key battles where the
smallest edge may tip things in one’s favour. The old barriers to entry that provided
some certainty and stability in the past are no longer as high as they used to be. So,
in a new world with minimal barriers and many options, which will be the decisive
factors? These will range from the usability, which can involve some nuanced
subjective feelings about the experience, to the far more objective performance in
hard numbers. It is therefore crucial for organisations to understand every dimension
of this innovation and make the right moves at the right time.
This book covers the key issues related to robo-advisors, covering both the finan-
cial and technological dimensions. Using robo-advisors effectively may involve
using the latest versions of generative AI or applying completely commoditised
solutions with an effective business model. There isn’t one answer, but it is
necessary to understand this service and more broadly the role of Fintech in
disrupting finance. To be successful, those from finance must understand robo-
advisors as a technology and as an innovation, while people from a technology
background must understand the financial dimension. In addition to the typical
service of portfolio management, other common services are retirement planning,
financial planning tools, fractional share investing, thematic and ESG investing,
dividend reinvestment, crypto investments, estate planning, insurance advice and
debt management.
Yet the evolution from rule-based to AI-powered advisory is far from linear.
Some platforms continue to rely on predefined rules and rigid categorisation, offer-
ing only superficial customisation. Others are beginning to exploit the capabilities of
generative AI to provide more intuitive and responsive user interactions, including
real-time adjustments based on behavioural data and market changes. The gap
between what the most advanced technologies can theoretically offer and what
is actually implemented at scale remains significant. Many robo-advisors trade
on the aura of AI innovation without deploying cutting-edge methods under the
hood. The adoption of robo-advisory systems reflects a mixture of push and pull
dynamics. From the “push” perspective, financial institutions and FinTechs are
driving adoption through business models that rely on automation for scalability,
cost-efficiency, and regulatory compliance. These platforms reduce the need for
human labour and standardise decision-making, appealing to firms under pressure
to do more with less. On the “pull” side, consumers, particularly millennials and
digital natives, are increasingly comfortable with technology-based solutions and
attracted to platforms that promise lower fees, greater transparency, and always-on
availability. This convergence of supply-side innovation and demand-side readiness
has accelerated the spread of robo-advisors into mainstream financial services.

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 7
Despite their growing popularity, robo-advisors are not without controversy.
Critics question their ability to handle nuanced financial situations, their trans-
parency in risk modelling, and their capacity to adapt to clients’ changing needs.
Others warn about the risks of over-reliance on algorithms, particularly when
users lack the financial literacy to critically assess the advice they receive. From
a regulatory standpoint, challenges include ensuring algorithmic accountability,
preventing discriminatory outcomes, and maintaining investor protection in the face
of opaque decision-making processes. Nonetheless, the benefits are considerable.
Robo-advisors make investing accessible to a broader population, including those
previously excluded due to high fees or complexity. They offer a scalable way to
provide financial advice that can adapt in real time, potentially reducing behavioural
biases and enhancing outcomes. They also increase transparency, as platforms often
include clear dashboards and performance metrics, allowing clients to monitor their
investments with unprecedented ease.
The rise of robo-advisors is also emblematic of deeper structural changes in
finance. Traditional barriers to entry such as regulatory capital, brand trust, or branch
infrastructure are eroding. Digital platforms can launch quickly, iterate rapidly, and
scale globally. At the same time, the ability to compare financial products and
services online puts incumbent institutions under pressure to compete not just on
performance, but also on usability, personalisation, and customer experience. In this
increasingly competitive landscape, having even a small technological or opera-
tional edge can be decisive. This book situates robo-advisory within the broader
evolution of FinTech and financial services. It explores the historical development
of digital investment tools, the transition from static rule-based systems to dynamic
AI-driven models, and the interplay between business strategy, user experience, and
regulatory frameworks. We argue that robo-advisors are not merely a new type of
financial product, but a lens through which we can understand the future of finance
itself where automation, data, and design converge to reshape how people save,
invest, and plan.
1.2 Drivers, Challenges, and the Road Ahead
Understanding robo-advisors requires more than just awareness of their growing
market presence. It demands an appreciation of both their technological under-
pinnings and financial logic. For finance professionals, this means engaging with
the mechanisms of algorithmic decision-making and user interface design. For
technologists, it means understanding risk management, asset allocation, and client
segmentation. This interdisciplinary perspective is vital to harnessing the potential
of robo-advisory while mitigating its risks. With such a disruptive technology,
operating on such a large scale, there are challenges for all the stakeholders, not
just the customers and the financial organisations, but also the regulators. For
consumers, a key challenge is trust (Zarifis and Cheng 2022), understanding how
a platform works, whether its advice is suitable, and whether they are protected in

8 A.Zarifisetal.
case of errors or unexpected outcomes. Financial literacy varies widely, and many
investors may not realise they are engaging with AI rather than a human advisor. For
financial organisations, the stakes are high: integrating robo-advisory into existing
operations requires balancing cost-efficiency with risk management and client
experience. Firms that fail to adopt may fall behind, while those that rush may suffer
reputational or regulatory consequences. Regulators, in turn, must navigate the twin
pressures of encouraging innovation and ensuring consumer protection. Questions
of explainability, algorithmic fairness, data use, and fiduciary responsibility are
central to regulatory debates. These issues raise urgent research questions: How
should we evaluate robo-advisory outcomes? What kinds of disclosures should
platforms provide? Can regulatory frameworks evolve quickly enough to match the
pace of innovation? Ultimately, robo-advisors are part of a broader trend towards
digital transformation in finance. Their success depends not only on algorithmic
accuracy but also on trust, transparency, and alignment with human goals. In the
chapters that follow, we examine how these platforms are built, adopted, regulated,
and evaluated, offering insights for academics, practitioners, policymakers, and
users alike. As this field evolves, the balance between innovation and accountability
will determine whether robo-advisors fulfil their promise or fall short of it.
2 Evolution from Traditional Advisors to AI-driven Models
The evolution of financial advisory services from traditional human advisors to
AI-driven robo-advisors represents a paradigm shift in how financial guidance is
conceptualised, delivered, and experienced. This transformation is underpinned
by broader trends in digitalisation, disintermediation, and datafication that are
reshaping financial markets and institutions. Historically, financial advice was a
high-touch, relationship-based service delivered by trained professionals, often
operating under commission-based models or fee-based structures. Clients sought
human expertise, not only for investment allocation but also for reassurance,
trust, and behavioural coaching. However, this model was inherently limited by
its cost, scalability, and access, especially for retail or low-net-worth investors.
The emergence of robo-advisors in the post-2008 financial crisis era marked a
response to these limitations. Early platforms such as Betterment and Wealthfront
in the USA began offering algorithm-driven investment portfolios with lower fees,
minimal entry thresholds, and a high degree of automation. These platforms aimed
to democratise financial advice by using technology to reduce overheads and
pass on savings to clients. As the market matured, incumbents like Vanguard and
Schwab introduced their own hybrid robo offerings, blending automated models
with optional human support.
A key driver of this shift has been the rapid development of financial algorithms
and the availability of structured data on investor behaviour, market trends, and
macroeconomic conditions. Initially, the algorithms were grounded in Modern
Portfolio Theory (MPT) and offered asset allocations based on risk questionnaires

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 9
and time horizons. However, the growing sophistication of machine learning and
natural language processing has enabled robo-advisors to evolve from passive
allocators to proactive, adaptive financial agents. AI-powered systems can now
interpret textual data from news and social media, recognise sentiment shifts, and
factor real-time economic indicators into investment decisions (Gomber et al. 2018;
Sironi 2016).
Unlike their human counterparts, robo-advisors can scale effortlessly across
geographies and client segments. They operate with 24/7 availability, consistent
logic, and a high degree of transparency. While traditional advisors may offer a more
holistic, empathetic, and customised approach, their performance and advice quality
can vary significantly depending on individual skill, incentives, and behavioural
biases. Robo-advisors, in contrast, offer standardisation and predictability, albeit
with some loss of nuance and human judgement. Nonetheless, recent empirical stud-
ies suggest that the portfolio outcomes from robo-advisors are often comparable to
those produced by traditional advisors, especially for passive investment strategies
(Belanche et al. 2020; Fein 2015).
One of the turning points in this evolution has been the integration of behavioural
finance principles into robo-advisory interfaces. Traditional advisors have long
played a behavioural coaching role, helping clients resist herd behaviour, panic
selling, or overtrading. Modern robo-advisors increasingly incorporate nudges,
visual dashboards, and predictive alerts to guide users towards better financial
habits (Lo 2017). This incorporation reflects a convergence of psychological
insights, data analytics, and interface design, placing robo-advisory at the nexus
of finance, computer science, and behavioural economics. At an institutional level,
the evolution towards AI-driven advisory also reflects changing cost structures
and regulatory pressures. With tightening margins, banks and asset managers
view robo-advisory as a tool for operational efficiency and client segmentation.
For example, high-net-worth clients may continue to receive bespoke advisory
services, while entry-level clients are channelled through automated platforms. This
“barbell” strategy allows firms to optimise resources and expand their reach without
compromising compliance. According to Deloitte (2018), nearly half of wealth
managers globally were investing in robo capabilities by 2020, with most adopting
a hybrid advisory model.
Importantly, the rise of AI in financial advisory does not imply the obsolescence
of human advisors. Instead, a “human + machine” model is emerging in which
algorithms handle routine tasks, such as rebalancing, tax-loss harvesting, and risk
profiling, while human advisors focus on complex financial planning and emotional
engagement. This shift parallels trends in other professional services where AI
augments rather than replaces human expertise. As pointed out by Brynjolfsson and
McAfee (2014), the highest value lies not in pure automation but in collaborative
intelligence, where machines enhance human decision-making. The transition to
AI-driven models has also sparked ethical and regulatory debates. Concerns have
been raised about algorithmic transparency, data privacy, and fairness in portfolio
recommendations. Regulators are increasingly scrutinising the use of personal
data, algorithmic biases, and the fiduciary responsibilities of robo-advisors (Baker

10 A.Zarifisetal.
and Dellaert 2019). While some jurisdictions have embraced innovation with
regulatory sandboxes, others have taken a more cautious stance, imposing stricter
licensing and disclosure requirements. This variation reflects broader tensions in
global financial governance between fostering innovation and ensuring investor
protection. The evolution from traditional to AI-driven financial advisors is not a
linear replacement but a multifaceted transformation. It reflects broader shifts in
technology, economics, and client expectations. While traditional advisory models
continue to hold relevance in certain segments, the future of financial advice will
likely be hybrid, data-informed, and increasingly digital. The next frontier involves
not only refining the algorithms that drive these platforms but also enhancing their
capacity for trust, adaptability, and ethical alignment.
3 Differentiating Rule-based and AI-powered Systems
The field of robo-advisory encompasses a wide spectrum of technological sophis-
tication, from static rule-based systems to dynamic learning-based AI models.
Distinguishing between these two categories is essential to understanding not only
how robo-advisors function, but also their capacity for personalisation, adaptability,
and long-term value creation. Rule-based systems, while often labelled as “robo-
advisors”, differ substantially in capabilities and risks compared to AI-powered
platforms. Rule-based robo-advisors are grounded in predefined decision trees,
heuristics, and fixed allocation models. These systems typically use structured
inputs such as client age, income, risk tolerance, and investment horizon to
generate asset allocations based on Modern Portfolio Theory (MPT). The advice
is deterministic: given the same input, the system will always produce the same
output. This structure ensures consistency, transparency, and regulatory clarity. For
example, platforms like Vanguard Personal Advisor Services or early versions of
Betterment followed this approach to offer low-cost, diversified portfolios built
around passive investment strategies (Fein 2015).
Despite their simplicity, rule-based systems offer several advantages. First, they
are easier to audit, explain, and regulate an important consideration in a highly
scrutinised industry. Second, they are cost-effective, making them suitable for
entry-level investors. Third, they reflect a conservative approach to technology
deployment, limiting potential risks arising from opaque algorithms or spurious
correlations. However, this rigidity also means that rule-based advisors often fall
short in handling complex financial situations, adjusting to market shifts, or learning
from new data. As Belanche et al. (2020) note, users may become disengaged
over time if the system does not evolve with their preferences or behaviour. In
contrast, AI-powered robo-advisors leverage machine learning, natural language
processing, and other forms of artificial intelligence to deliver more adaptive and

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 11
personalised services. Rather than relying solely on static inputs, these systems
can incorporate unstructured data (e.g. financial news, social media sentiment),
behavioural cues (e.g. login frequency, withdrawal patterns), and even voice or chat
interactions to refine recommendations. This dynamic capability allows AI-based
platforms to recognise emerging trends, predict customer needs, and proactively
suggest financial actions (Gomber et al. 2018).
One of the key features of AI-powered systems is continuous learning. Algo-
rithms can update their models as new data becomes available, allowing the advisor
to recalibrate portfolios based on market volatility, client behaviour, or updated
macroeconomic forecasts. For example, systems using reinforcement learning can
optimise asset allocations over time based on the outcomes of previous decisions,
improving performance while adapting to evolving investor preferences. As Sironi
(2016) suggests, the most advanced robo-advisors behave more like “financial
assistants” than mere portfolio generators.
However, these advantages come with trade-offs. AI-based systems are often less
transparent, raising concerns about explainability, algorithmic bias, and account-
ability. Users may not fully understand how recommendations are generated,
especially if the underlying models are black-box neural networks. Regulatory
bodies such as the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) have called
for greater algorithmic transparency in digital finance, highlighting the tension
between innovation and investor protection. Baker and Dellaert (2019) argue that
the fiduciary responsibilities of robo-advisors must be reinterpreted in light of AI’s
growing role in decision-making. There is also the question of data privacy and
ethical use. AI systems require large volumes of personal and behavioural data
to function effectively. The more data they have, the better they can personalise.
But this raises risks related to data breaches, misuse, and surveillance issues
that are increasingly salient in jurisdictions with strict data protection laws like
GDPR. Furthermore, the performance of AI-powered advisors can be uneven across
different client segments. While tech-savvy users may appreciate adaptive interfaces
and real-time insights, other investors may find them confusing or intimidating.
This raises an important strategic decision for platforms: should they prioritise
automation and sophistication, or maintain simplicity and clarity?
In practice, many robo-advisors fall somewhere along a continuum. Hybrid
models combining rule-based decision trees with machine-learning enhancements
are becoming increasingly common. Some firms also offer “human-in-the-loop”
designs where advisors oversee AI recommendations and intervene when necessary.
This approach aims to balance scalability and precision with human judgement
and empathy. Ultimately, the differentiation between rule-based and AI-powered
systems is not just technical; it reflects deeper questions about trust, control, and the
nature of financial decision-making. As the industry matures, the challenge will be
to develop systems that are not only intelligent but also interpretable, secure, and
aligned with investor values.

12 A.Zarifisetal.
3.1 Emerging Themes in Robo-Advisory
Robo-advisory services have evolved from niche innovations into robust, multi-
functional financial tools embedded within the wider digital finance ecosystem.
As the field matures, several key themes have begun to shape its trajectory. These
emerging patterns are not only technological but also behavioural, regulatory, and
ethical, revealing the expanding responsibilities and possibilities associated with
algorithmic financial advice.
One of the most notable developments is the hybridisation of services. Early
robo-advisors positioned themselves as fully automated alternatives to traditional
financial planners. However, as adoption broadened, it became clear that many
users, especially those with complex financial needs, preferred having some level
of human interaction. In response, leading platforms have adopted hybrid models
that combine algorithm-driven portfolio management with optional access to human
advisors. This blended approach enhances trust, supports client retention during
market turbulence, and acknowledges the psychological dimensions of financial
decision-making (Jung et al. 2018). Rather than replacing human advisors outright,
robo-advisors now often complement them, streamlining routine tasks while pre-
serving empathy and flexibility for nuanced cases.
Another defining theme is the integration of behavioural finance into platform
design. Traditional risk tolerance questionnaires are increasingly being replaced or
supplemented by goal-based planning interfaces that reflect users’ evolving life con-
texts. Rather than focusing narrowly on asset allocation, these platforms now guide
users through savings milestones, retirement planning, and behavioural nudges
designed to reduce impulsive decisions. Features such as progress dashboards,
auto-reminders, and scenario planning tools are increasingly common, aligning
robo-advisory interfaces with behavioural design principles that support financial
well-being (Lo 2017).
Closely related to this is the rise of personalisation through alternative data.
AI-powered robo-advisors now have the capacity to move beyond traditional
demographic inputs. By analysing behavioural data, lifestyle patterns, and even
psychometric signals, platforms can offer more refined and responsive investment
strategies. This allows advisors to tailor portfolios based not just on income and
age, but on personality traits, spending habits, and digital engagement profiles. Di
Maggio et al. (2020) note that such approaches can significantly enhance portfolio
alignment with investor goals, but they also raise ethical questions around data
privacy, user consent, and algorithmic profiling. The promise of personalisation
must therefore be balanced with responsible data governance.
Robo-advisors are also broadening their scope beyond investment management.
What began as a service focused on low-cost, passive portfolios has now evolved
into a suite of financial planning tools. Many platforms offer tax optimisation,
debt reduction strategies, ESG screening, insurance matching, and estate planning,
all within a unified digital interface. This shift reflects a strategic move towards
lifecycle financial coaching, where the robo-advisor becomes a long-term partner

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 13
in financial decision-making (Sironi 2016). The bundling of services also supports
platform stickiness, as users are more likely to stay engaged when their broader
financial lives are integrated into a single system.
Trust and transparency have simultaneously emerged as central concerns. As
algorithms become more complex and less interpretable, users may feel uncertain
about how decisions are made on their behalf. To address this, many platforms are
now incorporating explainability features such as visualisation of allocation logic,
plain-language disclosures, or simulation tools that show how portfolios respond to
different market scenarios. This development is not merely cosmetic. Research has
shown that perceived fairness and trustworthiness of algorithmic decisions improve
when users understand how those decisions are made (Kleinberg et al. 2020).
Regulators are also pressuring platforms to meet higher standards of disclosure,
particularly under rules like GDPR and MiFID II, which directly address automated
decision-making.
Finally, there is a growing emphasis on inclusion and accessibility. Robo-
advisors have the potential to democratise finance by reducing entry barriers,
offering multilingual interfaces, and lowering minimum investment thresholds. In
developing economies, mobile-first robo-advisors are bringing investment services
to new populations, bypassing the need for traditional banking infrastructure
(Arner et al. 2016). Yet, challenges remain. Digital illiteracy, algorithmic bias, and
accessibility limitations may still prevent marginalised groups from fully benefiting.
Therefore, platforms must not only offer inclusive access but also be designed with
diversity in mind, ensuring that users of varying backgrounds, ages, and digital
proficiencies can engage meaningfully with the service. Together, these themes
mark the expansion of robo-advisory from a narrowly defined technological solution
to a broader institutional and behavioural phenomenon. The platforms are no longer
only defined by their algorithms, but by how they engage users, address regulation,
incorporate data ethics, and adapt across cultures and markets. Understanding these
shifts is essential to grasping the future of digital financial advice not only in terms
of innovation, but also in terms of responsibility, reach, and resilience.
4 Key Players and Market Trends in Robo-Advisory
In the future, there may be a small number of global robo-advisors, but currently,
due to regulation and cultural differences, different robo-advisors are popular in
each country. If we just take Europe as an example, in the UK, robo-advisors include
Nutmeg; in German-speaking countries, Scalable Capital and Whitebox are popular;
in France, there is Yomoni; in Spain, there is InbestMe; and in Switzerland, there
is Simple Wealth. Countries that are known as financial innovators and are strong
in Fintech and crypto, such as Singapore, are also particularly strong in providing
several successful robo-advisors, such as StashAway and Endowus.
In North America, the robo-advisory space is led by early pioneers like Better-
ment and Wealthfront, which remain dominant due to first-mover advantage and

14 A.Zarifisetal.
consistent innovation in user experience. These platforms focus heavily on passive
investing and automated tax-loss harvesting, offering a clean, intuitive interface for
millennials and tech-savvy investors. However, major incumbents such as Vanguard,
Fidelity, and Charles Schwab have also entered the space with hybrid models that
combine algorithmic allocation with optional human advice. The success of these
incumbents underscores a broader market trend: robo-advisory is no longer the
exclusive domain of startups, but a capability that is rapidly being absorbed into
the core offerings of traditional financial institutions.
Market penetration and client acquisition strategies vary by region and provider.
In developed economies, most robo-advisors target digitally native retail investors,
especially those in younger age cohorts with long investment horizons but limited
capital. Conversely, in emerging markets, platforms are experimenting with alter-
native business models, including subscription-based plans, micro-investing, and
integration with mobile wallets to reach users outside the traditional banking system.
For example, platforms in India and Indonesia are leveraging partnerships with
telecom providers and mobile-first banks to offer robo-investing services via super
apps. These strategies reflect the adaptability of the robo-advisory model to different
regulatory environments, financial infrastructures, and consumer behaviours.
Consolidation is another emerging trend. As the market matures, smaller robo-
advisors are being acquired by banks, asset managers, or private equity firms seeking
to expand their digital capabilities. This wave of mergers and acquisitions suggests
a convergence between FinTech innovation and institutional finance, driven by the
need for scale, trust, and regulatory compliance. At the same time, new entrants
continue to emerge, particularly niche robo-advisors focused on ESG investing,
Sharia-compliant portfolios, or crypto-asset management. These specialised plat-
forms cater to increasingly segmented investor preferences, illustrating the potential
for robo-advisors to not only generalise but also differentiate within the digital
advice space.
These developments suggest that the future of robo-advisory will be both
global and fragmented. While a few dominant players may emerge at scale, the
landscape is likely to retain a diverse mix of local champions, hybrid models, and
niche providers. The dynamics of trust, regulation, cultural fit, and technological
infrastructure will continue to shape how robo-advisory evolves in different markets.
Rather than converging towards a single model, robo-advisory is likely to diversify,
reflecting not just financial logic, but also social, legal, and behavioural contexts
unique to each region.
4.1 Digital Transformation in Finance and Emerging Business
Models
The effectiveness and popularity of financial robo-advisors do not just depend
on the technology they utilise but also on the broader strategy they are part of.

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 15
Digital transformation in finance is an ongoing process, but there are six AI-focused
business models that have been proven and should stand the test of time. The six
business models proven to be ideal for a modern organisation with AI at its centre
(Zarifis and Cheng 2023, 2024) are: (1) an incumbent focusing on one part of the
value chain and disaggregating, (2) an incumbent absorbing AI into an existing
model, (3) an incumbent expanding beyond the current model to fully utilise the
opportunities of AI and access new data, (4) a startup disruptor focused on one
sector, built from the start to be highly automated, (5) a disruptor focused on tech
adding a new service like insurance, and (6) a disruptor that is not necessarily tech-
focused, with an extensive user or fanbase.
Robo-advisors are central to all six business models, but they will be used very
differently depending on the chosen strategy. The business model may influence
the technology and the data used by the robo-advisor. For example, if the strategy
is to keep the business model the same and adapt technology to it, there will
typically be some in-house customisation of the robo-advisor. The priority is that
the robo-advisor accurately represents the organisation as opposed to fully utilising
its capabilities.
As shown in Fig. 1, the deployment of robo-advisory services varies significantly
depending on the business model of the financial organisation. These six AI-
focused models illustrate not only how firms structure their operations around
automation but also how they leverage data, scale, and customer engagement.
The distinction between incumbents and disruptors, each adopting AI in different
ways, highlights that there is no one-size-fits-all approach. Some models prioritise
legacy integration, while others are built from the ground up with digital-native
strategies. Understanding where a robo-advisor fits within this typology provides
crucial insight into its strategic potential, technological constraints, and long-term
sustainability in an increasingly competitive financial ecosystem.
The influence of the business model on the data available to the robo-advisor
is important. The AI-focused business models put more emphasis on data than the
older, outdated models they are replacing. It is not simply a case of more or less data;
the different data make the assessment different. For example, the first three business
models involve incumbents that have data on their customers and their investment
results in the past that can inform the analysis the AI does. The fourth model is a
startup that does not have its own data. The fifth is a tech-savvy company with data
from its existing customer base, and the sixth is a company that is not tech-focused
and has data from its existing customer base. If the customer behaviour available is
not financial, it can still be useful in understanding their perspective on things like
risk, trust, the point they are at in their lives, and their goals.
4.2 Robo-Advisors in Cryptocurrency Investment
In the context of cryptocurrencies, the concept of robo-advisory extends beyond
simple portfolio rebalancing. Given the 24/7 nature of crypto markets and their

16 A.Zarifisetal.
Fig. 1 Six financial services business models with AI at their centre

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 17
extreme volatility, algorithms must adapt to rapid price movements, liquidity
shocks, and regime change challenges much more severe than in traditional markets
(Luo et al. 2021). The integration of blockchain analytics, sentiment data, and
real-time volatility metrics into advisory algorithms allows these tools to provide
dynamic recommendations. For example, research has shown that ML-based trad-
ing strategies for cryptocurrencies significantly outperform simple buy-and-hold
approaches, underscoring the importance of adaptive algorithmic design in this
domain (Cohen 2023;Lietal.2 025). Thus, the evolution of robo-advisors for digital
assets reflects not only the democratisation of investment management but also the
technological sophistication required to operate effectively in decentralised markets,
which exhibit distinct long-memory properties, trading environments, and arguably
different investor behaviours.
While traditional robo-advisors (e.g., in equities or bonds) have been widely
discussed (Judijanto 2025), the growing popularity of digital assets has prompted
several fintech and wealth management platforms to expand their offerings into
cryptocurrency investment. Several mainstream robo-advisory platforms, such as
Betterment, have begun to offer diversified crypto-asset portfolios, while specialist
firms like Bitwise Asset Management provide dedicated algorithmically managed
crypto index funds. Other platforms, such as Wealthfront and SwissBorg, offer
more limited or niche crypto exposure, indicating a spectrum of service depth in
the robo-advisor crypto space. These systems utilise quantitative risk models to
allocate investments between major cryptocurrencies, stablecoins, and occasionally
DeFi assets, aiming to provide exposure while mitigating downside risks.
However, the operational logic of crypto robo-advisors differs significantly from
that of traditional counterparts. Unlike equity or bond portfolios that rely on
established valuation metrics and long-term fundamentals, crypto portfolios require
real-time sentiment analysis, on-chain network data, and liquidity assessments (Li
2023). This complexity challenges the robustness of standard mean-variance opti-
misation frameworks and prompts developers to adopt hybrid models that combine
algorithmic rebalancing with heuristic or rule-based triggers. Consequently, robo-
advisors in the crypto domain embody a fusion of classical portfolio theory and
behavioural-fintech adaptation to a novel asset class.
Robo-advisors offer a potential antidote to the behavioural biases that pervade
cryptocurrency investing. Retail investors often fall victim to emotional trading,
driven by fear of missing out (FOMO), loss aversion, and herding effects. By
delegating portfolio decisions to an algorithm, investors may reduce impulsive
behaviour and maintain more disciplined, long-term strategies. Automated systems
also eliminate the cognitive overload caused by the high-frequency and often
contradictory information flow within crypto markets.
Yet, reliance on algorithmic advice introduces its own psychological complex-
ities. Some investors may develop an “illusion of control”, assuming that the
algorithm guarantees superior outcomes, while others may experience discomfort
with the lack of human interaction or transparency in decision-making. Moreover,
algorithmic biases embedded in model training data could reproduce systemic
errors, particularly if models rely on historical patterns that are poorly suited to

18 A.Zarifisetal.
the rapidly evolving crypto environment. Thus, while robo-advisors can mitigate
emotional biases, they simultaneously create new cognitive dependencies that
warrant careful study (Filiz et al. 2022).
The regulatory landscape surrounding robo-advisors in traditional finance is still
evolving, and the inclusion of cryptocurrencies further complicates the picture.
In most jurisdictions, robo-advisors must comply with fiduciary and suitability
requirements, ensuring that automated recommendations align with clients’ profiles.
However, when the underlying assets are decentralised and globally traded, the reg-
ulatory jurisdiction becomes ambiguous. Platforms offering crypto robo-advisory
often face challenges in meeting disclosure standards, anti-money laundering
(AML) compliance, and investor protection obligations.
The regulatory frameworks governing digital assets and artificial intelligence
are rapidly evolving, shaping the environment in which robo-advisors operate. In
the European Union, the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA) (Regulation
(EU) 2023/1114) represents a milestone in the legal recognition and supervision of
crypto-asset activities. MiCA establishes harmonised rules for issuers of crypto-
assets and for crypto-asset service providers (CASPs), introducing obligations
related to investor protection, transparency, and operational governance. Robo-
advisory platforms that offer automated investment strategies involving crypto-
assets may fall within the MiCA definition of a CASP, particularly when providing
portfolio management or investment advice. This means they must adhere to
MiCA’s authorisation, conduct-of-business, and disclosure requirements. The reg-
ulation also emphasises the need for algorithmic transparency and the management
of technology-related risks, indirectly setting expectations for the explainability
and accountability of AI-driven decision-making tools used in automated advisory
services. In this sense, MiCA not only brings regulatory clarity to the crypto market
but also indirectly establishes governance standards relevant to algorithmic and
data-driven investment technologies.
Ethical concerns also arise from the opaque nature of algorithmic decision-
making. Investors seldom understand how recommendation engines weigh different
variables or respond to market stress, leading to a potential lack of accountability.
Data privacy adds another dimension of risk, particularly when algorithms rely
on personal financial data combined with blockchain analytics. Addressing these
ethical and legal challenges is critical for building investor trust and ensuring the
long-term sustainability of robo-advisory models in cryptocurrency markets.
The performance of robo-advised cryptocurrency portfolios remains a contested
issue. Empirical evidence is still emerging, but early analyses suggest that algo-
rithmic rebalancing can improve risk-adjusted returns by enforcing diversification
and disciplined trading. In particular, automated systems can respond to volatility
spikes more efficiently than human investors, reducing exposure during downturns
and re-entering positions systematically. These advantages position robo-advisors
as effective tools for smoothing returns in an otherwise turbulent market.
Nonetheless, algorithmic strategies are not immune to systemic risk. Model over-
fitting, delayed responses to black-swan events, and cascading sell-offs triggered
by simultaneous algorithmic signals can amplify market instability (Paulin et al.

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 19
2019; Gort et al. 2022). The absence of standardised benchmarks also makes it
difficult to assess performance objectively. In highly correlated markets such as
cryptocurrencies, where diversification benefits might be limited within the crypto-
assets ecosystem, robo-advisors may inadvertently provide a false sense of risk
management. Therefore, continuous monitoring and adaptive-learning mechanisms
are essential for maintaining robustness and investor confidence.
Looking ahead, the convergence of robo-advisory, decentralised finance, and
artificial intelligence heralds a new phase of autonomous wealth management.
Smart contracts could soon enable fully decentralised robo-advisors that operate
without intermediaries, executing trades and rebalancing portfolios transparently on
blockchain networks. Integration with decentralised oracles and predictive analytics
could further enhance these systems’ ability to anticipate market shifts, offering
real-time, self-executing financial guidance.
However, the expansion of robo-advisory into crypto ecosystems also raises
questions about inclusivity and systemic risk. While automation can democratise
access to sophisticated investment tools, it might also lead to herding behaviour
if thousands of investors follow identical algorithmic signals. Balancing efficiency
with diversity, and automation with human oversight, will define the next stage
in the evolution of robo-advisory technology. As digital assets mature, the key
challenge will be ensuring that these innovations enhance financial stability and
investor welfare rather than amplify speculative excesses.
5 Conclusion
Robo-advisory represents one of the most transformative developments within the
broader FinTech revolution. As this chapter has shown, the shift from traditional
human advisors to digital, and increasingly AI-driven, platforms is not simply a
technological progression; it is a systemic change in how financial services are
conceptualised, delivered, and consumed. This evolution reflects deeper shifts in
client expectations, regulatory pressures, and institutional strategies, signalling a
redefinition of the advisor–client relationship in the digital age. From their early
days as low-cost, rule-based tools offering passive investment portfolios, robo-
advisors have grown into complex, multifaceted platforms capable of delivering
personalised and dynamic financial guidance. Today, many are embedded with
machine-learning capabilities, natural language interfaces, and behavioural insights,
enabling them to serve as adaptive financial companions rather than static allocation
engines. The transition from deterministic models to predictive, data-driven systems
illustrates how innovation in this space is driven not only by advances in technology
but also by the growing demand for accessible, responsive, and transparent financial
solutions.
At the same time, the chapter has highlighted that this transformation is not
uniform or universal. Robo-advisors span a wide spectrum, from simple decision
trees to sophisticated AI-driven assistants, and their capabilities, cost structures,

20 A.Zarifisetal.
and user experiences vary accordingly. This variation is shaped by a number of
factors, chief among them the business model of the organisation deploying the
technology. As Fig. 1 illustrates, six dominant models define how institutions
integrate robo-advisory into their broader digital strategies. Whether these platforms
are developed in-house by incumbents or launched by digital-native startups, the
role of data, scalability, and trust is central to their success. Market structures
and regulatory environments also play a critical role in shaping the landscape.
Robo-advisory growth is uneven across geographies, with different players gain-
ing traction depending on local consumer behaviour, cultural preferences, and
compliance requirements. From Nutmeg in the UK to Betterment in the USA, to
StashAway in Singapore, providers are adapting their models to meet regional needs
while leveraging global technological trends. This duality, global convergence of
digital finance with localised execution, will likely define the next decade of robo-
advisory expansion.
Importantly, the rise of robo-advisory is not without risks and unresolved ten-
sions. As outlined in this chapter, questions remain around transparency, algorithmic
bias, user understanding, and regulatory oversight. The very features that make
robo-advisors efficient and scalable—automation, opacity, and reliance on data—
are also those that generate ethical and operational challenges. These tensions
underscore the need for an interdisciplinary approach to evaluating robo-advisors,
one that incorporates insights from finance, computer science, psychology, and law.
What also emerges clearly is that success in robo-advisory cannot be reduced to
technology alone. Platforms that thrive are those that blend usability with regulatory
compliance, technical capability with behavioural insight, and scalability with
personalisation. As we move further into the age of algorithmic finance, the key
differentiator will likely be trust: platforms must not only deliver strong outcomes
but also provide users with confidence in how those outcomes are achieved.
This chapter has laid the groundwork for understanding the rise of robo-advisory
by tracing its origins, differentiating its technological forms, examining its business
contexts, and highlighting its most pressing challenges and opportunities. In the
chapters that follow, we delve deeper into the architecture, governance, and societal
implications of robo-advisory platforms. We examine not just how they work, but
how they are adopted, regulated, and evaluated across different stakeholder groups.
Ultimately, robo-advisory is not merely a financial tool; it is a test case for how
artificial intelligence, behavioural design, and digital infrastructure can be combined
to reshape one of the most human of endeavours: making decisions about money,
risk, and the future.
6 Overview of the Chapters
This book is organised into five interconnected parts that collectively examine how
robo-advisory technologies are transforming the finance industry. It begins with the
foundations of this transformation and then explores the behavioural and ethical

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 21
dimensions of investor interaction, the regulatory and risk frameworks that underpin
system integrity, the technological innovations driving new applications, and finally,
the sustainability and future trajectory of AI-driven financial services.
Part I: Foundations and Market Evolution
The opening part establishes the conceptual and market foundations of robo-
advisory. It charts the field’s evolution within the broader FinTech movement and
introduces the drivers that shaped its emergence. This chapter introduces the rise of
robo-advisory, situating it within the broader context of the digital transformation
of financial services. It examines how artificial intelligence, behavioural design,
and data analytics have converged to democratise access to financial advice. The
chapter concludes with a framework of six AI-driven business models that reveal
the strategic diversity of robo-advisory across traditional and disruptive financial
firms. Chapter “Current Trends for Robo-Advisors” continues by mapping current
trends and developments in digital wealth management. It highlights the industry’s
shift from fully automated to hybrid advisory models that blend algorithmic
precision with human insight. The discussion underscores how global adoption,
client sophistication, and regulatory adaptation are collectively maturing the sector
into a resilient and customer-centric ecosystem.
Part II: Behavioural and Ethical Dimensions
The second part turns to the human and ethical aspects of robo-advisory. It examines
how cognitive biases shape investment decisions, how artificial intelligence can
personalise advice, and how trust and transparency determine user adoption.
Chapter “Behavioral Biases in Investment Decisions” analyses behavioural biases
such as overconfidence, herding, and loss aversion that distort investor judgment and
market efficiency. Drawing on insights from behavioural finance and neuroscience,
it links these biases to financial instability and discusses AI-based techniques that
can correct or reduce them responsibly. Chapter “AI in Personalized Financial
Decision-Making” explores the growing role of artificial intelligence in tailoring
financial advice to individual preferences and behavioural tendencies. By applying
machine learning and reinforcement learning, robo-advisors can anticipate investor
responses and adjust recommendations dynamically. The chapter also warns of
ethical concerns around consent, fairness, and privacy, urging a balance between
innovation and investor protection. Chapter “Building Trust in Financial Robo-
Advisory and Overcoming Ethical Challenges”addresses the central challenge of
building trust in financial automation. It outlines five key dimensions—human
oversight, transparency, accuracy, usability, and human-like interaction—and pro-
poses specific strategies to strengthen confidence and ethical reliability in AI-
based financial systems. Chapter “A Theory of Investment Simplification and an
Experiment with AI Large Language Models” moves the discussion towards the
complexity of digital finance itself. Through an experimental comparison of human
advisors and large language models, it demonstrates that advanced AI systems can

22 A.Zarifisetal.
simplify decision-making and even outperform humans in navigating the diversity
of advisory platforms.
Part III: Regulation, Compliance, and Risk Management
Part III focuses on governance, risk, and accountability. It explores how AI
introduces new risk categories, how regulators are adapting, and how auditing and
cybersecurity frameworks evolve to maintain market integrity. Chapter “Identifying
and Ranking the Eight Risks of AI for Each of the Six Main AI Focused Fintech
Business Models” identifies eight key risks facing AI-focused FinTech business
models, ranging from data privacy to strategic misalignment, and ranks their
significance using a Delphi methodology. The analysis reveals that while established
models reduce some forms of risk, they remain vulnerable to technological and
ecosystem dependencies. Chapter “Regulatory and Compliance Issues in AI-
Driven Financial Services” examines the regulatory and compliance issues that
shape AI-enabled advisory services across major jurisdictions. It translates global
regulatory expectations such as those of the SEC, FCA, ESMA, and MAS into
actionable control frameworks, demonstrating how firms can integrate compliance
into product design, testing, and deployment. Chapter “Robo-Advisory and Audit-
ing: Internal and External Controls” explores how AI is reshaping both internal
and external auditing. It introduces a dual-layer model that combines real-time
technological oversight with ethical and governance assurance, positioning auditing
as a continuous, predictive, and trust-building function in AI finance. Chapter
“Cybersecurity risk and Robo-advisory” delves into the cybersecurity challenges
of digital advisory systems. It explains how adversarial machine learning, data
leaks, and model manipulation create new vulnerabilities and proposes a defensive
architecture built on explainable AI, encryption, and zero-trust principles. Chapter
“Progress in Contemporary Fraud Detection through the Fintech Application of
Artificial Intelligence” extends the discussion to fraud detection and prevention. It
highlights AI’s potential to enhance financial transparency and reduce misconduct
while stressing that lasting progress depends on ethical accountability, regulatory
vigilance, and responsible innovation.
Part IV: Technological Innovations and Financial Integration
This part investigates the technological frontier of robo-advisory from data-driven
forecasting and market microstructure to the transformative promise of quantum
computing. Chapter “Enhanced Cryptocurrency Volatility Forecasting via Local
Linear Forests” evaluates Local Linear Forests as a machine-learning approach for
forecasting cryptocurrency volatility. The findings demonstrate that these models
outperform traditional econometric frameworks, particularly in unstable market
phases, offering practical insights for investors and regulators. Chapter “Fee Struc-
ture and Order Flow Informativeness in the Cryptocurrency Market” studies how
trading fees influence the efficiency of digital markets. Using Binance’s policy
shift from zero to commission-based trading as a natural experiment, it shows that
modest transaction costs enhance the informativeness of order flow and improve
price discovery. Chapter “Quantum Computing and the Next Generation of Robo-

TheRiseofRobo-AdvisoryinFinTech 23
Advisory” explores quantum computing as a transformative force in financial
modelling. It explains how quantum algorithms can advance portfolio optimisation,
risk simulation, and data encryption while also acknowledging the current technical
and adoption challenges that accompany this emerging paradigm.
Part V: Sustainability, Market Impact, and Future Directions
The final part looks towards the broader implications of robo-advisory for sus-
tainable finance and market evolution. It considers how AI-enabled platforms
contribute to ESG integration, investor alignment, and the long-term viability of
the digital wealth sector. Chapter “Sustainable Investing and the Role of AI-Driven
Robo-Advisors” discusses the intersection of sustainability and technology in asset
management. It highlights how AI-driven robo-advisors enhance ESG investing
by improving data consistency, transparency, and adaptability while helping mit-
igate greenwashing and aligning with evolving sustainability standards. Chapter
“Robo-Advisory Under Review: The Market’s Verdict” concludes the volume by
examining how markets have responded to the emergence of robo-advisory services.
By contrasting the withdrawal of several incumbent institutions with the success of
specialised digital platforms and the rise of robo-advisory in emerging economies,
it identifies the strategic and regulatory conditions under which digital advice will
thrive.

Current Trends fo r Robo-Advisors
Fabio Silva Di as
Abstract FinTech innovation and changing customer demands for more affordable,
always-available, and user-friendly services are driving a significant global trans-
formation in the wealth management sector. Robo-advisors, which are automated
investment platforms that use quantitative algorithms to manage portfolios, first
appeared in the USA but have since quickly expanded throughout Europe and
Asia. These platforms have solidified their position in digital wealth management
by going beyond basic advice to provide full portfolio management, which now
includes trade execution, monitoring, and automated rebalancing. In order to
manage the growing complexity of clients and finances globally, the market is
clearly maturing from fully automated services to more intricate hybrid models that
combine technology and human expertise. This chapter explains the fundamental
shift from purely automated services, which dominated the initial phase of the
industry’s development, towards more complex models that offer a careful balance
of technology and human expertise.

1 Introduction and Ove rview
The emergence of robo-advisors can be attributed to their fundamental role in
democratising investment through automated services. These online platforms,
which were first envisioned as inexpensive substitutes for conventional human
advisors, automatically create and manage client portfolios using algorithms. In the
years after the global financial crisis of 2007–2008, this democratisation process
was accelerated because of stricter regulations on established banks and the rapid
adva ncements in computer science, which strongly encouraged technology-based
financial firms to create non-bank solutions. Mass market investors can now open
accounts,getfinancialadvice,andautomatetheirinvestmentdecisionsmoreeasily
and affordably thanks to robo-advisors, which drastically reduce the financial
barrierstoentry.
The earliest and simplest iteration of these platforms was the pure robo-advisor
model, characterised by a fully automated investment advisory process driven
by algorithms with no direct human interaction for the user. This pure approach
prioritised cost reduction and scalability, enabling providers to service a large
number of retail investors with limited capital amounts. However, as the industry
matured and competition intensified, providers began to recognise the inherent
limitations of a model devoid of human touch, especially for handling complex
or emotionally charged financial decisions. The industry began a discernible shift
towardsmodelsthatofferedabalanceoftechnologyandhumanexpertise,seeking
tomaintainefficiencywhileovercomingthechallengesofcompleteautomation.
This market evolution has resulted in the increasing prevalence of the hybrid
robo-advisor model, which deliberately combines automated methods with addi-
tional human oversight in varying degrees. The hybrid structure allows for addi-
tional human interaction in the financial advisoryprocess,acomponentthatmany
investors, including wealthier and older clients, actively desire. A study of the US
market by Metzler et al. (2022) clearly illustrates this split, showing that many
of the largest players have adopted a hybrid approach to service their extensive
client bases. This development highlights that the evolution of robo-advising is not
a mov etowardsacompletereplacementofhumanprofessionals,butrathertowards
apartnershipwheretechnologyaugmentsandenhancestheadvisor’srole.
Table 1, derived from an analysis of major US-based providers, demonstrates
the early success and client acquisition of both pure and hybrid models, though
hybrid systems often dominate the top tier of assets under management due to
their appeal to high-net-worth individuals. The data shows that the largest firms

This evolving business model directly influences how firms structure their value

1.1 Defining the Hy bridModel
The hybrid model represents a strategic and practical combination of automated
algorithms with human financial advisors, aiming to capture the best attributes of
both service delivery methods. The core premise is that algorithms are deployed for
their inherent efficiency and scalability, excelling at quantitative tasks that require
speed and consistency. These automated systems perform key activities su ch as
continuous portfolio monitoring, trade execution, and the systematic rebalancing
ofassetstomaintaintargetedrisklevels.Thismachine-basedapproachdramatically
lowersoperationalcostsandensuresthatstandardinvestmentprocessesareexecuted
withouthumanbiasorerror.
Conversely, the model purposefully integrates human financial advisors to
provide a personalised touch and nuanced understanding, qualities that are fun-
damentally challenging for current technology to replicate. The human component
is typically reserved for complex, non-standard situations, such as comprehensive
financialplanning,debtmanagement,taxstrategy,and,mostimportantly,providing

28 F.S.Dias
emotional guidance during periods of market volatility. This additional human
advice gives advisors the authorisation to discuss personal preferences and even
override the algorithm’s portfolio allocation, injecting a necessary element of
flexibilityandtailoredjudgement.Jungetal.(2018) underscore the reality that most
investors still feel a need for an additionalhumanadvisor,reinforcingtheviability
ofthisblendedapproach.
This structural composition is designed to address a critical tension in the market:
the investor desire for both cost-effectiveness and human expertise. Pure robo-
advisors meet the cost-effectiveness need but often fall short when clients face
complex life events or require empathetic counsel, prompting them to seek external
validation or control. By offering various service tiers, often including premium
subscriptions with permanent access to an advisory network via phone or chat,
hybrid firms capture segments of the market that demand higher-touch service
withoutpayingthefullpriceoftraditionalprivatewealthmanagement.Furthermore,
the customisation capabilities inherent in this model, explored in research such as
FaloonandScherer(2017), are greatly enhanced, moving beyond simple risk profile
questionnaires to offer highly individualised portfolios developed through human
consultations.
From an academic perspective, this hybridisation trend reflects a maturation of
digital business models within the financialdomain.Theframeworkintroducedby
OsterwalderandPigneur(2010), the Business Model Canvas, provides a structured
lens through which Metzler et al. (2022) analyse the differing characteristics of
pure versus hybrid RAs. Their analysis demonstrates that hybrid RAs strategically
differentiate themselves through superior value propositions like ‘additional human
portfolio advice’ and specific ‘human advisory networks’. This requires them to
manage a different infrastructure, including slightly higher staff payment costs
comparedtothe‘verylowstaffpayment’characteristicoftheirpurecounterparts.
The differences extend directly into the customer interface, where hybrid RAs
target customer segments that often require a ‘mostly high capital minimum’ and
maintain ‘additional personal communication’ channels beyond purely automated
ones.Ultimately,thehybridmodel,ashighlightedbyRühretal.(2019), addresses
the psychological trade-offs in automation by ensuring users feel they have a level
of control and personal recourse, which is vital for building trust in the management
of long-term wealth. The hybrid model thus serve s as a contemporary benchmark
for digital investment management, offering a comprehensive and psychologically
reassuringservicethattechnologyalonecannotyetdeliver.
2 The Rise and Mechanics of Hybrid Robo-AdvisoryModels
The evolution of digital wealth management has been marked by a critical strategic
pivot: the shift from the purely algorithmic efficiency of the original robo-advisors
to the balanced, client-centric design of the hybrid model. This model, which
combinesautomatedtechnologywithhumanfinancialexpertise,israpidlybecom-

CurrentTrendsforRobo-Advisors 29
ing the industry standard, particularly for firms targeting the mass affluent and
high-net-worth segments. The mechanics of the hybrid approach are built upon a
complementary division of labour, where machines handle the routine, quantitative
tasks, and human advisors focus on the complex, qualitative aspects of financial
well-being. This symbiotic relationship not only enhances efficiency but also
addresses the fundamental psychological needs of investors who often require the
reassuranceofahumanexpertduringturbulenttimesormajorlifetransitions.
2.1 Components of a H ybridRobo-AdvisorModel
The hybrid model in wealth management takes advantage of the best parts of
both automated and human advisors. The automated system can do things like
portfolio monitoring, rebalancing, and tax-loss harvesting that are quantitative and
can be done repeatedly. This lowers the cost of providing services and makes
it possible to reach the mass affluent market. On the other hand, the expensive
human advisor focusses on qualitative, relationship-dependent tasks like complex
financial planning, behavioural coaching, and custom problem-solving. These tasks
build trust, give clients peace of mind, and provide emotional support that keeps
clients through market fluctuations. This strategic integration helps businesses get
around the problems with standalone models and build a complete, affordable,
and strong service architecture that meets the needs of all types of wealth,
providing clients with both affordable institutional-grade investment management
andpersonaladvicethatishigh-touch.
The automated component forms the technological backbone of the hybrid
robo-advisor, primarily leveraging Artificial Intelligence (AI) and machine learn-
ing (ML) capabilities. These technologies are tasked with executing routine, high-
volume tasks with speed, precision, and consistency that human advisors cannot
match. Key functions include continuous portfolio rebalancing, where algorithms
monitor deviations from the client’s target asset allocation and automatically
execute trades to restore balance, often using sophisticated techniques like dynamic
rebalancing thresholds. The system is also responsibleforextensivedataanalysis,
processing vast amounts of market information, economic indicators, and client
transactiondatatogeneratepredictiveinsightsandsuggestpotentialoptimisations.
This data-driven approach underpins all investment decisions, ensuring portfolios
are managed according to quantitative models such as Modern Portfolio Theory
(Markowitz1952), thereby eliminating emotional bias from the investment process.
Furthermore, the automated engine handles critical administrative functions, such as
tax-loss harvesting in taxable accounts, seamlessly identifying opportunities to sell
assets atalosstooffsetcapitalgains,whichisakeyvaluepropositionforclients.
In contrast, the human advisor role is strategically repositioned to focus
exclusively on activities that require emotional intelligence, nuanced understanding,
and bespoke solutions. Rather than spending time ontradeexecutionorrebalancing,
the human expert concentrates on relationship building, establishing the trust

30 F.S.Dias
necessary to retain clients through market cycles. A primary focus is complex
financial planning, covering areas far beyond simple investment returns, such
as estate planning, where an advisor helps structure wills and trusts; significant
life events, such as inheritance, divorce, or business sale; and long-term goal
setting for intergenerational wealth transfer. Crucially, the advisor p rovidesessential
emotionalsupportandguidance,actingasabehaviouralcoachtodissuadeclients
frommakingimpulsivedecisionsdrivenbyfearorgreedduringperiodsofmarket
volatility. This human touch addresses the finding by Rühr et al. (2019) that
many investors value a level of control and personal recourse, which the human
advisor effectively provides by interpreting the algorithm’s recommendations and
communicatingtheminapersonallyrelevantcontext.Metzleretal.(2022) confirm
that this advisory network, often composed of Certified Financial Planners (CFPs),
is a key value driver andcostcentredifferentiatinghybridmodelsfromtheirpurely
digitalcompetitors.
The distinction between the roles can be summarised as a strategic separation
of the mechanical and the conceptual. The automated system is the efficient
engine of execution and monitoring, while the human advisor is the perceptive
strategic planner and empathetic communicator. This is evident in the fact that while
the algorithms manage the daily performance of the portfolio, the human advisor
takes the lead in discussing non-standard products, complex debt strategies, and
the integration of external accounts to form a truly holistic financial picture. The
humanadvisor’sabilitytoengagewithclientpsychologyandlong-termmotivations
ensures the financial plan remains aligned with the individual’s evolving personal
andfinancialcircumstances.Thesuccessfulimplementationofthisdualityiswhat
definesthenextgenerationofdigitalwealthmanagement.
2.2 Integration of InsuranceProducts
A critical element of the hybrid model’s advanced value proposition is the seamless
integration of insurance products into the comprehensive financial planning
service. Traditionally, investment management and insurance planning have been
siloed, handled by separate professionals or institutions, which often results in frag-
mented and incomplete client financial health. The hybrid robo-advisor is uniquely
positioned to bridge this gap, shifting the focus from a narrow concentration on
inve stmentgrowthtothebroadernecessityofaholisticfinancialplanthatincludes
a thorough insurance needs review. This integration acknowledges that securing a
client’scurrentassetsandfutureincomeagainstunexpectedrisksisjustasvitalas
growingtheircapital.
The hybrid advantage in this area is powered by the synergistic relationship
between the machine and the human advisor. The automated system identifies
potential insurance gaps by analysing client data ingested during the onboard-
ing process, which includes income stability, marital status, dependent children,
mortgage debt, and existing policies. Using algorithms, the platform can quickly

2.3 Catering to Individual Inv estorNeeds
The flexible service delivery inherent in hybrid models allows them to effectively
segment and cater to the diverse needs of the modern investor base, offering a
broad spectrum of engagement based on comfort, complexity, and budget.This
adaptability is a key commercial advantage, enabling firms to service a wider range
of clients than either traditional advisors (who often require high minimum assets) or
purerobo-advisors(whomaystruggletoretainclientsastheirwealthandfinancial
complexity grow). The ability to scale the human touch up or down, based on
a client’s stage of life and financial magnitude, is the central mechanism of this
customisation.
For digitally native investors, who are typically younger and highly comfortable
with technology, the service leans heavily on the automated features for day-to-
day management. These clients rely on the platform for portfolio monitoring and

32 F.S.Dias
automated rebalancing, appreciating the convenience and low cost. They reserve
human advice for major milestones, such as structuring investments for a new
home purchase, planning complex educational savings, or consolidating various
retirement accounts. The human advisor acts as an occasional consultant for
validation and specialised guidance, a service that is often bu ndled into a low-
cost subscription or offered for a nominal fee. This approach provides the digital
generation with the professional assurance they need without compromising the
seamlessonlineexperiencetheyprefer.
Conversely, higher-net-worth individuals receive a significantly different ser-
vice, with regular consultations with a human advisor becoming the norm, if
not the expectation. For these clients, the digital platform functions primarily as
a sophisticated analytical and execution tool; it provides detailed performance
reporting, advanced scenario planning, and real-time access to their holdings, which
can be critical for large, multi-faceted portfolios. The advisor uses the platform’s
analytical outputtoinformface-to-faceorvideo-conferencediscussionsonintricate
topics like philanthropic giving, complex options trading, or trust administration.
The advisor–client relationship here is central, allowing the firm to capture the
higher advisory fees associated with customised, high-touch wealth management.
Thistieredapproach,asdiscussedbyJungetal.(2018), allows the firm to generate
significant and differentiated value fromdifferentcustomersegments.

reintroducing the human element. It combines the individualised knowledge of

Due to this integration, businesses ar eabletoprovideatieredapproachthatappeals
