AI in Personalized Financial
Decision-Making
Narmin Nahidi
Abstract This chapter explores the transformative role of artificial intelligence
(AI) in personalized financial decision-making, highlighting how robo-advisors
utilize advanced machine learning to detect and respond dynamically to investor
behavioral biases such as loss aversion, overconfidence, anchoring, and recency
effects. By employing predictive analytics and reinforcement learning models,
robo-advisory platforms can anticipate investor behavior and proactively tailor
interventions, significantly improving both financial outcomes and user satisfac-
tion. Real-world case studies from wealth management and retirement planning
illustrate the successful deployment of hyper-personalized strategies, demonstrating
AI’s capacity for nuanced portfolio adjustments and behavioral nudges. Despite
promising advancements, the chapter addresses critical ethical challenges, including
transparency, informed consent, data privac y, and the risks of reinforcing demo-
graphic biases or manipulative practices. The chapter concludes by advocating
continuous refinement of AI strategies to balance technological sophistication
withethicalresponsibility,ensuringpersonalizedfinancegenuinelyservesinvestor
welfareandmarketintegrity.

Behavioralnudges · Predictiveanalytics · EthicalAI · Dataprivacy · Investor
welfare

1 Introd uction
Artificial Intelligence (AI) has profoundly reshaped the landscape of personal
finance, shifting the emphasis from generic financial advice to finely tuned, user-
specific strategies. As the democratization of investment services accelerates,
robo-advisors AI-powered digital platforms have emerged as pivotal agents of this
transformation. Initially designed to provide low-cost, algorithm-driven portfolio
management, these platforms have evolved into sophisticated systems capable
of complex behavioral modeling. No longer limited to static portfolio recom-
mendations, today’s robo-advisors actively learn from individual user behavior,
integratingbehavioralfinanceprinciplesintotheiralgorithmstoofferincreasingly
personalizedexperiences(Jungetal.2018). This evolution reflects a broader trend in
financial services: leveraging AI to address the cognitive and emotional biases that
traditionally impair financial decision-making. Importantly, this technological shift
is not simply about automation; it is about fundamentally redesigning the advisory
process to align better with how individuals think,feel,andactwhenmanagingtheir
finances.Consequently,AI’sroleinpersonalfinanceisnotmerelyoperationalbut
alsodeeplycognitive,aimingtoimprovebothoutcomesandexperiences.
Central to this shift is the ability of AI systems to detect and respond to behavioral
anomalies that manifest in financial decision-making. Cognitive biases such as loss
aversion, overconfidence, anchoring, and recency ef fects often lead investors to
make suboptimal choices, particularly under conditions of uncertainty or market
volatility (Baker and Ricciardi 2010). Traditional advisory models struggled to
consistently identify these biases, relying heavily on self-reported data and periodic
advisor–client interactions. In contrast, advanced machine learning models now
enable robo-advisors to monitor user behaviors in real time, using digital footprints
such as changes in asset allocation preferences, trading frequency, or reactions
to market news to infer the presence of biases. Sophisticated behavioral profiling
techniques allow these systems to build dynamic models of each inves tor’s psy-
chologicaltendencies,updatingcontinuouslywithnewdatainputs.Recentstudies
suggestthatAI-drivendetectionmechanismsnotonlyimproveindividualfinancial
outcomes by mitigating bias-driven errors but also increase client satisfaction and
retentionbyprovidingasenseofbeinggenuinelyunderstood(Jungetal.2018).
Beyond the detection of biases, AI’s capacity for targeted behavioral intervention
has opened new frontiers in personalized finance. Robo-advisors are now increas-
ingly designed to adapt their communication strategies, portfolio recommendations,
and even timing of advice delivery based on inferred user biases. For example,
investors displaying loss aversion might receive notifications framed to highlight
potential long-term gains rather than short-term losses. Similarly, clients prone to
overtrading due to overconfidence could be gently nudged toward more passive
investmentstrategies.Theseadaptiveresponsesarerootedinbehavioraleconomics
theories but are significantly amplified by AI’s ability to scale these interventions
across millions of users simultaneously (D’Acunto et al. 2019). Unlike traditional
human advisors who must manually adjust their strategies for each client, AI

AIinPersonalizedFinancialDecision-Making 77
systems automate this personalization at unprecedented levels of precision and
responsiveness. Importantly, these nudges are often subtle, designed to preserve
user autonomy wh ile encouraging more rational decision-making, a balance that
continuestobeasubjectofethicaldebatewithinthefield.
At the heart of these developments lies the application of machine learning
models specifically designed for behavioral finance. Predictive analytics models,
for instance, analyze historical behavioral data to forecast the likelihood of specific
future actions, such as panic selling during a downturn. Natural language processing
(NLP) algorithms assess sentiment in client communicationsorsocialmediaactivity
togaugeemotionalstatesthatmayinfluencefinancialchoices.Reinforcementlearn-
ingmodels,inparticular,standoutfortheirabilitytooptimizeadvisorystrategiesby
learningfromrepeatedinteractionsandfeedbackloops(Sironi2016). Unlike static
predictive models, reinforcement learning allows robo-advisors to dynamically
adjust their approaches in real time, rewarding strategies that yield better client
outcomes while penalizing those that do not. The fusion of these technologies
signals a major paradigm shift in the advisory model, moving beyond retrospective
performance analysis toward anticipatory guidance. As a result, machine learning
notonlyhelpspredictindividualbehaviorbutalsoenablesproactiveshapingofthat
behaviortowardimprovedfinancialwellness.
Real-world implementations provide compelling evidence of the efficacy of
AI-driven personalized financial strategies. Leading robo-advisory firms such as
Betterment and Wealthfront now offer hyper-personalized portfolio management
services,adjustingassetallocationsdynamicallyinresponsetobothmacroeconomic
shifts and subtle user behavior changes (Belanche et al. 2020). These platforms
integrate user-specific data, such as cash flow patterns, employment status, and
spending habits, into their investment algorithms, creating a holistic picture of each
client’s financial life. Similarly, in the domain of retirement planning, AI-based
tools are increasingly being used to customize saving trajectories based on personal
longevity risk, expected healthcare costs, and even individual lifestyle preferences.
Importantly, these innovations are not restricted to high-net-worth indiv iduals;they
are increasingly being made accessible to a broader retail clientele, democratizing
accesstosophisticatedfinancialplanning.Suchdevelopmentshighlightthatperson-
alization,onceapremiumserviceavailableonlythroughprivatewealthmanagers,
isbecominganexpectedstandardfeatureindigitalfinancialservices.
Despite these promising advances, significant challenges remain in the deploy-
ment of AI in personalized financial decision-making. Algorithmic transparency
remains a pressing concern: clients often lack clear insight into how and why
specificrecommendationsaremade,raisingissuesoftrustandaccountability(Jag-
tiani and Lemieux 2019). Furthermore, the ethical use of behavioral data is under
increasing scrutiny, particularly regarding the fine line between helpful nudging and
manipulative steering. Differential performance across demographic groups also
poses challenges, as machine learning models trained on biased or incomplete data
may inadvertently reinforce existing inequalities in financial outcomes. Cultural
factors further complicate personalization efforts: strategies that work effectively
in one country or demographic group may fail or even backfire in another. As

78 N.Nahidi
such, there is a growing recognition that effective personalization must go beyond
technical sophistication to incorporate considerations of fairness, inclusivity, and
contextual sensitivity. This chapter addresses these complex issues by systematically
exploring how robo-advisors detect and respond to user biases, th e development
andapplicationofmachinelearningmodelsforbehavioralfinance,andreal-world
casestudiesillustratingboththepromisesandlimitationsofAI-drivenpersonalized
financialstrategies.
2 How Robo-Advisors Detect and R espondtoUserBiases
2.1 Detection of Behavioral Biases ThroughAI
The detection of behavioral biases in financial decision-making marks a critical
advancement in robo-advisory services. Traditionally, financial advisors relied on
questionnaires, interviews, and periodic reviews to infer client behavior. However,
these approaches were often limited by self-reporting biases, infrequent interactions,
and subjective interpretations. Robo-advisors, powered by artificial intelligence (AI)
and machine learning, now analyze va standdiversedatasets,includinguseractivity
logs, transaction histories, device usage patterns, and even cursor movement on
websites to infer user behavior in ways not possible before (Jung et al. 2018).
This allows them to detect subtle manifestations of biases such as overconfidence,
anchoring, or loss aversion without direct self-disclosure by users. Early detection,
often unnoticed by clients th emselves,becomescriticalbecauseevenminorbiases
cancompoundovertimetosignificantlyharmlong-termfinancialoutcomes.
Modern AI systems use supervised and unsupervised learning techniques to
uncover patterns that indicate the presence of biases. Deep learning techniques, par-
ticularly recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM)
models, have enhanced the detection of temporal patterns in investor behavior
(Baker and Ricciardi 2010). These models capture dependencies across time
allowing the system to recognize that an investor’s trading behavior after a series
of market losses may be driven more by emotions than by rational strategy. In
addition, clustering algorithms enable robo-advisors to create investor archetypes,
such as “risk-averse optimizers” or “momentum-driven traders,” without pre-
labeling users, offering a more nuanced understanding of how behavioral biases
manifestacrossdifferentsegments.Thistransitionfromstaticclientsegmentationto
dynamicbehavioralprofilingsignificantlyimprovesthesystem’sabilitytopreempt
problematicdecisionpatternsbeforetheyescalate.
Recent studies also highlight that real-time behavioral monitoring offers major
advantages over periodic behavioral assessments. Real-time detection enables
systems to track emotional volatility, sudden deviations from established investment
preferences, or impulsive reactions to news events, allowing for immediate and
context-specific interventions (Belanche et al. 2020). Techniques such as senti-

AIinPersonalizedFinancialDecision-Making 79
ment analysis through Natural Language Processing (NLP) have enabled some
robo-advisors to gauge user emotions from support chat interactions or feedback
responses, further enriching the behavioral data pool. Importantly, such approaches
reduce reliance on self-reported risk tolerance questionnaires, which have long been
criticized for their lack of predictivevalidity.Behavioraldata,continuouslyupdated
and passively collected, provides a more authentic and adaptive measure of the
investor’strueriskattitudesandemotionalresilience.
However, while AI-based bias detection offers significant promise, it also
presents technical and ethical challenges that merit careful consideration. Detection
models are only as good as the data and assumptions they are built on. If training
data lacks demographic diversity, the model’s predictions may systematically
misinterpret or overlook important cultural or socioeconomic variations in financial
behavior. Furthermore, the risk of “labeling” clients prematurely based on early
behavior patterns can create self-fulfilling prophecies, whereby users are nudged
into behavioral categories they might have otherwise grown out of. Addressing
theselimitationsrequirescarefulmodelvalidation,periodicretrainingwithupdated
datasets,andacommitmenttomaintainingaflexibleratherthandeterministicview
of client behavior (Jagtiani and Lemieux 2019). Thus, while detection is a critical
first step, its efficacy dependsonbothtechnicalrigorandethicalsafeguards(Fig.1).
In the framework for behavioral bias detection by robo-advisors, the financial
journey begins with the continuous acquisition of client behavioral data. This
data, encompassing transaction histories, trade frequencies, emotional reactions
inferred through digital interactions, and evolving risk appetite, is more granular
and dynamic than what traditional risk-profiling questionnaires could ever capture
(Baker and Ricciardi 2010). AI-driven systems process this vast and noisy data
landscape using a combination of advanced machine learning methods: recurrent
neural networks (RNNs) to identify temporal behavioral patterns, clustering algo-
rithms (such as k-means and hierarchical clustering) to categorize investors based
onsharedbehavioraltraits,andsentimentanalysisvianaturallanguageprocessing
(NLP) to detect emotional volatility from user interactions (Jagtiani and Lemieux
2019; Jung et al. 2018). These techniques allow the system to construct dynamic
investor profiles that continuously update in r esponse to real-time actions rather
thanrelyingonstatic,outdatedassumptions.
Once user behaviors are modeled, the system identifies specific behavioral biases
such as loss aversion, overconfidence, anchoring effects, and recency bias, all of
whichhavebeenempiricallyshowntodistortfinancialdecision-making(D’Acunto
et al. 2019). By mapping behavioral triggers and recognizing bias-prone patterns,
robo-advisors can develop tailored intervention strategies. Adaptive interventions
include subtle nudges framed to counteract specific biases, such as emphasizing
long-term gains to mitigate short-term loss aversion or designing “cooling-off”
mechanisms to temper overconfident trading behaviors. These interventions are
groundedinbehavioraleconomicsandchoicearchitecturetheoriesbutaredynam-
ically applied at scale through AI personalization engines (Belanche et al. 2024).
Importantly, the system does not merely provide one-off advice but continuously

The ethical dimension of such AI-driven behavioral correction systems deserves
careful attention. As Martin (2019) discusses, algorithmic decision systems in
finance raise critical issues around transparency, informed consent, and the potential
for manipulation. While personalized nudging can empower investors to make better
decisions, it also introduces the risk that poorly designed or opaque systems might
steer clients in ways that benefit the platform ra ther than the user. Therefore, the
frameworkimplicitlyrequiresrobustgovernancestructures,ongoingfairnessaudits,
and clear user disclosures to ensure that bias correction remains aligned with the
client’sbestinterests.
The conceptualization outlined here not only synthesizes behavioral finance
insights with modern AI capabilities but also opens new avenues for future
development. Particularly, reinforcement learning models could be layered on top
of bias detection to dynamically adjust nudging strategies based on real-world
outcomes(Sironi2016). Similarly, more sophisticated emotional modeling, drawing
on advances in affective computing, could enhance the system’s ability to detect
early signs of behavioral instability before they translate into harmful financial
actions. Such innovations could further improve the long-termfinancialwell-being
ofinvestorsbyevolvingbeyondreactiveinterventionstowardpredictivebehavioral
supportecosystems.
2.2 Adaptive Responses and Nudges byRobo-Advisors
After detecting behavioral biases, robo-advisors deploy a range of adaptive
responses designed to improve client decision-making without restricting their
autonomy. Drawing on choice architecture and behavioral economics, these
platforms im plement “nudges” subtle modifications in how choices are presented
to influence behavior without altering the actual options available (D’Acunto et
al. 2019). For instance, investors prone to panic selling during downturns may
receive encouraging notifications that reframe volatility as a normal, temporary
phenomenon, helping to reduce anxiety-driven reactions. Similarly, investors
exhibiting confirmation bias—favoring information that supports their existing
beliefs—may be ex posedtobalancedmarketanalysisreportsthatgentlyintroduce
alternative viewpoints. These interventions aim to recalibrate decision frames at
criticaljunctureswithoutappearingintrusiveorpaternalistic.
Personalization of nudges is a critical differentiator enabled by AI. Rather than
applying uniform nudging techniques across all clients, advanced robo-advisors tai-
lor interventions based on auser’sdetectedbehavioralprofile,historicalresponses
to past interventions, and evolving financial goals (Jung et al. 2018). Natural
Language Processing (NLP) techniques fine-tune the language, emotional tone, and
timing of messages to fit individual preferences, making advisory interactions feel
more organic and less scripted. For instance, users identified as highly loss-averse

82 N.Nahidi
may receive reassurance-focused updates after market dips, while overconfident
investors may be nudged toward educational modules emphasizing the value of
diversification. Reinforcement learning models continuously optimize these nudges,
testingvariationsandlearningfromwhichonesresultinimproveduserengagement
andbetterfinancialdecisionsovertime.
Several practical examples illustrate the effectiveness of AI-driven adaptive
responses in financial advisory contexts. Platforms like Betterment, Wealthfront,
and Nutmeg use algorithmic nudging techniques to automate tax-loss harvesting
reminders, encourage automatic rebalancing, and reinforce goal-based investing
behaviors. When users attempt to deviate from pre-set investment plans during
periods of high market volatility, gentle reminders emphasizing long-term invest-
ment horizons are automatically triggered (Belanche et al. 2020, 2024). Other
platforms have begun experimenting with gamification strategies, awarding virtual
badges or progress milestones when users adhere to disciplined saving or investment
behaviors. These subtle reinforcement mechanisms s erve to internalize positive
habits, transforming initially externally prompted actions into intrinsic behavioral
patternsovertime.
While the potential of AI-driven nudges is considerable, their design and deploy-
ment raise complex ethical issues. In particular, the line between helpful nudging
and manipulation can become blurry when systems are optimized purely for
engagementorprofitabilityratherthanclientwelfare(JagtianiandLemieux2019).
Transparency becomes essential: users must be informed when their behaviors are
being influenced by design choices, and they should retain meaningful opt-out
options if desired. Additionally, the risk of reinforcing harmful stereotypes, such
as assuming lower risk tolerance based solely on age or gender, without continuous
validation, must be actively managed through fairmodelpracticesandongoingbias
audits.Therefore,whileadaptiveresponsesrepresentapowerfultoolforimproving
financial behaviors, their success depends as much on ethical system design and
responsiblegovernanceasontechnicalsophistication.
3 Machine Learning Models fo rBehavioralFinance
3.1 Predictive Modeling of In vestorBehavior
The application of machine learning (ML) to predict investor behavior represents
a pivotal development in behavioral finance. Traditional financial theories assumed
rational agents operating with perfect information, but decades ofempiricalresearch
have demonstrated the pervasive influence of cognitive and emotional biases on
decision-making (Baker and Ricciardi 2010). Predictive modeling techniques aim
to bridge this gap by analyzing patterns in historical and real-time data to forecast
future behavior more accurately. Supervised learning algorithms, such as logistic
regression,decisiontrees,andgradientboostingmachines,arecommonlyemployed

AIinPersonalizedFinancialDecision-Making 83
to predict outcomes like trade frequency, asset class preferences, risk tolerance
shifts, or likelihood of panic sellingduringmarketdownturns(JagtianiandLemieux
2019). These models incorporate diverse inputs, ranging from macroeconomic
indicators to granular user-level data, offering a multidimensional view ofinvestor
psychologythatstaticquestionnairescouldnevercapture(Fig.2).
The conceptual framework for predictive modeling of investor behavior captures
the intricate process by which personal and market-level data are systematically
transformed into behavioral insights and financial recommendations. At the foun-
dational level, the system collects granular personal data such as income patterns,
age, past trading behaviors, and portfolio diversification history alongside broader
market data including volatility indices, interest rate trends, and macroeconomic
news sentiment. Unlike traditional econometric mo delsthatassumestablerelation-
shipsbetweeneconomicvariables,predictivemodelinginmodernfinanceleverages
machine learning algorithms like Random Forests, XGBoost, and deep neural
networks to uncover complex, nonlinear patterns across vast multidimensional
datasets (Belanche et al. 2020; Gomber et al. 2018). These models can flexibly
accommodate non-stationary relationships and behavioral drift, providing a richer
and more dynamic understanding of how external shocks and internal predispo-
sitions interact to shape investor decision-making. By structuring inputs at both
the personal and market lev els, the framework emphasizes that investor behavior
cannotbepredictedaccuratelywithoutconsideringbothmicro-levelpsychological
tendenciesandmacro-levelfinancialenvironments.
The predictive modeling process culminates in the generation of anticipated
investor behaviors, such as tendencies toward panic selling during downturns,
herding behavior in bubbles, overtrading driven by overconfidence, or inertia
characterized by the reluctance to rebalance portfolios even when optimal. These
predicted behaviors, informed by complex interactions between user-specific and
market-specific factors, allow robo-advisors and digital financial platforms to ta ilor
interventions proactively. Rather than waiting for biases to manifest in destructive
investment decisions, the system uses predictive signals to preemptively adjust
portfolio recommendations, risk profiles, or communication strategies (D’Acunto
etal.2019). As discussed inSect.3.1 of the chapter, this shift from retrospective to
anticipatory advisory models marks a profound departure from traditional financial
advising, positioning predictive analytics as a behavioral shield rather than a mere
diagnostic tool. The hierarchical structure of the framework flow ing from data
inputs through predictive modeling to behavioral outputs and personalized advice
maps logically onto the chapter’s theoretical emphasis on machine learning as a
behavioralfinanceaccelerator.
A deeper reflection on this framework reveals important ethical and technical
challenges that warrant attention. Predictive modeling raises concerns about algo-
rithmic bias, especially if training datasets underrepresent certain demographic or
behavioralgroups,potentiallyleadingtomispredictionsorunfairtreatment(Martin
2019). Furthermore, the opacity of complex models like deep neural networks can
obscure the logic behind specific behav ioral forecasts, undermining client trust
unlessexplainabilitymechanismsareintegrated(JagtianiandLemieux2019).

One of the notable strengths of predictive modeling in finance is its ability
to uncover nonlinear relationships between variables that traditional econometric
models often miss. For example, neural networks can model complex interactions
between inv estor age, income volatility, past investment experiences, and current
market sentiment to predict susceptibility to herding behavior during bubbles
(Belanche et al. 2020). Moreover, ensemble methods like random forests and
XGBoost improve prediction accuracy by combining multiple weak learners, miti-
gating overfitting risks commonly encountered with individual models. Researchers
have demonstrated that these techniques significantly outperform classical risk-
profiling methods in predicting investment decisions under stress scenarios, par-
ticularly when behavioral variables such as sentiment scores and trading inertia
are included as features (D’Acunto et al. 2019). Thus, machine learning offers a
more realistic and nuanced lens foranticipatingbehavioraldeviationsfromrational
benchmarks.
However, the success of predictive models in behavioral finance hinges critically
on the qualityandrichnessoftheunderlyingdata(Gomberetal.2018). Behavioral
signals are often noisy, context-dependent, and influenced by latent factors that
are difficult to observe directly. To address these challenges, financial technology
firms increasingly integrate alternative data sources such as mobile device usage
patterns,socialmediasentiment,geolocationdata,andwearabledevicemetricsinto
their models (Jung et al. 2018). While the incorporation of such data improves
predictive accuracy, it also raises important questions about user privacy, data
governance, and regulatory compliance. In response, some firms have adopted
privacy-preserving machine learning techniques, such as federated learning, which
allow model training across decentralized devices without transmitting raw data.
These innovations represent an important step toward balancing personalization
benefitswithethicaldatastewardshipinbehavioralprediction.
Another critical limitation of predictive modeling lies in its temporal stabil-
ity. Investor behavior is not static; it evolves in response to changing personal
circumstances, learning effects, and shifting macroeconomic conditions (Schoar
and Sun 2024). Models trained on past behavior may quickly become obsolete if
they fail to account for behavioral drift. Addressing this requires continuous model
retraining, adaptive learning architectures, andtheincorporationofonlinelearning
algorithmsthatcanupdatepredictionsbasedonthelatestbehavioralinputs(Sironi
2016). Additionally, explainability remains a major concern. Black-box models,
while often more accurate, risk losing client trust if their decision logic cannot be
adequately communicated. Recent research emphasizes the importance of adopting
explainable AI (XAI) frameworks that provide interpretable outputs, allowing users
and advisors alike to understand the behavioral factors driving model predictions.
Thus, while predictive modeling holds immense promise, its success ultimately
dependsondynamicupdating,ethicaldatausage,andtransparentuserengagement.

86 N.Nahidi
3.2 Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic FinancialAdvice
Reinforcement learning (RL) introduces a powerful paradigm for enhancing robo-
advisory services by enabling systems to dynamically adapt their financial advice
based on user interactions and outcomes. Unlike traditional supervised learning,
which predicts a static outcome basedonlabeleddata,RLalgorithmslearnoptimal
strategies by exploring different actions and receiving feedback through reward
signals (D’Acunto et al. 2019). In the context of financial decision-making, these
rewards can be defined in terms of user satisfaction, portfolio performance, or
behavioral improvements such as reduced trading frequency or increased savings
rates. Over time, the system re finesitsadvisorystrategiestomaximizecumulative
rewards, offering personalized, context-sensitive financial guidance that evolves
alongsidetheclient.
One of the key strengths of reinforcement learning in personalized finance is its
capacity for continuous learning and adaptation. In environments characterized by
uncertainty and dynamic user preferences, static models quickly become outdated.
RL frameworks, particularly those based on Q-learning and deep reinforcement
learning(DRL),allowrobo-advisorstoupdatetheirpolicyfunctionsinrealtimeas
newinformationbecomesavailable(Belancheetal.2020). For instance, if a user’s
risk tolerance decreases following a personal life event such as job loss or family
expansion, the RL agent can detect deviations from expected behavior and adjust
portfolio recommendations accordingly. Importantly, this adaptability enables the
system to remain aligned with the user’s evolving financial goals and emotional
states,providingalevelofpersonalizationthatstaticadvisorymodelscannotmatch.
Recent applications of RL in finance illustrate its potential for revolutionizing
client engagement strategies. For example, some robo-advisors use multi-armed
bandit algorithms to dynamically select the most effective nudging interventions
basedonreal-timeuserresponses(Jungetal.2018). Others employ policy gradient
methods to optimize asset reallocation strategies that balance expected returns
with behavioral considerations such as loss aversion. Furthermore, hierarchical
reinforcement learning models have been proposed to structure complex financial
advice tasks into subgoals, improving learning efficiency and user interpretability.
These de velopmentssuggestthatreinforcementlearningisnotmerelyanacademic
curiositybutapracticaltoolcapableofsubstantiallyenhancingadvisoryeffective-
ness,particularlyinvolatileorhighlypersonalizedclientenvironments.
Nevertheless, deploying reinforcement learning systems in financial services
entails substantial challenges. One major concern is the definition of appropri-
ate reward functions. If rewards are too narrowly tied to s hort-term portfolio
performance, the system may inadvertently encourage excessive risk-taking or
short-termism, undermining broader financial wellness objectives (Jagtiani and
Lemieux 2019). Additionally, exploration strategies necessary for the RL agent to
discover better advisory actions carry inherent risks; poorly timed or inappropriate
interventions can erode client trust and satisfaction. There are also regulatory and
ethicalconsiderations:howmuchautonomyshouldbedelegatedtoanAIsystemin

AIinPersonalizedFinancialDecision-Making 87
managing user finances? How should conflicts between user preferences and long-
term welfare be resolved? Addressing these challenges requires a careful blend
of technical safeguards, human over sight, and transparent client communication,
ensuring that reinforcement learning is harnessed responsibly and effectively in
personalizedfinancialdecision-making(Martin2019).
4 Case Studies on AI-Driven PersonalizedFinancial

4.1 Robo-Advisory Personalization in We althManagement
The deployment of AI-powered personalization in wealth management has rad-
ically altered the traditional client–advisor relationship, turning what was once
an elite, high-cost service into a widely accessible financial planning solution
(Puschmann 2017). A particularly illustrative example is Betterment, one of the
first and most successful robo-advisory platforms, which applies machine learning
algorithms to tailor portfolios based on individual client profiles. Betterment collects
detailed client information through onboarding questionnaires that assess risk
tolerance, investment horizon, and financial goals. Howev er, what sets it apart is
theplatform’sabilitytointegratebehavioraldatapost-onboarding,suchasdeposit
habits,withdrawalfrequencies,andemotionalresponsestomarketfluctuations,into
its continuous recommendation engine (Belanche et al. 2020). This results in a
dynamic investment strategy that evolves alongside the client’s financial journey,
adjusting asset allocations proactively rather than reactively. For instance, if a user
begins saving more aggressively than initially projected, Betterment’s algorithms
will recommend more aggressive equity ex posure if risk tolerance allows, or
alternatively may suggest moving surplus funds into new financial goals like a
travel fund or early retirement account (Anagnostopoulos 2018). Similarly, if a
user hesitates to rebalance a portfolio despite significant drift from the target asset
allocation, behavioral markers of risk aversion are flagged, and the system subtly
adapts itscommunicationstrategyusingreassuringlanguageormilestoneframing
toencouragecorrectiveactionwithoutcreatingclientanxiety(Gomberetal.2017).
Betterment’s Tax Loss Harvesting+ product further customizes after-tax returns by
monitoring portfolios daily for tax-optimization opportunities, a service that would
have required bespoke wealth managers in the past. Importantly, the success of
such personalization is not only technical but psychological: client surveys reveal
that userswhoperceivetheirfinancialadvisor(humanordigital)asunderstanding
theiruniqueneedsaresignificantlymorelikelytoadheretoinvestmentplansduring
volatilemarkets(JagtianiandLemieux2019). Therefore, platforms like Betterment
illustrate how AI personalization is not confined to portfolio construction alone but
extends into continuous behavioral adaptation and emotional support mechanisms
thatwereoncethesolepreserveofhighlytrainedwealthmanagers.

Wealthfront offers another compelling case study in advanced personalization,
particularly through the integration of real-world financial data into comprehensive
wealth-building advice. Wealthfront’s Path tool leverages machine learning models
to create detailed, customized life-planning simulations by ingesting granular user
data from bank accounts, investment portfolios, mortgages, and even credit card
spending(D’Acuntoetal.2019). Unlike traditional financial plans that offer static
projections based on generalized assumptions, Path adjusts in real time as user
behavior evolves, off ering continuous feedback loops that refine the retirement,
housing, and family planning forecasts (Stolper and Walter 2017). For instance,
if a user begins spending more heavily on travel or luxury goods, Path recalculates
the probability of meeting retirement goals and suggests either increased savings
rates or adjusted retirement dates to maintain financial sustainability. Furthermore,
Wealthfronthasincorporatedsophisticateddirectindexingoptions,replacingbroad
ETFs with customized baskets of securities tailored to client preferences, tax
situations, and ESG considerations (Brandl and Hornuf 2020). By enabling tax-
loss harvesting on individual securities rather than at the fund level, clients can
significantly improve after-tax returns, achievi ng a form of hyper-personalized
portfoliomanagementonceaccessibleonlythroughprivatebankingservices(Sironi
2016). Wealthfront’s behavioral nudging, such as automatic reminders to set finan-
cial goals or to capitalize on employer 401(k) matching programs, further ensures
that users are continuously engaged in beneficial financial habits. These features
demonstrate that the future of wealth management lies not merely in reducing
advisorycoststhroughautomationbutindeliveringhighlynuanced,individualized
financial ecosystems capable of adapting fluidly to the evolving contours of each
client’sfinancialandemotionallife.

calculators, which require manual input and assume linear progression of financial
variables, Personal Capital aggregates real-time financial data across all linked
accounts—bank savings, investment portfolios, real estate equity,debts,andpension
plans—and continuously feeds this information into a machine learning model to
simulatethousandsofpossibleretirementoutcomesunderdifferentmarketandlife
eventscenarios(Belancheetal.2020) (Fig.3).
The conceptual framework for AI personalization in retirement planning captures
the shift from static, one-size-fits-all models to dynamic, individualized financial
life management. The starting point of the process is the continuous collection of
real-timefinancial inputs,such as fluctuations inincome, spending habits,savings
contributions, and unexpected expenses, combined with the detection of life event

This conceptualization strongly supports the argument advanced in Sect. 4.2 of

to promotions, recessions, major purchases, or unexpected life events, dynamic
retirement planning models adjust in near real time, ensuring that retirement paths
remain viable and aligned with user goals. Moreover, behavioral reinforcement
mechanisms, such as nudges reminding users to save more aggressively after
pay raises or framing messages to reassure users during market volatility, are
embedded into these systems (Belanche et al. 2020). The framework highlights
that AI personalization is not merely about mathematical recalculations; it is
about integrating behavioral finance insights into dynamic financial planning. By
including emotional and psychological elements in the personalization engine,
AI-enhanced retirement planners address not only financial optimization but also
behavioraladherence,ensuringthatusersaremorelikelytostickwiththeirevolving

Reflecting deeper, the framework also points toward several critical ethical and
technical challenges. The personalization of retirement pathways based on AI raises
concerns about transparency and explainability: users must be able to understand,
at least at a conceptual level, how their retirement strategies are being adjusted,
particularly when major financial decisions are influenced by machine learning
algorithms (Martin 2019). Furthermore, there are risks of reinforcing biases if
the underlying models are trained on historically skewed data (e.g., systematically
lower savings recommendations for certain demographic groups). Future research
and practical development in AI retirement planning could involve reinforcement
learning models that adaptively learn from long-term success and failure rates of
different retirement strategies, offering even finer-grained personalization. Inte-
grating physiological data (such as stress indicators) or cognitive assessments
could eventually enhance retirement planning further, creating systems that are
not only financially adaptive but also emotionally intelligent. By offering this
layered,adaptive,andethicallymindfulperspective,theframeworkensuresthatAI-

alignedwithclientwelfareandbroadersocietalgoals.

This allows for a highly personalized stress-testing of retirement plans, dynami-
cally adjusting for changes such as unexpected health costs, early retirement desires,
or bear market scenarios. For example, if a user increases discretionary spending
after a major lifestyle change (such as marriage or moving to a more expensive
city), the Retirement Planner recalibrates forecasted retirement dates, suggests
adjusted savings targets, or recommends more conservative investment allocations
to safeguard retirement readiness. The system also flags shortfalls proactively
rather than reactiv ely, alerting users when spending behaviors threaten long-term
goals and offering actionable strategies to get back on track. Beyond numeric
adjustments,PersonalCapital’sinterfaceusesvisualizationslikeprobabilitybands
andworst-caseprojectionstomakecomplexuncertaintyintuitivelyunderstandable
to clients, thereby empowering more informed, emotionally resilient financial

real-time financial behavior, market uncertainty, and individualized psychological
patterns into a cohesive retirement strategy exemplifies how AI elevates retirement
planning from a static, spreadsheet-driven process into a dynamic, adaptive life
managementsystem.
Other platforms, like Fidelity’s Personalized Planning and Advice service,
extend the AI-driven retirement customization model even further by incorporating
behavioral segmentation into their retirement advice frameworks. Fidelity’s system
analyzes user behaviors such as login frequency, risk rebalancing hesitation, cash
flowvolatility,andsavingsconsistencytocreatepsychographicprofilesthatinform
retirement advice (Jagtiani and Lemieux 2019). Rather than assuming a uniform
decline in risk tolerance with age, the standard “glide path,” Fidelity’s AI adapts de-
risking strategies based on how individuals actually behave when confronted with
volatility. For instance, if a 60-year-old user displays the same emotional resilience
and savings aggressiveness as a typical 45-year-old investor, the model adjusts the
glide path to maintain higher equity exposure for longer, maximizing growth poten-
tial without unnecessarily increasing perceived risk. Conversely, users who exhibit
flight-to-safety behaviors during minor market corrections are steered toward more
conservative allocations well before traditional age-based models would suggest.
Importantly, this dynamic personalization also extends to communication strategies:
users prone to financial anxiety receive calming, reassurance-based updates framed
around long-term goals, while financially confident users receive performance-
drivenanalyticsdesignedtomaintainengagementwithoutintroducingunwarranted
risk appetite. Such levels of behavioral sensitivity ensure that retirement advice
remains not only financially sound but also emotionally attuned to the client,
increasing the likelihood of adherence to long-term plans. By integrating these
behavioralandfinancialdimensions,FidelityexemplifieshowAI-basedretirement
customization moves beyond portfolio optimization to support holistic financial

5 Conclusion
Artificial intelligence continues to redefine the boundaries of personalized financial
decision-making, particularly by enabling systems that not only react to user
behaviors but also anticipate and adapt to emotional and cognitive fluctuations. A
key advance liesintheintegrationofpsychographicdatainformation—aboutuser
lifestyles, values, and motivations—into AI advisory models (Bendig et al. 2018).
Unlike traditional demographic segmentation, psychographic profiling allows plat-
forms to predict how different users will respond to market turbulence, interest rate
shifts, or life events, thereby fine-tuning advice beyond purely financial variables.
Studies in behav ioral economics have long emphasized that financial choices
are often driven more by identity and life goals than by objective optimization
(Thaler and Sunstein 2008), and AI systems are increasingly capable of capturing
these dimensions. This shift aligns closely with the rise of goal-based investing,
where financial strateg ies are constructed around personalized milestones such as
homeownership,education,orearlyretirement,ratherthanabstractbenchmarkslike
portfolioalpha.
Beyond technical advancements, the deeper integration of behavioral finance
principles into AI systems marks a paradigm shift. Traditional financial advice
models operated under the assumption of stable risk preferences and rational
actor models, bu t empirical research reveals that investor preferences are fluid,
context-dependent, and heavily influenced by emotional states (Kahneman and
Tversky 2021) Modern robo-advisors increasingly utilize dynamic risk profiling,
wherein client risk tolerance is continuously assessed andupdatedbasedonbehavior
rather than static surveys (Imas 2016). For instance, observed trading hesitation
during volatile periods or increased liquidity hoarding can trigger an automatic
reassessment of a user’s risk profile, prompting adaptive portfolio rebalancing.
Such systems represent afusionofmachinelearningcapabilitieswithfoundational
theoriesfrombehavioraleconomics,operationalizingconceptslikeprospecttheory
intoreal-timefinancialadvising.
However, the deployment of AI in personalized finance also introduces signif-
icant ethical complexities. Concerns about transparency, fairness, and informed
consent are magnified in environments where user data is not only passively
collected but actively used to steer behavior (Martin 2019). For example, if an
AI advisor detects increased financial anxiety, it might nudge the client toward
more conservative investment choices. While this appears benevolent, it also raises
the risk of systematically disadvantaging certain groups if not carefully audited.
Disparitiesindataavailabilityandmodelperformanceacrossdemographiccohorts
can inadvertently reinforce financial inequalities, a phenomenon well-documented
in the broader AI fairness literature (Cowgill et al. 2020). Addressing these
issues demands robust bias detection frameworks, transparency in advisory logic,
and the development of standards for ex plainable AI in finance, ensuring that
personalizationenhancesclientagencyratherthanunderminingit.
Another underexplored challenge in personalized financial AI is the risk of
“overpersonalization.” Whiledynamicadjustmentisvaluable,excessivesensitivity

AIinPersonalizedFinancialDecision-Making 93
to short-term behavioral signals can cause frequent, destabilizing changes to
financial advice (Wang et al. 2018). For instance, a temporary spike in market
anxiety could trigger a series of increasingly conservative portfolio adjustments,
locking users into suboptimal strategies. Balancing personalization with strategic
consistency requires careful calibration of model responsiveness thresholds and the
integration of countercyclical behavioral nudges. Moreover, firms must recognize
that not all deviations from optimal financial behavior are inherently irrational; users
may haveprivateinformationorlifecircumstancesunknowntothemodel.Thus,AI
systemsmustbedesignedtoaccommodateadegreeofuserautonomyanddissent
withoutcategorizingitimmediatelyasanerrortobecorrected.
Looking forward, future research in AI-driven personalized finance could benefit
from integrating emotional AI and affective computing techniques (Lemke et al.
2011). These technologies aim to detect and respond to user emotions in real
time, offering an even deeper layer of behavioral understanding. For instance,
physiological indicators such as heart rate variability or galvanic skin response,
captured through wearable devices, could provide additional inputs into financial
advice algorithms, allowing them to detect stress or excitement before these
emotions manifest behaviorally. Combined with advancements in reinforcement
learning, such systems could optimize not just financial metrics but emotional
resilienceandwell-beingaspartoftheiradvisorygoals.However,suchcapabilities
would necessitate even stricter ethical guidelines around consent, data usage, and
emotional manipulation risks. By embedding emotional intelligence into financial
advisory systems,thenext generation of personalized finance could offer notonly
smarterbutmorehumaneandempatheticfinancialguidance.

Building Trust in Financial
Robo-Advisory and Ove rcoming Ethical
Challenges
Alex Zarifis and Manuel Nunes
Abstract Previous research identified five areas where trust could be built for
financial robo-advisors. This research identifies the specific methods for building
trust for each of these five areas. Building trust with human oversight can be done in
three specific ways: (1) oversight of AI model and service it provides, (2) human
explanations for advice and processes, and (3) regular human communication
outside specific processes. Building trust with transparency and control can be
done by: (1) recognise that there are beliefs that do not immediately lead to
action, (2) explain actions and demonstrating ability and integrity, and (3) balance
automation with control to avoid disempowering users. Building trust with accuracy
and usefulness can be done by: (1) accurate and relevant information conveying
competence and integrity, (2) usefulness supported by back testing and multiple
methods, and (3)enhancedusefulnessthroughpersonalisation.Buildingtrustwith
ease of use and support can be done by: (1) achieve ease of use while keeping
all the necessary functionality, (2) support time management with nudges, and (3)
usefulandreliableservicewithhighperformance.Buildingtrustwithahumanlike
interaction can be done by: (1) utilise the latest sentiment analysis and longest
contextualmemory,(2)therobo-advisorshouldhaveaclearpersona,and(3)build
arelationshipandafeelingoffriendshipandpartnership.

1 Introd uction
Most financial institutions can meet their short-term targets by offering competitive
services that are attractive. The best financial institutions go beyond simply meeting
short-term targets and build strong relationships. Even in the age of AI and data-
driven decisions, evidence of the value of building strong relationships is all around
us. Both retail customers and organisations show trust and loyalty to financial
institutions they have a deeper emotional connection with. Until now, this usually
happenednaturallywiththeface-to-faceinteraction.Evenwhenweinteractedwith
systemsontheinternet,untilrecentlythesesystemsdidnotuseAIbuthumanlogic

AI implementation is naturally good at many aspects of financial services, but it is
not naturally effective at building trust. Typically, some human intervention, such
as supervised learning and specific instructions given before every answer the AI
gives, are necessary to create an interaction that builds trust. Unfortunately, trying
to get the AI to build trust in the way humans build trust doesn’t usually work.
ThereisextensiveevidencethatAIbehavingasahumancanoftenbackfireoreven
becreepy,sonewmethodstobuildtrustarenecessary(Mori2012). This research

technologysothatitdeliversaservicepeopletrust.
The capabilities of AI increase on a weekly basis but implementing AI in a way

consider the other aspects of the financial institution as additional layers. All these
technical and business layers to the ‘financial robo-advisor stack’ must be aligned
toatrust-buildingstrategy.AIcanofferusmanythingssuchasnear-infinitescaling

Previous research has identified four issues that affect trust in robo-advisors for

While identifying these five areas is helpful, they are not specific methods to

2 Theoretical Fo undation
This section first looks at the challenges to trust in financial robo-advisors before
identifying the five issues that build trust in robo-advisory that form the basis for
thedatacollection.
2.1 The Challenges to Trust in FinancialRobo-Advisors
Despite the impressive performance of generative AI transforming finance (Chui
et al. 2023), receiving financial advice from a robo-advisor still raises several

98 A.ZarifisandM.Nunes
challenges to trust. From the user’s perspective, there are several risks, each of
which requires that they have trust in apositiveoutcome.Wherethereisrisk,trustis
needed(Lanktonetal.2015; McKnight and Chervany2002). The risks from using a
financial robo-advisor include that the AI does not understand their real motivation
and intentions, t echnology supporting the robo-advisor does not work correctly,
receivingdamagingfinancialadvice(Dietzmannetal.2023), their sensitive personal
information leaking, and having acybersecuritybreach(Jainetal.2023). All these
risks are exacerbated by the feeling a user can have that a human on the side of the
financial institution is not responsible and anything that happens can be explained
awayasatechnicalissue.
There is also the additional potential risk of the robo-advisor making the
consumer feel uneasy or even creepy. When we interact with traditional information
systems, the interaction is similar to using a tool that has no thought process. When
the user interactswitharobo-advisor,itmaycommunicateinaninappropriateway,
andthiscancreateanadditionalfeelingofinsecurityorevencreepiness(Mori2012;
Rajaobelina et al.2021).
2.2 The Five Issues That Build Tr ustinRobo-Advisory
Research has found that when interacting with generative AI the nature of the task or
questionscaninfluencetheperceptionofriskandtrust(Chengetal.2021). Previous
systems that used static code and not AI were limited to specific processes, such as
reporting the price of a share. Because robo-advisors are more versatile and do not
operate in a rigid way, they handle a breadth of questions and interact in a quasi-
social way (Cheng et al. 2024). While there are many different questions asked,
in terms of trust building, an important distinction must be made between specific
and vague questions. There is a prov endifferenceinhowtobuildtrustinthesetwo
differentscenarios(Fig.1).
Recent research has identified four issues that affect trust in robo-advisors for
specific financial questions, and five t hat affect trust in robo-advisors for vague
financial questions (Zarifis and Cheng 2024). The four issues are the same for
both specific and vague questions, but vague questions have one additional issue.
The four issues that affect trust in all financial questions are human oversight,
transparency and control, accuracy and usefulness, ease of use, and support. The
additional, fifth issue that builds trust in vague questions is humanlike interaction.
These fiv e trust-building areas are the starting point for this research, which will
explore each of them further. These five areas should be further investigated to
identifythespecificpracticalwaystobuildtrust(Fig.2).

3 Me thod
This research attempts to identify specific practical steps to build trust. Previous
research identified fiveareaswheretrustcanbebuilt(ZarifisandCheng2024), so
this research attempts to find realistic ways practitioners can implement them. For
this reason,aqualitativeapproachwithfourfocusgroupswasimplemented.

100 A.ZarifisandM.Nunes
3.1 Data Collection
The participants of the focus groups are professionals working in financial insti-
tutions. They are the kind of professionals who deal with these issues as part
of their role. This ensures that the methods identified are realistic and can be
applied. They do not all have the same role, but they are in roles that influence
the implementation of the financial robo-advisor. The participants were from IT-
relatedroles(9),financialroles(8),management(5),andmarketing(5).Theywork
fortraditionalbanks,born-onlinebanks,andtraditionalinsurersinEUcountries.
The original data collection plan was to implement four focus groups and then
add more if this was necessary, but after the third focus group, the to picswereindeed
saturated.Thefourthfocusgroupdidnotaddsomethingsignificantlydifferent,so
noadditionalfocusgroupswereadded.
Before the online focus groups, a researcher presented the purpose of the research
and the topics that were being explored. The rest of the focus group was divided into
the five trust-building areas. So that an honest discussion is made, ‘Chathamhouse
rules’wereusedsonorecordingsweremadeandonlynotesweretaken.Thenotes
didnotrecordtheidentitiesoftheparticipants,justthemainpointsthatweremade.
3.2 Data Analysis
The data was analysed using the NVivo software to im plementathematicanalysis
(BraunandClarke2006; Miles andHuberman1994). As transcripts were not taken,
only notes, the thematic analysis was done based on the notes. The high-level themes
were the fiv e trust-building areas. Several trust-building themes were identified
beneaththem.
4 Analysis and Discussion
This section identifies the practical ways to build trust for each of the fiv e areas
identified in previous research (Zarifis and Cheng 2024). There are four areas to
build trust in both vague and specific questions, and one additional area that only
helps for vague questions. There are some common themes such as transparency
and having extensive safeguards and checks in place, but each area also has its
idiosyncrasies and attempting to oversimplify these issues will not bring the best
results.Eachofthesefiveareasneedstobehandledindividuallyforthebestresults.
4.1 Human Ove rsight
Despite the many challenges in keeping a human in the loop, including the problems
humans can make, this is still the best way forward. Keeping humans in the loop

BuildingTrustinFinancialRobo-AdvisoryandOvercomingEthicalChallenges 101
ensures a more human character to the process. Despite the capabilities of AI, a
real person’s judgement and empathy are beneficial. Equally importantly, someone
always needs to be responsible. Those using robo-advisors to make financial
decisions need to know who is behind the tool they are using. They should also
know where the responsibility of those creating and maintaining the chatbot starts
andends,andwheretheirresponsibilitystartsandends.Humanoversightneedsto
beimplementedeffectivelyandthencommunicatedeffectively.
Having a team of humans in the loop, in itself, does not guarantee any benefit; it
needs to be implemented in a targeted way. Those involved in the human oversight
will almost inevitably also b e involved in troubleshooting unexpected day-to-day
problems,whichoftentakemanyprofessionalsmoretimethantheyplantospend.
4.1.1 Oversight of AI Model and Serv iceItProvides
The first way to build trust is the oversight of the AI models. The model needs to be
regularly checked by humans in quantitative and qualitative ways. Tests can be made
for AI model drift, but humans can also regularly go through the process themselves.
The ‘mystery shopper’ has been an effective method to check quality and fix issues
that could damage trust before AI emerged, and it is still entirely relevant. AI cannot
empathise with the problems the people that use it have. AI cangivetheappearance
thatitempathises,butitbenefitsfromsupervisedlearningandhumaninstructions
before each response it makes to do this effectively. Additionally, a robo-advisor
maybewellsuitedfortheregulareventsitdealswith,butlesscommoneventssuch
ascyberattacksmayneedsomehumanintervention.
If these proactive oversight processes are in place this will reduce problems,
but reactive oversight will still be needed. It is inevitable that those that use robo-
advisors will have both valid and less valid complaints. There will be complaints
that are not valid, but the users believe them to be valid. The processing of these
complaints should not be done with the priority to achieve efficiency. AI offers scale;
these processes should focus on empathy and human interaction. Users must feel
there is an organisation fullofexpertsbehindthemachinetheyareinteractingwith,
notjustaserverroomandanorganisationleftonautopilot.Theproblemescalation
pathshouldbeclearandaspainlessaspossible.Itshouldbeseenasanopportunity
to touch bases, not a process that should be stripped down to its most basic and
automated.
This layer of human oversight managing the AI model and the service should
be overseen by a team of middle managers w ith a range of expertise, including
anunderstandingofthetechnical,business,psychological,andsociologicaldimen-
sions.
4.1.2 Human Explanations for A dviceandProcesses
In marketing literature, they emphasise the importance of the specific ‘touchpoints’
a user has with an organisation.Themainvalueoffocusingontheinteractionsthe

102 A.ZarifisandM.Nunes
user has with the organisation is that those resonate more than advertising or back-
officeoperationsnotvisibletotheuser.
There are opportunities during the process of using financial robo-advisors to
get the best of both worlds, the performance of AI and the human touch. As
already happens in some implementations, an explanation written by a human can
accompany some advice. It does not have to be made for a specific question but for a
type of situation, such as an unexpected event. Processes implemented with AI and
automation are often effective in providing a good service when the user has their
regular needs but often underperform when the user wants to make abigchangeto
whattheyaredoingsuchachangingtheirroleinanorganisation,orwhentheyhave
a major change in their life. The effectiveness of generative AI is partly down to
rememberingpreviousconversationswithauserbutwhenthereisasharpchange,
thesepreviouspatternsareahindrance,notahelp.
Clear accountability that is regularly communicated is also important. There are
no tricks to building trust; the humans in the financial institution cannot hide behind
the robo-advisor. There should be regular updates that include the name of the
human who wrote them. Any checks made by a human can also be logged with
theperson’sname.Theaccountabilitydoesnotalwaysneedtobecommunicatedto
theuser,insomecasesitjustneedstobethereincasetheyneedit.
4.1.3 Regular Human Communication Ou tsideSpecificProcesses
It is human nature to not only build an impression of a financial institution, but even
give it human attributes such as traditional, aggressive, innovative, caring, friendly,
kind, or unreliable. These human attributes we associate with an organisation
influence trust. The performance of the organisation inevitably affects these issues,
but it is not just about the performance. The communication should conve y a
coherent message and character both when reacting to requests and outside of
specific processes.Thisiswhatthebestorganisations withstrongvalues achieved
before AI dominated the interaction with the user, and this is what should still
happentoday.
The communication must outline how experienced professionals with a suc-
cessful track record are developing and validating the portfolios and handling
exceptions. The more specific this is, th e better. Including names, pictures, and
wheretheirofficeisemphasisesthatthesearerealpeople(Table1).

is the benefit of transparency? Similarly, if there iscontrolbutnotransparency,how
can the user utilise the control they have effectively? Financial professionals and

4.2.1 Recognise That There Are Beliefs That Do NotImmediatelyLead
toAction
The fashion of being ‘data-driven’ based on users’ actions often misses people’s
feelings as they don’t always act on them immediately. However, bad feelings
building up can lead to negative actions further down the line. Feelings of a lack
of transparency and control may not immediately be apparent in the data that come
from measuring behaviour. Consumers can often be trapped in a situation where
they do not have better options, so they do not change their behaviour for some
time.However,assoonasanalternativeappearstheywillchangetheirbehaviour.It
iscommonforpeopletoexpectlinearchangeinbehaviour,butthisisnotalwaysthe

104 A.ZarifisandM.Nunes
case. There is often a sudden inflection point in behaviour that came from longer-
held beliefs. Feelings are not always easy to understand when the interaction is
online; we cannot read the persons face for example, but they are powerful and
decisive.
It is important to appreciate that AI effectiveness is not enough on its own,
as even with an excellent financial robo-advisor there will be both valid and less
valid concerns and fears. All these things are dealt with instinctively when humans
interact with each other. A professional in insurance or finance would do these
without thinking. When we moved to online services these relationships were
weakened but people knew that, ultimately, humans were making the decisions as
theymadethecodeandthealgorithms.Thisappliestoallfiveareasoftrustbuilding,
butitisparticularlyimportantfortransparencyandcontrol.
4.2.2 Explaining Actions and Demonstrating AbilityandIntegrity
The robo-advisor can make an excellent recommendation, but the user may still
feel some anxiety and uncertainty. For example, if AI makes a change to a user’s
investment portfolio, a short explanation of why this was done is necessary. This is
an opportunity for the robo-advisor to explain what methods it uses and how capable
it is. If therobo-advisormakesasignificantchange,thenitneedstoinformtheuser.
Theusermustnotbeleftinuncertainty.Asfaraspossible,theexplanationmustbe
inplainEnglishavoidingspecialisedterminologyandacronyms.
A separate section on the website can be dedicated to more information on the
methodologies behind the actions and recommendations. If the user wants more
information beyond the messages they receive, they will be able to find it at this
methodologyhub.Theseformsofcommunicationnotonlyreduceuncertaintyand
theperceivedriskinvolved,buttheybuildmorerealisticexpectations.
4.2.3 Balancing Automation with Control to Avo idDisempoweringUsers
The robo-advisor must make it easy for the user to be in control by providing a range
of tools. These are usually simple but give the user a quick way to take action to
implement their will. A slider can enable them to adjust the risk level. Switches can
be used to make typical investment exclusions such as weapons manufacturers, or
organisations that are considered unethical such as cannabis and alcohol producers.
There should also be a button that can be pushed that stops each process such as
a new investment until it is checked by the user and confirmed. Additional buttons
should enable the user to pause or undo a decision. The line between work and
leisure time has been blurred and both professionals and retail investors may be
making decisions when they are not entirely in their work mindset. This is the
current reality so the financial robo-advisor must make it as easy as possible to
understandtheimplicationsofdecisionsandcorrectmistakeswherepossible.These
featurescreateapsychologicalsafetynetforusers.

4.3 Accuracy an dUsefulness
It is not a surprise that the accuracy and usefulness of the information build trust in
the robo-advisor. The role accuracy and usefulness play in this context, however, is
worth exploring further. Understanding their ro leinthisspecificcontextwillmake
iteasiertodevelopacomprehensiveapproachtobuildingtrust.
4.3.1 Accurate and Relevant Information Conv eysCompetence
andIntegrity
The robo-advisor must provide precise, reliable, and relevant information. There are
many things an organisation can do to convey their competence, but if the accuracy
is not there, all the other measures will be in vain. If there is accuracy, then other

106 A.ZarifisandM.Nunes
measures, such as communicating the value of the advice, can reinforce the feeling
of competence. This is an obvious point but it needs to be made as AI often struggles
with accuracy, especially if it is bringing a lot of information together such as
the user’s risk tolerance, fees, and so on. If there is a lack of accuracy, it may be
perceived as a lack ofcompetence,oralackofintegrity,orboth.Alackofaccuracy
inanyaspectmaybeperceivedasdishonestyandmaydamagetrust.Withtherisk
involvedinfinancialdecisionspeopleareparticularlysensitivetothepossibilityof
beingmisled.
4.3.2 Usefulness Supported by Back Te stingandMultipleMethods
Generative AI has impressive capabilities, but the accuracy of the most popular
generative AI most people use is achieved by implementing unsupervised and
supervised training, along with several special commands. For financial questions,
additional layers must be added on top of these typical layers. For example, AI
can identify patterns in a wide range of data that influence risk. An example is
that some insurers track alternative behavioural data such as a user typing speed,
as slow typing has been linked to higher risk. These strengths of AI must be
combined with traditional methods and back testing to prev iousscenarios.Finance
andinsuranceareparticularlychallengingforgenerativeAI,whosecharacteristics
bringbothstrengthsandweaknessesinthisarea.Therearemanyunexpectedsudden
twists in these areas that are hard to predict by AI if it just plays to its natural
strengths. The multiple AI models and methods will enhance the usefulness. The
saying‘twomindsarebetterthanone’couldbeadaptedhereto‘multipleAImodels
andmethodologiesarebetterthanone’.
4.3.3 Enhanced Usefulness Thro ughPersonalisation
While AI has both strengths and weaknesses in making financial predictions,
personalising a service is something AI is naturally very strong at. The obvious
strength of AI here is bringing data on the user’s behaviour together to understand
their specific needs. Less obvious is that AI can encourage more interaction from
the user, so they keep sharing their needs as they evolve. In addition to measuring
behav iour, surveys, and other opportunities to encourage feedback can be used.
Thisdialoguecanbeelicitedwhenthereisunexpectedperformanceorunexpected
events. This should not come across as nudges but as opportunities for the user to
havetheirsay(Table3).
4.4 Ease of Use andSupport
When there is a big disruption with new technologies and new capabilities emerging,

An attempt at humanness that is out of place, or in any other way ineffective,

5 Conclusion
Previous research has identified four issues that affect trust in robo-advisors for
specific financial questions, and five th at affect trust in robo-advisors for vague
financial questions (Zarifis and Cheng 2024). The four issues that affect trust in
all financial questions are human oversight, transparency and control, accuracy and
usefulness, ease of use, and support. The additional, fifth issue that builds trust
in vague questions is humanlike interaction. Knowing these five areas is helpful,
but in o rder to take action, specific methods to build trust for each of them are
necessary. Therefore, this research identified the specific methods to build trust in
robo-advisorsforeachofthefiveareas.
This research finds that building trust with human oversight can be done in
three specific ways: (1) oversight of AI model and service it provides, (2) human
explanations for advice and processes, and (3) regular human communication
outside specific processes. Building trust with transparency and control can be
done by: (1) recognise that there are beliefs that do not immediately lead to
action,(2)explainactionsanddemonstratingabilityandintegrity,and(3)balance
automationwithcontroltoavoiddisempoweringusers.Buildingtrustwithaccuracy
and usefulness can be done by: (1) accurate and relevant information conveying

BuildingTrustinFinancialRobo-AdvisoryandOvercomingEthicalChallenges 111
competence and integrity, (2) usefulness supported by back testing and multiple
methods, and (3) enhanced usefulness through personalisation. Building trust with
ease of use and support can be done by: (1) achieve ease of use while keeping
all the necessary functionality, (2) support time management with nudges, and (3)
useful and reliable service with high performance. Building trustwithahumanlike
interaction can be done by: (1) utilise the latest sentiment analysis and longest
contextualmemory,(2)therobo-advisorshouldhaveaclearpersona,and(3)build
arelationshipandafeelingoffriendshipandpartnership.
Yet these trust-building methods do not operate in isolation. Algorithmic bias
and ethical trade-offs represent systemic risks that can undermine client confi-
dence if left unaddressed. Bias can enter robo-advisory systems through data,
features, model design, and deployment choices, producing suitability failures,
excess trading costs, and inappropriate drawdown exposure. Practitioners must also
navigate genuine tensions between personalisation and fairness, transparency and
proprietary interest,automationandhumanoversight,andpredictiveaccuracyand
interpretability. The governance architecture of model risk management, suitabil-
ity assurance, fairness monitoring, and documentation provides the institutional
foundationwithoutwhichthepractitionerstrategiesidentifiedinSect.4 cannot be
sustained atscale.
This analysis carries implications for investors, firms, and regulators alike.
Investors benefit from understanding that robo-advisory trust is multidimensional
and that the presence of sophisticated technology does not guarantee aligned
interests. Questions about oversight, transparency, and fairness monitoring are
reasonable to ask and material to the advisory relationship. Firms benefit from
recognising that trust-building is not merely a marketing exercise but requires
genuine investment in governance infrastructure, bias testing, and explainability.
The competitive advantage of robo-advisory, scalable personalised advice at low
cost, can only be sustained if clients believe the system operates in their interest.
Regulatorsbenefitfromtheframework’semphasisonoutcomesratherthanprescrip-
tiverules.Suitability,fairness,andtransparencycanbeassessedthroughthelensof
clientexperienceanddistributionalanalysis,withoutrequiringdetailedalgorithmic
auditsthatmaybeimpracticalatscale.
The chapter began by observing that trust, built naturally through face-to-face
interaction in traditional advisory relationships, must be deliberately constructed in
theageofAI-drivenfinancialservices.Thetrust-buildingareasidentifiedinSect.2
and operationalised inSect.4 provide the conceptual and practical architecture for
this construction. They offer a comprehensive approach to building financial robo-
advisory systems th atarenotmerelyefficientandscalable,butgenuinelyworthyof
clientconfidence.

A Theory of Investment Simplification
and an Experiment wi th AI Large

J. Indigo Jo nes
Abstract The complexity of investing in financial markets creates demand to
simplify it; but competition to meet this demand creates a new layer of complexity,
restarting the cycle. Robo-advisors are but one link in a long chain of financial
technology seeking to scale and simplify access to financial markets, and there are
now too many to know them all. The next link in the chain of creative destruction is
the robo-“robo-advisor”-advisor: A technology which helps retail investor chooses
the right robo-advisor for them. One non-AI advisor and five AI large language
models (LLMs) are tested to see whether at least one can provide complete advice
that can nav igate complicated jurisdictional problems and robo-advisor service
heterogeneitywithoutproducinghallucinations.Sincetherearenoswitchingcosts,
onlyoneisnecessary.FouroutoffiveLLMsoutperformthehumanteam,andwith
a sophisticated prompt, Anthropic’s Claude can solve this problem without error.
Thepromptisprovidedsuchthatreaderscanbenefitdirectlyfromthisresearch.
