1 Introd uction
In 1924, there was only one mutual fund. For the layman, investing in financial
markets suddenly became simpler: Just invest in MITTX. Then competitors started
offering different kinds of mutual funds. This broadened the choice set for investors,
which is always good, but as a byproduct of having to understand the differences
among the mutual funds in order to make an informed choice, investing in financial
markets became complicated again. Then in 1975, there was only one index fund.
For the layman, investing in financial markets suddenly became simpler: Just invest
in VFIAX. Then the cycle repeated—bond indexes, the Wilshire 4500, maturity
dates.Thenin1993,therewasonlyoneExchangeTradedFund(ETF):Justinvest
inSPY.Andthecyclerepeats:inverse,leverage,tilt.Thenin2008,therewasonly
one robo-advisor: Just invest with Betterment. Rinse and repeat: REITs, crypto,
tax-lossharvesting.Thisiscreativedestruction(AghionandHowitt1990), where a
financial innovation’s proliferation sows the seeds of itsowneventualreplacement.
Two stylized facts emerge from this brief history: Investors demand both
simplification and diversification. But these two demands are in conflict. The
demand for simplification is met by a supplier with a financial innovation: mutual
fund, index fund, ETF, robo-advisor, whereas the demand for diversification is met
by multiple suppliers with specializedservicescateringtoaspecificportfolioneed,
investor demographic, or wealth bracket. This is the situation in which the latest
evolutioninthishistory,robo-advisors,findsthemselvesin.
Could generative AI, and specifically large language models (LLMs), help build
this hypothetical robo-“robo-advisor”-advisor? Capable of referencing the breadth
ofthepublishedcontentontheInternetandeminentlyscalable(List2022), but also
prone to hallucinations, LLMs may or may not becapableofperformingthisrole.
The outline of this chapter is as follows. Section 2 reviews the literature on
simplifying financial technology and describes the complex current state of robo-
advisors.Section3 considers a theory of conflict between demand for simplicity and
diversity in investment options. Section 4 describes the methods used to construct
the task for the experiment with the AI LLMs and their comparison with human
financialadvisors.Section5 states the results of the experiment with adiscussionin
Sect.6. Section 7 concludes by placing this study within a wider economic contex t
ofautomatizationoffinancialadvice.
In this chapter, five of the most popular LLMs are given a complex intellectual
task of recommending a robo-advisor to an investor, and their answers are compared
against a baseline of human financial advisors. Because these LLMs are all free and
giving them this task is as simple as copying and pasting it from this study, there
are no upfront or switching costs among theLLMs.Assuch,ifthereisatleastone
LLMthatiscapableofsolvingthetask,thentherobo-“robo-advisor”-advisorexists.
Thehumanfinancialadvisorsfailedthetask.AsdidfourofthefiveLLMs.Butone
LLM,Anthropic’sClaude,producedadvicewithouterror.

ATheoryofInvestmentSimplificationandanExperimentwithAILarge... 115
This study contributes to the literatures of financial technology (FinTech), human
financial advisors compared to robo-advisors, and the extent to which AI can
replace professional services. Furthermore, this study provides an economic theory
explaining the cyclical evolution of simplifying financial services, a framework for
thinking through stumbling blocks and edge cases when choosing a robo-advisor,
and a specifically engineered prompt which readers can use to recover their lost
utilitypredictedfromthetheory.
2 Literature Rev iew
2.1 The Steady March To wardSimplification
Owning and maintaining a diversified portfolio is more complicated than holding a
single stock, but investors accept this additional complication because the lowered
risk is worth the trade-off in expectation. Nobel prize-winning economist Harry
Markowitz (1952) outlined that an investor could construct a portfolio which
maximizes an expected return for a given level of risk through diversification of
nonperfectly correlated assets, inventing modern portfolio theory (MPT). MPT
largely replaced the naive diversification strategy that investors used prior to its
invention.ExtensionsofMPT,suchasthecapitalassetpricingmodel(CAPM)by
Nobel prize-winning economist William Sharpe (1964) or the three- or five-factor
model by Nobel prize-winning economist Eugene (Fama and French 1992, 2015),
are industry standards. If only th iswaseasier.
Saving is common, and the benefits of diversification are well-known, but
building and especially maintaining a scientifically diversified portfolio that suits
an investor’s unique financial situation is difficult. Therefore, financial technologies
have been invented to make diversification easier. Since at least 1924, inv estorshave
pooledtheirresourcesanddelegatedthetaskofmanagingadiversifiedinvestment
portfolio, called a mutual fund (Farina et al. 1969). However, the fees associated
with paying the manager and reimbursing their trades meant mostmutualfundshad
below-averagereturns(Sharpe1966). Furthermore, mutual funds that outperformed
in 1 year rarely maintained this streak in subsequent years (Carhart 1997). This
is predictable. In any given trade, the average return of the buyer and seller is
slightly negative: One makes a profit and the other make s a loss, but they both
pay transaction fees. If financial markets are efficient (Fama 1970), an imperfect
but plausible and widely held view, the fact that few managers can reliably earn
above-average returns after deducting transaction fees logically follows. To address
this shortcoming with the typical mutual fund, Jack Bogle launched Vanguard in
1975 with a mutual fund called a n “index fund,” which gives up the chance of
outperformancetoguaranteeaveragereturnsbytrackingabroadstockmarketindex
such as the S&P 500 (Bogle 1999). Further financial technologies improved on

116 J.I.Jones
this model. Buying and selling shares of a mutual fund can be tricky, so exchange
traded funds (ETFs) were invented in 1989 to make trading index funds easier.
Eventually, there were so many ETFs on the market that inve stors needed help
choosing among them, so robo-advisors were invented in 2008 to give advice on
andmanageportfolioscomposedpurelyofETFs(Fischetal.2019).
With each new simplifying technology, portfolio diversification becomes more
accessible to and inclusiveofdiverseaudiences(seeChatterjee2020). Whereas once
only the wealthiest institutions and individuals could access sophisticated diversi-
fication, with ETFs and especially robo-advisors, the financial and informational
barriers to entry have been greatly reduced. Just as other technologies which have
reduced the barriers to stock market participation have raised participation rates
(Bogan2008), robo-advisors are bringing new entrants into financial markets aswell
(ReherandSokolinski2019). Choi (2022) summarized that across eight dimensions,
consensus popular and academic household finance agreed on just one: to investin
passiveindexfunds,e.g.,withrobo-advisors.
2.2 The Benefits of Robo-Advisors
The actions taken by these untrained, middle-class individuals are of great interest to
governments, regulators, asset managers, financial markets, and academics exactly
because they are so typical of the median person, a person who has either very
little experience in finance or has not yet even entered financial markets. As more
peopleentertheglobalmiddleclass(Kochhar2015), as stock market participation
rises acrossmanycountries(Campbell2006), and as more individuals’ pensions are
covered by defined contribut ion instead of defined benefit plans (Broadbent et al.
2006; Gomes et al. 2021), the number of household investors participating in the
stock marketwillonlygrow.
The question then is how to properly advise this growing stream of new investors,
those without ex perience and uncertain financial literacy, cost-effectively at scale
(List2022). Here, there is a large cleavage between popular and academic household
finance. If popular household finance is pessimistic about the ordinary person’s
capabilities, academic household finance is optimistic. To avoid taking on debt,
Dave Ramsey (2013) encourages his readers to rent until they have the money
to buy their primary residence in cash because they cannot be trusted with debt.
Meanwhile, Ando and Modigliani (1963) assume that people can solve lifetime
consumption optimization problems or at least behave as if they hav edoneso.These
twoperspectiveshavelittleincommon.
Robo-advisors can improve upon human performance (including well-trained
financial managers) in many ways. In r eality,investorsunderdiversify(Benartziand
Thaler 2001). Investors hold too much company stock (Benartzi 2001) and home-
country stock(FrenchandPoterba1991), and trade excessively (BarberandOdean
2000, 2001). Perhaps this is the bounded rationality mentioned by Simon (1955),

ATheoryofInvestmentSimplificationandanExperimentwithAILarge... 117
regular humans’ limited omniscience. But investors do not always do much better
with human financial managers. Certain flaws among human financial advisors
have been well documented. To start, human financial advisors can advise their
clients to hold portfolios that reflect their own portfolios (Foerster et al. 2017;
Linnainmaa et al.2021). This is not necessarily good advice. Not only is each client
in need of different advice that fits their unique financial situation, in the words
of Linnainmaa et al. (2021), human advisors can “trade frequently, chase returns,
prefer expensive, actively managed funds, andunderdiversify.”ChalmersandReuter
(2020) found that the portfolios of clients who sought financial advice from brokers
underperformed target date funds, in part because advisors steered clients toward
higher fee products. Human advisors can steer their clients to high fee, often self-
servingfinancialinstruments(Mullainathanetal.2012). Mullainathan etal.(2012)
also documented evidence of age and gender discrimination towardclients.Sharpe
(1966) observed that the average mutual fund performed below the market average;
half a century later, it is still the case that the average human financial advisor
underperformsthemarketandsometimesevennaiveretailinvestorswithoutadvice
(Hackethaletal.2012; Chalmers andReuter2020).
Robo-advisors do not have these problems. It is not surprising then that even
when retail investors like and trust th eir financial advisor, they may seek a second
opinion with robo-advisors (Zhang et al. 2021). Some users prefer robo-advisors
because they are more accountable (Philippon 2019), objective Jung et al. (2019),
precise (Wexler and Oberlander 2021), or convenient (Mesbah et al. 2019) than
human financial advisors. Robo-advisors can also act as infinitely patient AI
teachers, demonstrating to investors how to better diversify their portfolio without
necessarilytakingupthetimeoforreplacingahumanfinancialadvisor(Loosetal.
2020).
2.3 The Limits of Having HundredsofRobo-Advisors
Up to this point, robo-advisors have been presented as a natural evolution in the
journey to make modern portfolio diversification a la Markowitz (1952) or Fama
and French (2015) simple enough for retail investors to perform en masse. But that
is speaking of robo-advisorsasageneralconcept:Howdoesitlookinthefield?
Because of the Foreign Account Tax Compliance Act (FATCA), an American
living in France cannot open an account with Betterment. Nor can a Frenchman
living in the United States open an account with Yomoni. Automatic rebalancing
is standard practice with most robo-advisors, but not Amundi’s. Furthermore,
Amundi’s robo-advisor is business to business (B2B), as are Advize, FundShop,
Fundvisory, and many others. By default, Nalo’s portfoliosoperateliketargetdate
funds, decreasing stock market exposure over time, though this option can be
deactivated. As a promotional offer at time of writing, SoFi automated investing
matches individual retirement account (IRA) contributions at 1%. Ramify allows

118 J.I.Jones
investment in art. Every portfolio with Fidelity Go includes cryptocurrency. Acorns,
Ellevest, SoFi, and Stash have no minimum investment threshold. Some robo-
advisors have ESG options, some do not; Goodvest has exclusively ESG portfolios.
There are no fees at either Schwab Intelligent Portfolios or at SoFi; 6% of a Schwab
portfolio is kept in cash that is then loaned out, while SoFi directs its investors to
its proprietary ETFs that have relatively high expense ratios. Speaking of Schwab,
tax-loss harvesting is ava ilable above $50,000 in assets under management. Can
the average robo-advisor client handle this complexity? If they can, then it is
questionablesuchafinanciallyliterateinvestorwouldevenneedarobo-advisor.If
theycannot,thenthereisalatentdemand,anunmetneed,forthenextsimplifying
financialtechnology.
Retail investors employ financial advisors because they want help understanding
and managing an investment portfolio. Robo-advisors automate this transaction,
making it more transparent and accessible. But now there are hundreds of robo-
advisors, each with their own services, entry barriers, and jurisdictions. Robo-
advisors aim to simplify ETFs, a technology aimed to simplify mutual funds, which
itself is a technology aimed to simplify trading individual stocks. The next stage
inthisevolution of simplification, indeed thenext stepfor robo-advice itself,isto
adviseretailinvestorswhichrobo-advisortochoose.
There is room for improvement in robo-advisors. Mutual funds were simple until
there were hundreds of them. ETFs were simple until there were hundreds of them.
The same has happened to robo-advisors. How can a retail investor with barely a
concept of compound interest possibly choose among the hundreds of robo-advisors
today, which compete with each other on services like tax-loss harvesting and
exposuretorealestateinvestmenttrusts(REIT)?Eachincrementalinnovationinthe
robo-advisorymarketincreasestheriskofchoiceoverload(Chernevetal.2015) and
thus reduces the scalability of the underlyingtechnology(Al-Ubaydlietal.2019).
The logical next step is for retail investors to seek an advisor to help them choose
a r obo-advisor: a “robo-advisor”-advisor. Reasonably, this advice could itself be
automated:arobo-“robo-advisor”-advisor.
3 Theory
3.1 A Theory of Inve stmentSimplification
A few key financial concepts such as adding and subtracting currency are taught in
elementary school and are essential fo r life. The classic three-question financial
literacy survey by Lusardi and Mitchell (2011) measures a population’s rate of
understanding of just slightly more advanced financial concepts, with around half
of the population answering correctly depending on the country. Meanwhile, tests

ATheoryofInvestmentSimplificationandanExperimentwithAILarge... 119
Fig. 1 Logarithmic
distribution of financial
knowledge
used to qualify professionals to give investment advice such as the certified financial
analyst (CFA) or certified financial planner (CFP) exams are much longer and
much more difficult, with very few people earning these credentials (Terry and
Vibhakar2006). A stylized fact can be extrapolated from this information: Financial
knowledge has a logarithmic distribution, as described in Fig.1, which plots th e
equationlog (x)+2as an ex ample.
10 .
If stock returns are inexplicably high and Treasury bill returns are inexplicably
low, then one would expect that all households in an economy of rational agents
wouldholdsomeequity.Indeed,thisisanimplicationofMPT(Markowitz1952).
But this is far from the case, and this incongruity is known as the stock market
participation puzzle (Mankiw and Zeldes 1991). No plausible rational explanation
exists for the stockmarketparticipationpuzzle(HaliassosandBertaut1995). Stock
market participation rates in the United States have doubled since the puzzle was
first identified, but the current rate of around 50% participation i s still far below
100%,andmanyotherwealthycountrieshaveparticipationratesnear0%(Campbell
2006).
Because of dramatic episodes like the Great Depression and the Great Financial
Crisis, it has become common knowledge that people can lose money in financial
markets. A risk-averse and particularly a loss-averse individual, with anunderstand-
ing of financial markets that they themselves judge to be insufficient, might then
rationally choose not to participate (Kahneman and Tversky 1979). Innovations
which reduce information costs have been shown both theoretically and empirically
toincreasestockmarketparticipationrates(Bogan2008).
If a simplifying financial technology reduces the financial knowledge threshold
for participating in financial markets (moves from right to left in Fig.1), then a

120 J.I.Jones
greater share of the population will feel confident enough to participate (moves from
top to bottom in Fig.1). However, as competition enters the market with slightly
differentiated products based on the original financial innovation, distinguishing
among these products makes financial knowledge more, not less, important. As
such, the financial knowledge threshold fo rparticipatinginfinancialmarketsmoves
back to the right and once again discourages some of the population away from
participating.
One concrete example of this cycle of simplification and diversification is ETFs.
The original ETF, SPY, is based on the S&P 500, which is a broad market index of
U.S. large cap stocks. SPY is a highly diversified fund, and a portfolio that contains
nothing butSPYisexposedtolittlespecificriskorliquidityrisk.Feelingconfident
enoughtoinvestinSPYrequiresknowledgeoftheaforementionedconcepts,which
is more than what is tested by Lusardi and Mitchell (2011) but not exceptionally
difficult. Much later, 2x-, 3x-, even 10x-leveraged version of the S&P 500 index
were put on the market. Are these wise investments? To answer this question, the
retail investor must have all of the previous financial knowledge necessary to choose
to invest in SPY plus knowledge of what it means to be leveraged. A choice set
of ETFs that contains nothing but variations on the S&P 500 can wind up being
intimidating(Chernevetal.2015). Such may be the case forrobo-advisorstoday.
4 M ethods
4.1 Human Financial Advisors’Attempt
The robo-“robo-advisor”-advisor already exists: Investing in the Web gives retail
investors a questionnaire to determine which robo-advisors would be right for them.
Inve sting in the Web also has a companion website aptly named Robo-Advisor
Finder.1 This tool can be used as a baseline of professional, educated, experienced
human performance against which to compare LLM performance. As a form of
qualitative research, I explored this tool until I exhausted it of all the advice it could
give, testing different situations and noting any mistakes that it made. At the time
of writing, Investing in the Web’s service has at least three flaws that prevent it
from working effectively: jurisdictional blindness, heterogeneity insensitivity, and
incompleteness.
First, jurisdictional blindness. After filling out the survey, I was suggested four
robo-advisors, none of which would accept me as an American client. Investing
in the Web does not know about FATCA. Nor does it know about the regulations
about Passive Foreign Investment Companies (PFIC)—investing with any of the
companies suggested would likely trigger this tax penalty. I tried once again,
wondering whether Investing in the Web knew about the sanctions imposed on
1 The website for Robo-Advisor Findercanbefoundinhere.

ATheoryofInvestmentSimplificationandanExperimentwithAILarge... 121
investment by Russian citizens and residents. Investing in the Web suggested Sarwa;
Sarwa lists on its website that it does not accept Russian resident clients. Investing
in the Webhasaverylimitedunderstandingofjurisdiction,steeringclientstoward
robo-advisorsthatdonottakethemasclients.
Second, heterogeneity insensitivity. Investing in the Web groups unlike robo-
advisors together, and the minimum investment threshold is a clear example of this.
The lowest minimum investment threshold an investor can specify with Investing in
the Web is “less than 500 [of a currency, e.g. $ or ],” which obscures the distinctions
among robo-advisors with no minimum (e.g., Acorns, SoFi), those with a $100
minimum (e.g., Vanguard Digital Advisor, Ally Invest Robo Portfolios), or a 300
minimum (e.g.,Goodvest,MonPetitPlacement).Itisamistaketopaperoverthese
thresholds. New retail investors may find it intimidating to deposit anything at all
intoanonlineinvestmentaccount,especiallywithaFinTechthatisnotahousehold
namelikeBankofAmericaorBNPParibas.
Third, incompleteness. Investing in the Web does not show France’s largest,
second largest, or third largest robo-advisors (Yomoni, Ramify, and Nalo), and it
isnotclearwhythesewouldbeomitted.
Investing in the Web represents humanity’s attempt at responding to investors’
demand to simplify robo-advisors, and it missed the mark in three ways: jurisdic-
tionalblindness,heterogeneityinsensitivity,andincompleteness.
Creating a complete robo-“robo-advisor”-advisor would clearly help retail
investors navigate the growing complexities of choosing a robo-advisor, but it
will not be easy. Very few financial professionals master the diversity of services
and the jurisdictional headaches that come with the territory of advising financial
services to all the world at once. Nor is any one person, even a team of skilled
professionals, likely to have the encyclopedic knowledge that keeping up-to-date
recordsonhundredsofworldwiderobo-advisorsentails.
In the next section, these shortcomings will be used to create a sophisticated
prompt to give to the AI LLMs. In this way, the responses of the LLMs can be
comparedwiththoseofInvestingintheWeb’shumanfinancialadvisors.

naive and one sophisticated. The naive prompt will ask the LLM to recommend a
robo-advisor in the way a naive, would-be newretailinvestorwouldaskforadvice.

6 Discussion
The human financial advisors’ shortcomings were used as a basis to create a task
against which five of the most popular free LLMs could compete. Because there are
no upfront or switching costs among the LLMs, all that matters is that at least one of
the LLMs is able to solve the task. Only one LLM failed in all of the same ways that
the human financial advisors failed: Microsoft’s Copilot. Three of the five LLMs
beat the human financial advisors in at least onedimension:OpenAI’sChatGPT-4o
mini,Mistral’sLarge2,andGoogle’sGemini.AndoneLLM,Anthropic’sClaude
3.5 Sonnet, solved the task without mistakes when given a sophisticated prompt.
This is surprising. Until recently, this was thought to have been impossible. One
LLMperformedaswellashumans,andfourperformedbetter,withoneperforming
perfectly.

ATheoryofInvestmentSimplificationandanExperimentwithAILarge... 129
The naive prompt did not provoke the LLMs to spontaneously give a complete list
of robo-advisor options or advice concerning an investor’s legal jurisdiction, though
four out of five mentioned that robo-advisors have heterogeneous minimum account
balances. Though the advice varied in length and complexity, only Microsoft’s
Copilot responded to the naiv e prompt with a request for more information. And
thespecific requestCopilotmade,abouttheinvestor’sgoal,isimportanttogiving
goodadvicebuthardlynarrowsdownthelistofoptions.
When given the sophisticated prompt, Anthropic’s Claude provided a complete
list of robo-advisors that cater to a client in a complicated jurisdictional situation
(US citizen non-resident), with appropriate caveats about minimum account balance
heterogeneity, and without any hallucinations. Compared to the other LLMs, which
all delivered hallucinations and which all failed in at least one of the three categories,
Claude’s performance is surprising. However, Claude’s response to the naive prompt
only tackles minimum account balance heterogeneity; it doesnotleadanewretail
investor to consider questions about jurisdiction or to ask for a complete list of
options.Therefore,whileClaudeperformedthebestinthehandsofasophisticated
user, a new retail investor may still struggle to use Claude to find the right robo-
advisorforthem.
To give good advice, a robo-“robo-advisor”-advisor must ask more questions.
To reduce the hundreds of robo-advisors to a manageable list, the best questions to
ask would be those that eliminate many robo-advisors from consideration in as few
questions as possible. Two important questions include the client’s legal jurisdiction
and minimum account balance. The only human-led robo-“robo-advisor”-advisor
effort, Investing in the Web’s Robo-Advisor Finder, poses these two questions,
though the advice the client receives is often inaccurate. Meanwhile, AI LLMs do
notsystematicallyaskthesetwoquestionsorgiveadvicesuchthatthesequestions
need not be asked. Furthermore, even if a sophisticated user brings up these two
questionsindependently,mostLLMsrespondedwithhallucinations.
Anthropic’s Claude stands out as an exception, giving decent advice without
error when given a sophisticated prompt, resulting in a complete list of robo-advisor
options for the user. Claude’s acceptable performance as a robo-“robo-advisor”-
advisorshowsthatsimplifyingrobo-advisorsfurtherstillisnotthefuture,itisthe
now.AIcandoit.
Though the abject failure of Microsoft’s Copilot, which did not meet any
objective in either test and still produced misinformation on top of that, offers
a sober warning to anyone trusting the output of an LLM out of hand. To an
inexperienced judge, the outputs of Claude and of Copilot are indistinguishable.
AIcandoit—buthowcanoneknow?
In addition, new retail investors must also be informed of the availability of
financial instruments such as ETFs or REITs or financial technologies such as
automatic rebalancing and tax-loss harvesting, and they must be given explanations
as to what all of these concepts mean for them. In this respect, neither the non-AI
nor AI options to date fully fill the void of a human financial advisor or a robo-

advisor’s website and sign-up questionnaire. AI LLMs are not currently prepared
to spontaneously teach new retail investors what they really need to know before
openinganinvestmentaccount.
7 Conclusion
For over 100 years, investors have demanded financial services be both simple
and diverse. The result of these two conflicting demands is a cycle of simplifying
financialinnovationfollowedbycomplexifyingcompetition.Astheglobalmiddle
classcontinuestogrow(Chatterjee2020) and stock market participation continues
to rise (Bogan 2008), new investors with less capital and financial literacy enter
the arena of investment. Inheriting the lineage from mutual funds to index funds to
ETFs, robo-advisors are the most recent link in the chain of financial technology
simplifying scientific diversification—but surely not the last. Now that there are
hundreds of robo-advisors competing in different legal jurisdictions and with many
complicated services, a new need has arisen to simplify the search for robo-advisors.
For the moment, this is a rather specific niche. If this advice is to exist at scale, a
machine wo uld have to give it. While a traditional database of robo-advisors may
suffice, this need for another layer of simplification happens to coincide with the
popularization of AI. Can AI LLMs be the robo-“robo-advisor” advisor? Can AI
meettheneed?ThispapershowsthatatleastoneLLMcan.Andsincethereareno
upfrontorswitchingcostsforusingthisLLM,“atleastone”isenough.
All this indicates that the new role of robo-“robo-advisor”-advisor might be best
filled by a “boutique” AI LLM trained specifically to give financial advice. Current-
gen AI LLMs that new retail investors are likely to use are all general purpose. But
from the consumer’s perspective, all that may be necessary to solve the question
ofAItrustworthinessisastrongsignalofitsdomain-specificcompetence(Loand
Ross2024). Examples of these such “boutique” AIs have been popping up all over
industry, from traditional finance behemoths such as Moody’s Research Assistant
to small FinTech startups such as Odonatech’s LiLa. One or another may one day
becomethereference.
Acemoglu and Restrepo (2018) indicate three broad effects of technology:
reinstatement (creating jobs), productivity, and displacement (removing jobs). In
this chapter, the effect of AI was to displace the team behind Investing in the
Web’s Robo-Advisor Finder. Though it may make robo-advisors more productive
as LLMs funnel investors into more appropriate wealth managers. And as apositive
externality,financialmarketswouldbecomeincrementallymoreproductivedueto
increased liquidity. To say nothing of the marginal investor who uses an LLM to
startinvesting.
In living memory, robo-advisors shook up the financial advice industry, stoking
fears among financial advisors that algorithms would put them all out of work.
Somewhereincyberspace,AIhasgivenarobo-advisorachilldownitsspine.

Part III
Regulation, Compliance, and Risk
Management

Identifying and Ranking the Eight Risks
of AI for Each o f the Six Main
AI-Focused Fintech Business Models
Alex Zarifis and Xusen C heng
Abstract This research explores the implications for risk of six AI-focused Fintech
business models identified in the previous research. While each of the six business
models has been validated in previous research, their typical influence on risk has
notbeensufficientlyexplored.
A Delphi method with two stages is used. In the first stage, the semi-structured
interviews with experts identify the main risks each of the six models faces. For the
second stage the participants are presentedwithasummaryofalltherisksidentified
byalltheparticipants,andtheyareaskedtorankthemfortheirspecificmodel.
Eight risks related to the application of an AI-focused business model are
identified: (1) direct AI risks, (2) technology integration risk, (3) third-party vendor
risk, (4) technology infrastructure risk, (5) data protection and privacy risk, (6)
cybersecurity risk, (7) fraud and identity theft risk, and (8) strategic misalignment
risk.Theeightrisksapplytoallsixmodels;however,theyarenotequallysignificant

The six business models reduce risk in two main ways: Firstly, because they
are proven models and secondly because they have a proven place in the ty pical

1 Introd uction
AI in robo-advisors and elsewhere in financial institutions bring risks that must
be addressed at the business model level. Fintech has reduced risks and crime
in the physical world, but increased technology-related risks such as cybercrime
(Jain et al. 2023). Financial institutions are not only faced with technology that is
changing rapidly but rapid change across the environment they operate in. The rate
of change and the fact that it often has far -reachingimplicationsmeansthatfinancial
institutionsneedtoadapttheirbusinessmodelfarmoreregularlythanintherecent
past(Jorziketal.2024). Business model innovation needs an understanding of the
process of changing a business model, and what business models typically work
(Tucci 2022). Failure to innovate in the best way can cause long-term damage
and make future attempts harder (Välikangas et al. 2009). With these fundamental
changes to technology and the broader environment financial institutions need
to identify a new business model that addresses the many challenges while not
increasing risk. The risk still comes from all the usual sources but the lack of a
shared vision at many levels is increasing risk. This lack of a shared vision is
partly due to competing visions, but it is also due to a lack of clarity on what an
organization’s business model should be in five years’ time and what the sectors
of the economy they are engaged in will look like in five years’ time. Therefore,
havingclarityonthebusinessmodelnotonlyhelpsinternallyinimplementingthe
operationsbutalsoexternallyincreatingasharedvision.Theimplicationsforrisk
of the Fintech business model chosen must be merged into the vision. If a shared
visionisnotpossibleatleastithelpsthestakeholdersunderstandtheorganization’s
futuremodelandadapt.
When the pace of change was slower most financial institutions gradually
evolved, with more dramatic changes to the business model such as pivots to
something new much rarer. The primary consideration was to continue to utilize
the skills and capabilities within the organization. With the technologies today,
especially AI with its near-infinite scalability, the main driver behind the choice
of business model is no longer what the existing skills and capabilities are. The
key driver behind a business model now is to identify the best business model
for the current environment irrespective of what the current capabilities are. The
most obvious example is from outside finance, but it illustrates this point clearly:
Elon Musk bought Twitter and changed its business model from the first week.
He was not motivated by what the current strengths of Twitter were, such as
moderating discussions, but he was primarily motivated by what the best business
model would be for today. Whether Elon Must is right or wrong time will tell but
thedecisiveredesignofthebusinessmodelisnecessaryinthefast-changingworld.
Organizations must be prepared for a purposeful leap to a new model, not just a
gradualevolution.
The slower and less far-reaching change in the past meant there was more time
to understand the risks directly and indirectly affecting an organization. The role
oftechnologywassmallerandmorepredictablethanAI.Now,duetotheneedfor

IdentifyingandRankingtheEightRisksofAIforEachoftheSixMainAI... 139
more regular strategic adjustments, there is a need to have a broader understanding
of risk and understand how changes to the business model can affect it. Both AI
and the broader environment can be very unpredictable. While the capabilities of
AI are irrefutable, there is a trade-off between more predictable and transparent
AI and unleashing AI’s full capabilities but losing some control, predictability, and
transparency. In terms of the broader environment, after a period where countries
hadadegreeofbuy-intosomekindofsharedvisionofglobalizationthereseemsto
befarlessagreementonasharedvision.Theimportanceofriskismultifacetedas
understandingitbettercansupportotherkeydecisionsrelatingtosustainabilityof
theorganizationandbuildingtrust.
This research explores the implications for risk of six AI-focused financial
business models identified in previous research (Zarifis and Cheng 2024). These
business models reduce risk firstly because they have been repeatedly proven to be
effective and secondly because they have a provenplaceinthetypicalecosystems
thatemerge.Therefore,theresearchquestionsare:
How do the six prominent AI-focused financial bu sinessmodelsinfluencerisk?
What are the most important risks for each of the si x prominent AI-focused
financialbusinessmodels?
The six AI-focused finance business models as identified by previous research
are (1) disaggregate, concentrate on a reduced number of financial services and
a smaller part of the value chain, (2) keep business model unchanged and absorb
AI into existing processes, (3) incumbent in finance expanding beyond their current
model, (4)dedicatedfinancedisruptor,typicallyastartup,(5)techcompanyoffering
financial services, and (6) disruptor not focused on technology with large user-
base offering new financial services (Zarifis 2025). The first three models involve
organizations that have been offering financial services for many years. The last
three involve organizations that did not off er financial services in the past but are
utilizingthecapabilitiesofAItostartofferingthem.
Eight risks related to the application of an AI-focused business model are
identified. These are (1) direct AI risks, (2) technology integration risk, (3) third-
party vendor risk, (4) technology infrastructure risk, (5) data protection and privacy
risk, (6) cybersecurity risk, (7) fraud and identity theft risk, and (8) strategic
misalignment risk. The second stage of the data collection asked participants to
ranktheeightrisksfortheirspecificbusinessmodel.Theeightrisksapplytoallsix
models;however,theirsignificanceisdifferentforeachmodel.
This research finds that the six business models do indeed offer clarity and
reduce several risks. Clarity on the business model reduces risk. While the Fintech
business models do not necessarily increase risk and may indeedreduceit,because
ofthechange inthenatureoftheriskinvolved,trustneeds tobebuiltwithallthe
stakeholders.
The next section is the theoretical foundation that covers three main areas. This
is followed by the methodology section that explains how the qualitative Delphi
method with two stages is implemented. This is followed by the findings, the
discussion and conclusion and finally the limitations and suggestions for future
research.

2 Theoretical Framewo rk
This research is guided by two broad areas of literature, digital transformation and
business model innovation, and the traditional and emerging risks in Finance and
Fintech. Based on this literature, an existing framework with the six AI focused
Fintechbusinessmodelsisadoptedandfurtherdeveloped.
2.1 Digital Transformation and Business Mo delInnovation
Digital transformation does not always necessitate business model innovation but as
the scale of disruption in finance is very high, transformation and business model
innovation are increasingly coming together (Liu et al. 2025). The organization
offering financial services must understand the implications of the transformation
and model innovation so that they can implement the changes to their organization
butalso,sotheyfullyunderstandwhattheirexisting,andemergingcompetitorsare
doing.
Digital transformation in finance is indeed drivenbyAI(Jorziketal.2024), but
more fundamentally it is driven by the sharing and processing of information which
is happening atalargerscalethanbefore(WuandPambudi2025).
While some argue that if one element of a business model is changing this can be
considered as business model innovation, this term isusuallyreservedforsignificant
changes that go beyond a gradual evolution (Tucci 2022). Companies offering
financial services for the first time, and existing insurers automating services and
calculating risk in a different way, certainly qualify as business model innovation.
Many of the typical building blocks of a model are being transformed. The typical
examples of business model building blocks are (1) va luepropositions,(2)customer
relationships, (3) customer segments, (4) channels, (5) cost structure, (6) revenue
streams,(7)keypartnerships,(8)keyactivities,(9)keyresources(Osterwalderand
Pigneur2010).
2.2 The Traditional and Emerging Risks in Fi nance
andFintech
There is a broad variety of risks that can impact a Fintech from those very closely
monitored such as the various financial risks to the less closely monitored risks such
as pandemics, often referred to as black swan events. While the wide variety of risks
should not be ignored, when looking at the effect of Fintech business models on
risk, therisksmorecloselyrelatedtothechoiceofbusinessmodelandtheprocess
of implementing that business model should be prioritized. These are risks that
have been either reduced or increased by the choice of business model. Framing

IdentifyingandRankingtheEightRisksofAIforEachoftheSixMainAI... 141
the most closely related risks in this way means focusing on the Fintech business
model risks. This is cover edmostlyinliteratureonFintech,riskandbusinessmodel
risk(Brillingeretal.2020; Dellermann et al.2017).
There is evidence that not going through the digital transformation causes risks
related to operating in an outdated inefficient way. While business model innovation
traditionally benefitted from a high tolerance to risk in this disruptive period, the
risks of not acting ma yevenbelarger.Atthesametime,theincreaseduseofFintech
hasbeenfoundtoincreaserisktakingbyanorganization(Tangetal.2024).
Literature on Fintech risk identifies five types of closely related risks (Tyagi
2024). These are technology, operational, compliance, strategic, and reputational
risks. These five topics capture the key risks for a Fintech that is heavily reliant on
AI. Beyondresearchpublicationsthesearehottopicspractitioners,andtheindustry
pressoftencoverthem.
The business model innovation in finance is primarily driven by trying to fully
utilize AI. Therefore, the new business model also brings with it a new relationship
with AI with all the benefits and new risks this involves. Given the increasing
volume of personal data processed, the increased ability to draw insight and the
increasedabilitytoactonthatinsightthereareincreasedprivacyconcernsandrisks
fortrust(Canhotoetal.2023).
2.3 The Six AI-Focused Fintech Business Models andNine
BuildingBlocks
In finance, it could be argued that all organizations in this area will meet the criteria
of a Fintech soon as the dependence on AI is constantly increasing and financial
technologyischangingbusinessmodels(Eliaetal.2023). While this may be true,
there is still a useful distinction to be made between a more traditional financial
organization with many offices, branches and many staff, and a leaner Fintech with
less offices and staff and a higher dependence on technology. Fintechs are also
typically created from the start with a business model designed to make the most
outofarecenttechnology.
Business models are defined in a variety of ways (Tucci 2022). This lack of
consensus is not necessarily a bad thing as some definitions of business models
are more useful in some situations and others in other situations. Even within an
organization there might be disagreement on what the business model is. While
the many different approaches should be welcomed, it must be made clear which
approachisbeingtakenandwhy.
So that this research can evaluate the influence of a business model on risk in
Fintech the prevailing business models need to be identified first. This research
adopts six business models of Fintechs identified in previous research so that the
implications of the business model to risk can be explored. This list has been
updated recently so it should be representative of most organizations in this area.

142 A.ZarifisandX.Cheng
The six Fintech business models are (1) disaggregate, concentrate on a reduced
number of financial services and a smaller part of the value chain, (2) keep business
model unchanged and absorb AI into existing processes, (3) incumbent in finance
expanding beyond their current model, (4) dedicated finance disruptor, typically a
startup, (5) tech company offering financial services, (6) disruptor not focused on
technologywithlargeuser-baseofferingnewfinancialservices(Zarifis2025;Zarifis
andCheng2024).
The first three models include organizations that are already active in the financial
sector. The last three models are organizations that were not involved in finance in
the pastbuthaveusedAIandothernewtechnologiestoofferservicestheycouldn’t
inthepast.Figure1 illustrates the similarities and differences of thesesixmodels.
3 M ethodology
This research attempts to capture the perspective of the experts working in Fintech
organizations and not other stakeholders, such as the consumers or shareholders.
The qualitative Delphi method is helpful in reaching a consensus among experts.
The Delphi method has been used extensively to gain consensus on the use of
technology (Gallego and Bueno 2014; Joia and Sily de Assis 2019), financial
innovation (Pengetal.2014), and business models (Effendietal.2024).
This research uses the Delphi method with two stages. In the first stage, the semi-
structured interviews with experts identify the main risks each of the six models
faces. For the second stage the researchers present the same participants with a
summary of all the risks identified by all the participants, and they are asked ifthey
want to revise their list of risks and if they can rank them from most serious, to
least serious. The Nvivo software was used to analyse the transcribed interviews
andidentifythemainthemes.
With this method this research can extend the research on the six AI-focused
Fintech business models. While each of the six business models has been validated
and ex plainedextensivelyinpreviousresearchtheirtypicalinfluenceonriskhasnot
beensufficientlyexplored(Fig.2).
The data collection had to ensure that the semi-structured interview participants
were professionals who had experience with one of the six AI-focused business
models. For th is reason, participants who worked for Fintech companies that
matchedoneofthesixmodelswereapproached.
Fintechs are heavily influenced by the geographic region they are active in, due to
several reasons such as the local regulation and culture. For this reason, companies
from one country, China, were targeted. While innovation in technology and finance
can come from many different places in the modern world, China is one of the
leaders in innovation in this area. Chinese Fintechs can be considered among the
mostadvancedintermsoftechnologyandbusinessmodels.

4  Findings
The purpose of the analysis is to identify and rank the main risks for each business
model. For each model the participants were asked about risks across technology,
operational, compliance, strategic, and reputational risks. These five categories of
riskareconsideredthemostsuitableforFintech(Tyagi2024). Eight risks related to
the application of an AI-focused business model are identified. These are (1) direct
AI risks, (2) technology integration risk, (3) third-party vendor risk, (4) technology
infrastructure risk, (5) data protection and privacy risk, (6) cybersecurity risk, (7)
fraud and identity theft risk, and (8) strategic misalignment risk. The eight risks
applytoallsixmodels;however,theyarenotequallysignificantinallmodels.
The second stage of the data collection asked participants to rank the eight
risks for their specific business model. Managers and their organizations have finite
resources so knowing which riskstoprioritizeisbeneficial.Therisksidentifiedfor
eachofthesixbusinessmodelsarediscussedhere.
4.1  The First Fintech Business Model and Its Risks: Foc us
onLessFinancialServicesandDisaggregate
The first business model relies heavily on an external value chain while only doing
a small part of the value chain internally. This characteristic of the first business
modelinfluencesmanyoftherisks.

146 A.ZarifisandX.Cheng
4.1.1 Direct AI Risks
There is a danger of basing financial and other decisions on inaccurate data. The
increased automation and the lack of face-to-face interaction can have a detrimental
effect on the quality of the data. One participant gave the example of the many
problems with people entering false information during the onboarding process.
While this usually stops short of becoming a security threat or a threat of fraud,
the false information is still processed leading to a skewed understanding. Given the
many partners involved, they may all allow some inaccurate information into the
ecosystem. Given the complexity of the ecosystem, it is hard to identify and fix the
problems with the data. One participant stated:
The onboarding needs speed, no security vulnerability, and OK for regulation, the range of
the data we get for analysis is not important.. . the wrong data from the onboarding makes
worse analysis.
Data sovereignty is one of the most important issues when trying to achieve
accurate and reliable results with AI. AI trained on a data set with very different
characteristics to the one it is analysing now may not make the best decisions.
For example, AI trained in one region, may not come to the best decisions with
data that is very different to what it was trained on. Using blockchain as a shared
infrastructure can provide clear provenance for the data across the ecosystem. One
participant stated:
who owns the datafortheAI,whoisallowedtochangeit,partnersshouldagreeonthethis
Artificial intelligence-driven risk assessment: AI is being used to personalized
financial products and calculate clients credit scoring. These processes have all
the typical risks of using AI, but some are more profound. Typical issues around
dataqualityarecompounded bythelackoftransparencyandcanleadtobreaches
of regulations and laws. The risks can be mitigated with more use of human
oversight, explainable AI, governance frameworks, guardrails, and quality checks.
Theseremediescanbehardertoimplementinabroadlydistributedecosystem.One
participantsaid:
Someprocessesarenotverysensitive,wecanrejectaclient,weareallowedtodothat,we
havenoobligation,otherprocessesaremoresensitive,veryregulatedorfinanciallyhigh
risk.AIautomatingriskassessmentandAIusingdifferentcriteriaaredifferent,ifclient
facingthenmustbemorecareful.
4.1.2 Technology Integration Risk
The Fintech ecosystem of many organizations is also a technology ecosystem with
many nodes that depend on each other to function properly. A problem in one of
the ecosystem’s nodes can cause the whole ecosystem to stop functioningproperly.
There needs to be alignment across the whole technology stack if possible. Using
blockchain as a shared infrastructure can reduce several risks when integrating
technology.

4.1.3 Third-Party Ve ndorRisk
This model creates a company narrowly focused on one part of the value chain such
as validating the identity of the clients. By specializing in one narrow part of the
value chain they can become very good at it and become a very appealing partner
to many organizations in the financial ecosystem. This strategy has a similar logic
to the very widely adopted strategy from IT of having the ‘best of breed’ for each
system. However, with the large number of partners, and the limited control over
them,thethird-partyriskincreases.Securityvulnerabilitiesoroutagesoftencome
from third-party vendors. These vulnerabilities often cause problems and are not
limitedtothehighprofilecasessuchastheoutagecausedbyCrowdstrikein2024.
There is often extensive jurisdictional fragmentation. This fragmentation can
mean that some members of the ecosystem are not fully aware o f the risks that
comefromthethird-partyvendorstheirpartnersuse.
Fintechs should take the security record of potential partners into account and
have contracts that require anyissuetobereportedacrosstheecosystem.
4.1.4 Technology Infrastructure Risk
Organizations trying to increase security and reduce the risks in their infrastructure
often find themselves in the situation where they have achieved strong internal
controls, but have less control over their external value chain. Keeping the shared
infrastructure secure can be more challenging than keeping the internal systems
secure. On the other hand, modern technologies can also offer solutions for this
model.Forexample,newpartnerscaneasilybeaddedtotheecosystembyutilizing
theblockchaininfrastructuretoshareinformation.
4.1.5 Data Protection and Priv acyRisk
Given that most people nowadays interact with Fintech on their phone and prove
their identity with the fingerprint, protecting this biometric data is very important.
There are different privacy requirements across different countries. EU countries
are far stricter than most other countries. For a distributed ecosystem this presents
challenges. The most common solution is to follow the strictest standards in
the ecosystem. Data and privacy governance frameworks, traceability and privacy
enhancingtechnologiescanhelp.
4.1.6 Cybersecurity Risk
Fintechs are very attractive targets for cybercriminals because of the money and data
they have. Unfortunately, with financial services there is atrade-offbetweensecurity
and accessibility, so some vulnerability is probably inevitable. Cybercriminals are

148 A.ZarifisandX.Cheng
skilled at identifying and targeting the weakness in a complex process, implemented
byacomplexecosystemoforganizations.
In many countries it is a regulatory requirement to report breaches. In addition to
this, the nature of the attacks, with many ransomware attacks, makes them public.
These breaches have become almost in evitable, and the effort is on limiting the
damage caused. Breaches can come from applications used, file transfer systems,
andcloudhosting.
4.1.7 Fraud and Identity T heftRisk
Financial institutions collect a lot of sensitive information. There is not only
sensitive information collected on customers such as their passport number, but
many insights can be deduced by how the customers spend their money. For
example, if someone looks at how a person spends their money over a month,
they can often draw insight about their current health based on medicines they
buy , and future health based on their eating habits. As this information is spread
acrosstheecosystem,theriskofitleakingoutandenablingfraudandidentitytheft
increases.Keepingdatasecureismorechallengingacrossanextensivelydistributed
ecosystem.

4.2.1 Direct AI Risks
If AI is adapted to existing processes, it may not be fully utilized. The existing
workflows were created in that way to fit the technology available at the time. This
raises the key question of whether the existing processes are worth retaining. If
the existing p rocesses are retained, then the current roles and people may also be
retained.Thiscancreateasituationwheretheorganizationispartlyoperatingwith
anoldmodelandpartlywithanewmodel.
The positive side of retaining some staff and existing processes is that they
can shape the new AI implementations with their experience and knowledge. For
example, an organization’s s taffusuallyknowtheircustomersbetterthananybody.
ThiscanreducetheriskofanAIimplementation.
4.2.2 Technology Integration Risk
The technical challenges may seem less, as it is more a case of evolution than
revolution, but the connections between the old and new infrastructure can be
fragile and cause problems. Maintenance may be more complicated and scaling
the operations in the future may be harder. The way legacy processes typically use
data and the way AI uses data are different. Legacy processes can involve several
complicated steps including manual decisions that prevent AI from functioning to
itsfullpotential.Oneparticipantsaid:

5 Discussion and Conclusion
The six business models discussed here are on a high level of abstraction and easy
to understand. However, when we look at the implications for risk of these business
models, things quickly become very complicated. In most cases, the risks are not
necessarily problems to be solved but delicate balances. While cybersecurity can
indeedbeseenasaproblemtosolve,inmostofthecases,theriskandthereward
cometogether.
The six AI-focused finance business models as identified by previous research
are (1) disaggregate, concentrate on a reduced number of financial services and
a smaller part of the value chain, (2) keep business model unchanged and absorb
AI into existing processes, (3) incumbent in finance expanding beyond their current
model,(4)dedicatedfinancedisruptor,typicallyastartup,(5)techcompanyoffering
financial services, (6) disruptor not focused on technology with large user-base
offering new financial services (Zarifis 2025). The first three models involve
organizations that have been offering financial services for many years. The last
three involve organizations that did not off er financial services in the past but are
utilizingthecapabilitiesofAItostartofferingthem.
Eight risks related to the application of an AI-focused business model are
identified. These are (1) direct AI risks, (2) technology integration risk, (3) third-
party vendor risk, (4) technology infrastructure risk, (5) data protection and privacy
risk, (6) cybersecurity risk, (7) fraud and identity theft risk, and (8) strategic
misalignment risk. The second stage of the data collection asked participants to
ranktheeightrisksfortheirspecificbusinessmodel.Theeightrisksapplytoallsix
models;however,theirsignificanceisdifferentforeachmodel.
5.1 Contribution to Theory
This research focuses on the impact of the choice of AI-focused business model on
risks. Initially the role o fabroadrangeofrisksacrossfinancial,legal,security,and
operational(Ryu2018) are explored. This research finds support for eight prominent
types of risk across all six Fintech business models. This suggests that these eight
types ofriskareusuallypresentwhenaFintechadaptstouseAImoreextensively.
Additionally, the experts interviewed came to an agreement ranking the signifi-
cance of the eight risks for their specific business model. This extends the literature
on the six AI-focused Fintech business models to also cover the typical risks that
come directly from how they apply AI. The areas of research on Fintech business
modelsandriskarelinked.

166 A.ZarifisandX.Cheng
5.2 Contribution to Practice
These findings are useful for companies that would identify themselves as Fintechs
and other financial organizations that rely heavily on AI. For financial institutions
the risks they were preoccupied with in the past were financial, and the solutions
to these risks were also financial, such as limiting credit. However, now one of the
main sources of risk is the AI used, and the solutions are not simply financial. The
solutions are not just about credit models but need to start at the business model
level. The Fintech leadership must integrate riskmanagementintothegoals,sothey
are not seen as competing priorities. This integrated approach will align values,
improveawarenessandengagement.AriskculturethatfitsthespecificAI-focused
business model can be created and this can lead to a resilient culture. A narrow
approach to risk management, not proactively shaping the AI focused business
modelisnotthewayforward.
While the Fintech business models do not necessarily increase risk and may
indeed reduce it, because of the change in the nature of the risk involved, trust needs
to be built with all the stakeholders. A Fintech can identify one of the six business
models that fits them, or a combination of two or more business models that captures
what they do. Based on their model, they can use the eight most importantrisksto
adapt their plans and constantly audit their implementation of AI. This research
enables Fintechs to target their finite resources more effectively to reduce risk.
Having thelinkbetween riskmanagement and thebusiness model, and constantly
developingbothtogethermeansthereislesschanceofunpleasantsurprises.
6 Limitations and Future Research
This research utilizes qualitative data collection from experts working in Fintech to
evaluate the typical risks when applying AI. This research extended research on six
AI-focused Fintech models. Future research can further extend these six business
modelsbyfocusingoneachoneindividuallyortestingtheminotherareas.

Regulatory and Compliance Issues
in AI-Drive n Financial Services
Narmin Nahidi
Abstract This section examines how regulation shapes the design, operation, and
oversight of AI-enabled and automated investment services (“robo-advice”) across
leading jurisdictions and distills the practical implications for firms building or
scaling these models. We map convergence among functional regulators the U.S.
Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), the UK Financial Conduct Authority
(FCA), the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), and the Monetary
Authority of Singapore (MAS)—showing that automation does not create a “lite”
regime: fiduciary/suitability duties, fair marketing rules, technology and outsourcing
controls, and record-keeping apply with equal or greater intensity when advice is
delivered by algorithms. Horizontally, the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act
(DORA) and AI Act tighten governance, transparency, and resilience expectations
that directly touch model development, deployment, monitoring, and rollback. We
translate these frameworks into operational control sets data capture and suitability
mapping (including sustainability preferences in Europe), model governance and
change control, performance and “AI” claim substantiation, digital engagement
practice (DEP) inventories, third-party/cloud oversight, and audit-grade books and
records illustratingeachwithrealenforcementandsupervisoryfindings.Thesection
also explores how to balance innovation and investor protection using sandboxes,
“targeted support”/simplified advice initiatives in the UK, outcomes testing under
the Consumer Duty, and DORA-style resilience drills, so product teams can
iterate safely. Case studies (Schwab cash floors; Wealthfront/Hedgeable feature
and marketing claims; Titan’s hypothetical performance controls; Betterment’s
TLHdisclosures;SoFiconflicts;SEC“AI-washing”)showrecurringfailuremodes
and durable fixes: promise carefully, evidence continuously, explain plainly, and
remediatefast.Theoverarchingmessageispractical:buildtothestrictestcommon
denominator across markets, wire compliance into the release pipeline, and treat

1 Intro duction
AI is now embedded across retail investing and wealth management, with robo-
advisers delivering onboarding, suitability assessment, portfolio construction, rebal-
ancing, and client updates through fully digital journeys. Regulators have largely
mapped these journeys onto existing investor-protection regimes rather than creating
bespoke robo rules from scratch. In practice, that means U.S. advisers (including
robo-platforms) operate under the Advisers Act’s fiduciary and anti-fraud standards;
UK firms face outcome-focused duties culminating in the FCA’s Consumer Duty;
EU firms must meet MiFID II suitability requirements updated by ESMA; and Sin-
gapore’s MAS applies a technology-agnostic licensing and conduct framework tai-
lored by pragmatic guidance for digitaladvisers.Acrosstheseregimes,thethemes
arestrikinglyconsistent:robustclientprofilingandevidencablesuitability;accurate,
balanced marketing (including tight controls for hypothetical performance and
honest“AI”claims);documentedalgorithmgovernance;andoperationalresilience
withvendor/Cloudoversight.Thischapterbuildsonthosepillarsandframeswhat
“good”lookslikeinday-to-dayproduct,model,legal,andcompliancework.
In the United States, robo-advisers are simply investment advisers, so the same
fiduciary duty and anti-fraud provisions apply to automated services and human
advisers alike. Recent SEC actions show where digital models and marketing
most often slip. The Schwab Intelligent Portfolios settlement in 2022 turned on
disclosures that did not plainly convey how mandated cash allocations could depress
expected returns; the three subsidiaries paid $187 million in disgorgement and
penalties, and the case became a touchstone for aligning algorithm economics
with client-facing language. The SEC’s ongoing Marketing Rule sweeps (since
2023) and the Titan case underscore that hypothetical performance shown to broad
audiences without strict controls is a violation; record-keeping, audience gating,
and net-of-fees presentation are now non-negotiable mechanics for any growth
team.Andin2024,theCommissionfinedDelphiaandGlobalPredictionsfor“AI-
washing,”makingclearthatclaimsaboutAIcapabilitiesaremarketingstatements
subject to the anti-fraud rule, like any other. If you say a model “does X,”
you must be able to prove it. Together, these actions set the U.S. perimeter for
robocompliance: don’t oversell the model, don’t misuse performance metrics, and
ensuredisclosuresmatchhowthealgorithmreallybehaves.

RegulatoryandComplianceIssuesinAI-DrivenFinancialServices 171
The United Kingdom has taken an outcomes-based approach that treats automa-
tion as part of normal business rather than a special case. The FCA’s 2018 multi-firm
review of automated investment services flagged weaknesses in profiling, suitability
evidence, and support for vulnerable customers; those gaps are amplified in click-
through experiences where firms may collect too little information or lean too hard
on defaults. Since July 2023, the Consumer Duty has raised the bar again: firms must
design and distribute products and communications that deliver “good outcomes,”
which squarely covers risk-profiling journeys, portfolio templates, nudges, and post-
sale support. Parallel policy work on the Advice–Guidance Boundary is creating
a pathway for “targeted support” and simplified advice so firms can serve mass-
market consumers without compromising protections; robo teams should monitor
these consultations to scope constrained-advice flows with clear eligibility rules,
human fallback, and audit trails. The direction of travel is clear: automation is
welcome, provided firms can demonstrate suitability, fair value, and accessible
communicationsintheround.
Across the European Union, MiFID II suitability remains the anchor for advice,
including algorithmic advice, while horizontal digital rules now bite operationally.
ESMA’s 2022–2023 suitability guidelines clarify how firms must gather and
use client information on knowledge/experience, risk tolerance, capacity for loss,
objectives, and (since 2022) sustainability preferences, and how those inputs should
flow through tools and recommendations. Two EU-wide frameworks now sit
alongside: the AI Act, which entered into force on 1 August 2024 with phased
application through 2025–2027 (including obligations for general-purpose AI from
August 2025 and full application in August 2026); and DORA, applicable from
17January2025,whichhardensICTriskmanagement,incidentreporting,testing,
andthird-partyoversightforfinancialentities.Forrobo-advisers,thattranslatesinto
day-to-dayobligationsaroundmodeldocumentationandchangecontrol,resilience
and failover testing, cloud/vendor governance, and clear, accessible disclosures,
especiallywhensustainabilitypreferencesdriveportfolioconstruction.
Singapore provides a concise, principle-based template that many Asia-Pacific
(APAC) markets reference. MAS’s Guidelines on the Provision of Digital Advisory
Services clarify licensing under the Securities and Futures Act/Financial Advisers
Act, set expectations for algorithm governance and back-testing, require ongoing
monitoring, and mandate human escalation paths for edge cases while keeping
the framework technology-agnostic so innovation isn’t chilled. MAS couples this
with a pragmatic stance on outsourcing and technology-risk controls, reflecting the
reality that robo-platforms depend on APIs and cloud prov iders;firmsmustevidence
vendorduediligence,performancemonitoring,dataprotection,andexitplans.The
net effect is a rules-light but expectations-clear environment: if a digital adviser
claims it can profile, recommend, and rebalance appropriately, it must be able to
showitsworkinglicenseinplace,modelsdocumented,controlslive,andcustomers
supported.
A fast-emerging cross-cutting issue is digital conduct the way app design,
prompts, and behavioral nudges embedded in digital financial platforms shape
investorbehavior.Internationally,IOSCOhasexaminedDigitalEngagementPrac-

highlighting how they can increase trading, leverage, or risk-taking if not governed.
The FCA has run controlled experiments showing that DEPs can materially

on customer understanding and foreseeable harm. For robo-advisers, this means
inventorying every engagement element across onboarding, portfolio selection, and

Enforcement history provides practical design lessons that teams can apply
immediately. The SEC’s first robo actions (Wealthfront and Hedgeable, 2018)
targeted false statements about tax-loss-harvesting controls and misleading perfor-
mance advertising, reminding firms that automation does not dilute the requirement
to be fair, clear, and not misleading. The 2023 Titan case and the 2023–2024
Marketing Rule sweeps cemented operational expectations for hypothetical per-
formance (audience gating, records, net-of-fees), which many growth teams had
historically under-engineered. And the 2024 “AI-washing” cases against Delphia
andGlobalPredictionstranslatecleanlytotoday’senvironment:inventoryyourAI

or advantage. A robust archive of marketing materials, model-change logs, and

An effective way to reconcile innovation with investor protection is to treat
compliance as product design. Embed legal, compliance, and model-risk spe-
cialists into sprints; maintain end-to-end documentation (data lineage, features,
training/validation, performance bounds, challenger models); define human-in-the-
loop triggers, particularly for vulnerable customers or edge-case recommendations;
and test resilience under DORA-style scenarios, including cloud outages and API
breaks. Align all client-facing statements with reality, especially “AI” claims, and
run pre-clearance for performance illustrations under the SEC Marketing Rule or
local equiv alents. As the EU AI Act phases in and DORA applies, and as the
FCAtightensexpectationsundertheConsumerDuty,firmsthatinstitutionalizethis
“compliance-by-design” approach will scale faster and safer across jurisdictions
becausetheycanshow,notjusttell,howtheirsystemsdeliversuitableadvice,robust
operations,andfairoutcomes.
2 Global Regulations on Robo-Advisory (S EC, FCA,ESMA,
MAS)
Across major markets, there is no “lite” regime for robo-advisors, the same investor-
protection rules that govern traditional advisers apply to automated services, with

RegulatoryandComplianceIssuesinAI-DrivenFinancialServices 173
extra scrutiny on how algorithms are designed, monitored, and explained. In
the United States, robo-platforms are investment advisers under the Inv estment
Advisers Act, owing fiduciary and anti-fraud duties alongside compliance and
recordkeeping obligations (SEC, 2022b). The UK’s Financial Conduct Authority
(FCA) supervises automated advice and online discretionary investment manage-
ment under outcomes-based principles,nowelevatedbytheConsumerDuty(FCA,
2022). In the European Union, MiFID II suitability rules refreshed by ESMA gove rn
profiling and recommendations whether human- or algorithm-delivered (ESMA,
2022). Singapore’s MAS sets a technology-agnostic framework that pairs licensing
withspecificexpectationsfordigitaladvisorycontrols(MAS,2018b). Conceptually,
this alignment reflects the academic view that robo-advice should be re gulated by
function,notform(Baker&Dellaert,2019).
In the U.S., the practical regulatory perimeter is defined as much by enforce-
ment as by statutes and formal rules. Robo-advisers must make accurate Form
ADV disclosures, operate under the Compliance Rule, and comply with the
Marketing Rule when using testimonials, endorsements, or any hypothetical or
back-tested performance (SEC, 2022b). Early enforcement actions against robo-
advisory platforms highlighted recurring compliance weaknesses. In 2018, the SEC
brought actions against Wealthfront and Hedgeable for misleading statements and
insufficient controls, including issues related to tax-loss harvesting claims, client
testimonials,andperformancecomparisons(SEC,2018). Subsequent enforcement
actions continued to emphasize similar risks, including cases involving SoFi Wealth,
Schwab Intelligent Portfolios, and Titan Global Capital Management concerning
conflictsofinterest,undisclosedportfolioallocationeffects,andmisleadinghypo-
thetical performance claims (SEC, 2018, 2022b, 2023, 2024). More recently, the
SEC pursued “AI-washing” actions against Delphia and Global Predictions for
misleading statements reg arding the use of artificial intelligence in investment
processes (SEC, 2024). The operational lesson for U.S. robo-advisory firms is
consistent: disclosures must align with actual model behavior, performance claims
must be substantiated, and any AI-related representation should be treated as a
regulatedstatementrequiringverifiableevidence.
The UK approach treats automation as business as usual but demands robust
evidence that retail clients receive suitable recommendations and fair value across
the full digital journey. The FCA’s multi-firm review of automated investment
services highlighted ga ps in data capture, suitability evidence, and support for
vulnerable customers, weaknesses that can widen in click-through experiences
if firms rely on defaults or shallow questionnaires (FCA, 2018). Since 2023,
the Consumer Duty has made “good outcomes” the standard for product design,
communications, and support, which squarelycoversrisk-profilingtools,portfolio
templates,nudges,andpost-saleprompts(FCA,2022). Parallel policy work on the
advice–guidance boundary seeks to enable “targeted support” and simplified advice
journeys without diluting protections, a live track that robo teams should monitor
whenscopingconstrained-scopeusecases(FCA&(Dasgupta,2021;FCA,2 024).
Within the EU, MiFID II suitability remains the anchor while horizontal digital
rules now shape day-to-day model operations. ESMA’s 2022 guidance clarifies

how firms should capture and use knowledge/experience, objectives, risk tolerance,
capacity for loss, and clients’ sustainability preferences and how those inputs must
flow into tools and recommendations, including algorithmic ones. Two EU-wide
frameworks overlay the advice rules: the AI Act (entered into force in 2024 with
phased obligations through 2025–2026) introduces governance and transparency
duties, including for general-purpose AI used inside advice stacks; and DORA
(applicable from January 2025) hardens ICT risk management, incident reporting,
testing,andoversightofcriticalthird-partyproviders(EuropeanCommission,2024;
EuropeanUnion,2022). For robo-advisers, that translates into model documentation
and change control, resilience testing, cloud/vendor ove rsight, and accessible
disclosuresalongsideclassicsuitabilityfiles(Table1).
2.1 U.S. Enforcement Trajectory
The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has taken the clearest
stance that robo-advisors are subject to the same fiduciary and anti-fraud duties
as traditional advisers, with enforcement actions setting the boundaries of per-
missible conduct. In In the Matter of Wealthfront Advisers, LLC (SEC, 2018),
the Commission charged the platform for misleading tax-loss-harvesting claims,
particularly the assurance that wash sales would be automatically avoided when, in
practice, controls were incomplete. In a parallel case, In the Matter of Hedgeable,
Inc. (SEC, 2018), false performance representations led to sanctions, reinforcing
that automated services cannot dilute the “fair, clear, and not misleading” principle.
Together, these early actions established that algorithmic advice is notexemptfrom
corefiduciarydutiesandthateveryclaimaboutautomationmustbeverifiableacross
alledgecases.
2.2 Conflicts and CashFloors
The 2022 Schwab case epitomizes how subtle algorithmic design choices can embed
conflicts of interest. According to the SEC (2022a), Schwab’s robo-portfolios
included mandated cash allocations that depressed expected returns relative to
alternatives, without prominently disclosing the impact or the affiliated benefits to
Schwab’s bank. The $187 million settlement demonstrated that regulatorswilltreat
cash “corridors” as material allocations that require plain-English disclosure and
robustgovernance.AsBakerandDellaert(2018) argue, conflicts of interest in robo-
advice are structurally harder for clients to perceive, making transparent disclosures
not merely desirable but necessary to preserve trust. This case remains the most
significant robo-advisory enforcement to date and sets a precedent for quantifying
andcommunicatingtheeconomicimplicationsofembeddedrules.
