2.3 Performance Claims an dHypotheticals
Marketing remains a persistent pressure point where growth imperatives collide with
regulatory boundaries. The Titan order in 2023 exemplifies this dynamic: the SEC
found that hypothetical performance was disseminated to retail audiences without
thegating,disclaimers,andreproducibilityrequiredundertheamendedMarketing
Rule(SEC,2023). Scholars note that retail investors often overweigh hypothetical
returns, leading to distorted expectations (Lusardi & Mitchell, 2014). Titan’s $1
million penalty shows that performance illustrations are treated as high-risk content,
requiring not only accurate assumptions but also robust distribution controls.
From a compliance-by-design perspective, this means embedding marketingreview
processes into content pipelines so that no chart, tweet, or landing page can
circumventregulatoryfilters.
2.4 AI-Washing as an EmergingFrontier
Most recently, the SEC’s 2024 cases against Delphia and Global Predictions
introduced the notion of “AI-washing” misleading statements about the use of
artificialintelligenceininvestmentprocesses(SEC,2024). This aligns with broader
concerns about “greenwashing” and other forms of exaggerated claims in finance.
By sanctioning firms for overstating AI capabilities, the Commission clarifiedthat
language such as “predicts” or “optimizes” is a regulated representation requiring
evidence. As Cruz et al. (2024) noted, this was the SEC’s first explicit action
targeting AI misrepresentation, and it signals that AI-related marketing will be
policed with the same rigor as performance advertising. For robo-advisers, this
introduces a new compliance perimeter: every AI-related phrase must be backed
bymodeldocumentation,validationresults,andcontemporaneousevidence.
2.5 UK Supervisory Approach
In contrast to U.S. headline fines, the UK’s Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) has
pursued supervisory reviews and thematic interventions. Its 2018 multi-firm review
ofautomatedinvestmentservicesflaggeddeficienciesinclientprofiling,suitability
evidence, and treatment of vulnerable customers (FCA, 2018). Although no fines
were imposed, firms were required to remediate weaknesses and demonstrate com-
pliance improvements. Since July 2023, the Consumer Duty has raised the bar by
obligingfirmstoevidence“goodoutcomes”acrossproductdesign,communication,
andpost-salesupport(FCA,2022). As Black (2008) emphasizes, the UK tradition
of “outcomes-based” regulation often relies on supervision and monitoring rather
than punitivefines,aimingtoshapefirmbehaviorsystemically.Forrobo-advisers,

178 N.Nahidi
this translates into deeper evidence-gathering and user-testing of digital fl ows,even
absentenforcementpenalties.
2.6 European Convergence an dHorizontalRules
At the EU level, MiFID II remains the anchor for suitability obligations, but
ESMA’s 2022 guidelines clarified howsustainabilitypreferencesmustbeintegrated
into suitability assessments, including algorithmic advice (ESMA, 2022). This
requirement adds a new layer of complexity, as robo-engines must now align
portfolio construction with clients’ environmental, social, and governance (ESG)
preferences. The horizontal frameworks of the Digital Op erational Resilience Act
(DORA)andtheAIActgofurther:DORAhardensICTriskmanagement,testing,
and vendor oversight (EU, 2022), while the AI Act mandates governance and
transparency obligations for “high-risk” AI , including general-purpose AI used in
financialservices(EU,2024). Scholars such as Gunninghametal.(2003) argue that
layered regulatory approaches combining sectoral rules with horizontal resilience
requirements create more robust guardrails but also increase compliance costs. For
robo-platforms, the implication is that operational resilience and AI explainability
arenolongeroptionalextrasbutregulatorynecessities.
2.7 Singapore’s Pragmatic Te mplate
Singapore’s Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has taken a technology-
agnostic but principle-heavy approach. Its Guidelines on the Provision of Digital
AdvisoryServicesrequirealgorithmgovernance,back-testing,ongoingmonitoring,
andescalationpathsforedgecases(MAS,2018a, 2018b). This is complemented by
the TechnologyRiskManagementGuidelines(MAS,2021), which stress scenario
testing, adversarial simulations, and vendor due diligence. As Tan (2020) notes,
MAS’s stance balances innovation encouragement with strict expectations that firms
prove controls in practice. Unlike the U.S., penalties have been rare, but licensing
conditions and supervisory scrutiny act as de facto enforcement tools. The lesson
is clear: robo-platforms in Singapore operate under a rules-light but expectations-
heavyregimewherecredibilitydependsondemonstrablegovernance.
2.8 Cross-Jurisdictional Lessons
Taken together, the global picture shows divergence in style but convergence in
substance. The SEC leads with visible penalties, making enforcement a signaling
device; the FCA and MAS rely more on supervisory engagement and guidance;

RegulatoryandComplianceIssuesinAI-DrivenFinancialServices 179
and ESMA leverages horizontal frameworks that embed digital resilience and
AI accountability into sectoral rules. As Baldwin et al. (2012) argue, regula-
tory strategies oscillate between “command-and-control,” “incentive-based,” and
“responsive” approaches. For robo-advisers operating cross-border, the safest path
is to build to the strictest denominator: SEC-style claim substantiation, FCA-style
outcome monitoring, ESMA-level sustainability and resilience documentation, and
MAS-grade vendor oversight. Th isapproachnotonlyreducesretrofitcostsbutalso
positionsfirmsastrustworthyplayersinamarketwhereinvestorconfidencehinges
ontransparencyandevidence.
Singapore provides a concise, principle-based template that many APAC firms
follow. The Guidelines on Provision of Digital Advisory Services confirm that
licensing is technology-agnostic and set expectations for algorithm governance,
back-testing, ongoing monitoring, and human escalation for edge cases (MAS,
2018a, 2018b). MAS complements this with Technology Risk Management guid-
ance on scenario testing, adversarial simulations, and incident response, and with
outsourcingexpectationsforcloudandcriticalvendors(MAS2021). The message is
clear: there is no robo carve-out, automate only what you can supervise andexplain,
andprovethatcontrolsworkinproduction.
Convergence is strongest around digital conduct and communications. Interna-
tional work on Digital Engagement Practices (DEPs) shows that prompts, default
settings, notifications, andgamifieddesigncanmateriallyinfluencerisk-takingand
tradingfrequencyinretailchannels(IOSCO,2024; IOSCO, 2025). UK experiments
echo these findings and link them directly to Consumer Duty expectations on
customer understanding and foreseeable harm (FCA, 2024). For robo-advisers,
that means cataloguing every engagement element across onboarding, portfolio
selection, and rebalancing; defining when a prompt might constitute a recommen-
dation; and governingDEPswiththesamecontrolsandapprovalsusedforfinancial
promotions(FCA,2022;ESMA,2 022).
Supervisors in all four jurisdictions increasingly expect compliance by design.
Product squads should embed legal/compliance and model-risk specialists into
sprints; maintain model cards, data-lineage documentation, challenger models,and
performance bounds; and operate change-control processes that tie code releases
toapprovals and client-facing disclosures (ESMA,2022; SEC, 2023). Operational
resilience is now table stakes: define RTO/RPO for rebalancing engines, drill
failover runbooks, secure audit and exit rights with cloud/data vendors, andmonitor
keyriskindicatorsthatlinkclientoutcomestomodelandplatformhealth(European
Union,2022;MAS,2021). When platforms operate across borders, building to the
strictest regulatory standard by default such as DORA-grade resilience, ESMA-lev el
suitabilityevidence,FCA-styleoutcomesmonitoring,andMAS-alignedtechnology
riskmanagementreducesretrofitrisk.
Innovation remains encouraged within guardrails. The FCA’s Innovation Path-
ways (and earlier Advice Unit), MAS’s sandboxes, and the AI Act’s requirement
for national AI sandboxes provide structured ways to test novel features under
supervisory visibility (FCA, 2022; MAS, 2 018a, 2018b; European Commission,
2024). The practical win is not a lower bar but earlier alignment on controls,

180 N.Nahidi
disclosures, and metrics that evidence client benefit. Teams that use these channels
while treating marketing language (especially “AI” claims and hypothetical results)
as regulated, and that hardwire suitability, resilience, and explainability into their
CI/CDpipelines,willmovefasterwithfewerregulatorysurprises(SEC,2023;FCA,
2022).
3 The Challenge of Ensuring CompliancewithFinancial
Laws
Ensuring suitability remains the core challenge because automated journeys mag-
nify both the benefits and the risks of scale. Firms must collect sufficiently granular
data on knowledge/experience, objectives, risk tolerance, capacity for loss, and,
since2022intheEU,sustainabilitypreferences,thenmapthoseinputstoportfolios
in a way that is explainable and evidenced (ESMA, 2022). UK supervision has
repeatedly found that digital flows can under-collect or over-rely on defaults, which
undermines suitability and the fair-value outcome now required by the Consumer
Duty (FCA, 2018; FCA, 2022). A robust control environment therefore includes
hard stops when inputs are incomplete, documented logic that links client attributes
to portfolio selection, periodic re-profiling triggers tied to life events or market
stress,andaclearhuman-in-the-looppathforedgecasesandvulnerablecustomers
(FCA,2018;ESMA,2 022).
Marketing and performance communications are the next pressure point because
they sit where growth targets meet regulatory obligations. Under the SEC’s
Marketing Rule, hypothetical and back-tested results require audience controls,
relevance filters, prominent limitations, and durable recordkeeping; fa ilures in
any of these mechanics have led to enforcement against digital advisers who
showcased eye-catching numbers to mass audiences (SEC, 2023). The broader
lesson is operational: performance content must be treated as a high-risk asset with
pre-clearance workflows, standardized disclaimers, net-of-fees presentation when
applicable, and monitoring to ensure sales channels don’t circumvent gating rules
(SEC,2023). UK and EU regimes reach similar conclusions through different legal
routes: communications must be fair, clear, and not misleading, and firms must
be able to evidence that customers genuinely understood key features and risks
(FCA, 2022; ESMA, 2 022). “AI” language is itself a regulated claim. In 2024,
the SEC sanctioned firms for making false or misleading statements about their
use of AI/ML, si gnalingthatclaimsaboutmodels,data,andpredictivecapabilities
mustbesubstantiatedlikeanyotherperformance-adjacentstatement(SEC,2024).
Practical compliance means maintaining an AI claims register that maps every
public assertion to internal evidence (data lineage, training/testing summaries,
validation metrics, and limits), enforcing pre-clearance of AI-related phrasing in
all channels, and aligning investor presentations with what the production system
actuallydoes.Whenphrasingimpliesadvantage“predicts,”“detects,”“optimizes,”

RegulatoryandComplianceIssuesinAI-DrivenFinancialServices 181
“learns” firms should expect to produce contemporaneous evidence on request
(SEC,2024).
Model governance ties the above together and determines whether the advice
engine is controllable at scale. Supervisors expect firms to define model pur-
pose, features, data sources and rights, training/validation methods, challenger
approaches, performance bounds, andchange-approvalthresholds;theyalsoexpect
drift,stability,andfairnessmonitoring,withdocumentedinterventionswhenthresh-
olds are breached (ESMA, 2022; European Commission, 2024). The EU AI Act
reinforces governance and transparency expectations, while DORA pushes financial
entities toward disciplined ICT controls and resilience testing that directly affect
model deployment and rollback procedures (European Union, 2022; European
Commission,2024). In APAC, MAS guidance makes the same point pragmatically:
keep algorithms explainable, back-test them, monitor them continuously, and be
readytoescalatetoahumanwhenthelogichitsitslimits(MAS,2018a, 2018b).
Operational resilience and third-party risk have shifted from “sound practice” to
mandatory in several jurisdictions, with particular implications for cloud-first robo
stacks. DORA requires formal ICT risk frameworks, incident reporting, threat-led
testing, and oversight of critical third-party prov iders expectations that map onto
architectural choices like multi-region deployment, controlled failover, immutable
config,andtestedrun-booksforadviceandrebalancingengines(EuropeanUnion,
2022). MAS’s Technology Risk Management and Outsourcing frameworks land
similarly, requiring scenario exercises, adversarial simulations, vendor due dili-
gence, audit/exit rights, and dataportabilitypracticalguardrailsforplatformsbuilt
on external APIs and cloud services (MAS, 2021; MAS, 2 018a, 2018b). Day-to-
day, this means defined RTO/RPO targets for advice functions, telemetry to detect
partial failures, and drill-proven incident communications to clients and regulators.
Digital engagement practices (DEPs) prompts, defaults, leaderboards, prize draws,
push notifications can tilt investor behavior and therefore attract conduct scrutiny.
IOSCO’srecentworkfindsthatDEPscanraisetradingfrequencyandrisk-taking,
whileUKexperimentsshowmeasurableshiftsfromsmalldesignchangesintrading
apps(IOSCO,2024; IOSCO, 2025;FCA,2024). Under the Consumer Duty, design
choices that predictably cause harm br eachexpectationsoncustomerunderstanding
and foreseeable harm (FCA, 2022). Compliance therefore extends beyond words
to interaction design: inventory DEPs, classify which elements might constitute a
recommendation, apply financial-promotion style approvals, and monitor behav ioral
outcomes (e.g., migration into riskier portfolios after a specific prompt), with
thresholdsforremediationandproductchanges(FCA,2022;ESMA,2 022).
Books and records complete the compliance perimeter and are often where
otherwise good programs stumble. The SEC’s sweeps routinely pair marketing
findings with recordkeeping lapses; the same risk exists in UK/EU regimes that
expect durable evidence of what clients saw, understood, and agreed to (SEC,
2023; FCA, 2022). For automated platforms, “records” must include versioned
screenshots of every in-app screen and disclosure, all variants used in A/B tests,
push-notification texts, social content, and app-store descriptions, plus model-
change logs tied to release identifiers. When combined with suitability files and

182 N.Nahidi
service-level telemetry, these artifacts let firms reconstruct the client experience and
the state of the model at any point—oftenthedifferencebetweenexplainingablip
anddefendingabreach(ESMA,2022; SEC,2023).
Table 2 builds on the enforcement history and supervisory case studies sum-
marized earlier by mapping four cross-cutting regulatory themes: suitability, truth-
fulness of AI and performance claims, digital conduct nudges, and operational
resilienceacrosstheSEC,FCA,ESMA,andMAS.
The intensity ratings inTable2 were derived from observable regulatory posture
rather than subjective judgment. A “High” intensity designation reflects either direct
enforcement actions with monetary sanctions (e.g., SEC penalties for misleading
tax-loss harvesting claims, hypothetical performance disclosures, or AI-washing) or
binding obligations with detailed guidance (e.g., ESMA’s MiFID II suitability rules
and the EU’s Digital Operational Resilience Act). “Medium” intensity indicates
areas where regulators have published thematic reviews or supervisory expectations
but have not yet imposed widespread penalties, such as the FCA’s Consumer Duty
monitoring of suitability and digital nudges, or MAS’s requirements for algorithm
governance under its 2018 Guidelines. Finally, “Emerging” denotes themes where
regulatory attention is visible through principle-based guidance or exploratory
reports but without targeted enforcement to date, as with DEPs in Singapore or
operationalresilienceintheUnitedStates.Theseclassificationscapturethepresent
regulatorystanceasof2024–2025andaredesignedtohighlightboththevariation
incurrentsupervisoryapproachesandthelikelytrajectoryoffutureenforcement.
Empirical evidence from U.S. enforcement actions confirms that marketing and
disclosure remain the dominant vulnerabilities in robo-advisory oversight. Since
2018, the SEC has repeatedly sanctioned firms for misleading statements, from
Wealthfront’sfalseclaimsabouttax-lossharvestingtoTitan’simproperpresentation
of hypothetical returns (SEC, 2018; SEC, 2023). The case against Betterment
in 2023 further reinforced that even partial misstatements about the frequency
and scope of tax-loss harvesting monitoring constitute breaches of fiduciary duty
(SEC, 2023). As Fig. 1 shows, these cases comprise the overwhelming majority
of enforcement activity, illustrating the SEC’s prioritization of transparency in
automated advice. Conflicts of interest form a second, though less frequent,
category. The SEC’s 2022 action ag ainst Charles Schwab subsidiaries highlighted
howplatforms’useofcash“floors”inautomatedportfolios—directedintoaffiliated
funds—createdhiddenconflictsthatdisadvantagedclients(SEC,2022a). Similarly,
SoFi Wealth was sanctioned for misstatements in its disclosures around investment
strategies (SEC, 2021). These cases demonstrate that even where robo-advisory
algorithms aretechnicallyfunctional,underlyingcommercialincentivescandistort
outcomes.Thesmallernumber ofconflictscasesinFig.2 suggests that regulators
treat these as significant but episodic breaches, requiring targeted penalties rather
than systemic reforms. A newer and growing frontier is the misrepresentation
of artificial intelligence capabilities, or “AI-washing.” In 2024, the SEC charged
DelphiaandGlobalPredictionswithmakingfalseandmisleadingclaimsabouttheir
use of artificial intelligence in investment processes (SEC, 2024). These actions
were the first of their kind and signaled a regulatory shift toward scrutinizing not

Taken together, the distribution in Fig. 1 underscores two broader points.
First, robo-advisory enforcement has been disproportionately concentrated on
information asymmetries—misstatements, omissions, and claims that impair client

the trajectory suggests a gradual expansion from tr aditional fiduciary issues (suit-

design. This pattern mirrors the regulatory dynamics described by Black (2008)
and Baldwin, Cave, and Lodge (2012): regulators initially focus on visible mis-
statements, but over time extend oversight to systemic design features. As the

Operational resilience and outsourcing rules are crystallizing most strongly in the
EU. DORA, applicable from January 2025, mandates ICT risk frameworks, incident
reporting, and oversight of critical third-party providers. The FCA integrates
resilience into its Consumer Duty monitoring, while MAS sets detailed expectations
for vendor oversight in its TRM (2021) and Outsourcing Guidelines (2018). The
SEC, by contrast, treats resilience largely through record-keeping and general
compliance obligations. Hence Table 2 records high intensity for ESMA, medium
for FCA and MAS, and emerging for the SEC. The clear future hotspot is cloud
and vendor failures, which regulators increasingly treat as systemic risk triggers.
Table 2 reframes robo-advisory oversight from a jurisdictional comparison to a
thematic diagnosis. Suitability and truthfulness are already highly policed, while
DEPs and resilience are the next enforcement frontiers. By incorporating a future-
hotspot lens, the table highlights where platforms should pre-emptively invest in
controls: AI claim substantiation, DEP inventories, ESG suitability mapping, and
DORA-grade vendor governance. The message is clear: firms that build to the
strictest denominator across jurisdictions are best positioned to scale safely while
avoidingretrofitcosts.

These drivers are translated into five operational pillars that together form the
backbone of compliance by design. Suitability processes ensure that KYC data,
risk profiles, and ESG preferences are captured with sufficient granularity to satisfy

back-testing, and continuous monitoring of models, consistent with both SEC

outcomes-based fa irness test under the Consumer Duty, making substantiation of

sory concerns raised by the FCA’s experiments on trading apps (FCA, 2024) and
IOSCO’s consultation on digitalengagementpractices(IOSCO,2024).
Each of these pillars generates tangible artifacts that regulators increasingly
demand as evidence. Suitability processes produce documented assessments of
investor preferences and ESG fit; algorithm governance yields validation files and
audit trails; client communication controls create marketing approval records and
AI claims registers; resilience frameworks produce stress test results and vendor
oversight reports; and nudge oversight generates DEP harmmetricsandrecordsof

evidence-based regulation, in which supervisory scrutiny hinges not on principles
alonebutonthedemonstrabilityofcompliance(Baldwinetal.,2012). The arrows

processes, whichinturngenerateverifiableoutputs.

4 Balancing Innovation and Investor Protection
Regulatory on-ramps exist to help teams test new ideas transparently rather than
quietly shipping and hoping for the best. The FCA’s Innovation Pathways gives
firms early engagement and structuredfeedbackonnoveladvice/guidancejourneys,
building on the Advisory Unit’s experience with automated models (FCA, 2022).
MAS offers Sandbox, Sandbox Express, and enhanced support that allow time-
boxed,parameterizedtestingwithclearexitcriteria(MAS,2018a). The EU AI Act
goes further by requiring each Member State to operate at least one AI regulatory
sandbox by the m id-2020s,creatingasupervisedspacetotrialAI-enabledfeatures
that affect suitability, monitoring, or communications (EU, 2024). None of these
lowers the bar on client protection; they reduce lega luncertaintyandaligncontrols
beforefulllaunch(FCA,2022;MAS,2 018a).
A practical way to widen access without diluting safeguards is to design
constrained-scope advice with crisp eligibility rules and overt boundaries. UK
policy work on the advice–guidance boundary is explicitly aimed at closing the
“advicegap”byenabling“targetedsupport”andsimplifiedadviceforwell-defined
needs, supported by Consumer Duty outcomes on customer understanding and
price/value (FCA, 2022). For robo teams, this translates into flows that clearly
signpost when a client is outside the scope, default to guidance rather than advice
when inputs are incomplete, and offer human fallback when the algorithm’s
confidenceorcoverageislow.Documentingthosedesigndecisionsandmeasuring
whethertheydrivebetteroutcomesareasimportantasthecode(FCA,2022).
Explainability is both a technical and a communications discipline. Internally,
model cards, data lineage, performance bounds, and challenger results anchor gov-
ernance; externally, firms must explain, in plain language, why a recommendation
fits a specific customer, including any sustainability-preference trade-offs required
byMiFIDII.UndertheConsumerDuty,“customerunderstanding”requirestesting
whetherdisclosuresactuallyland,notjustpresentingthem(FCA,2022). Effective
robo-platforms, therefore, pair algorithmic explainers with UX that lets clients
interrogate key drivers, risk capacity, horizon, sustainability preferences,andaccess
anescalationroutetoahumanwhensomethingdoesnotlookright(FCA,2022).
Test-first engineering helps teams innovate quickly without outsourcing risk to
end users. DORA expects EU firms to implement threat-led penetration testing
and incident playbooks; MAS TRM encourages scenario-based and adversarial
exercises (EU, 2022). For robo-advice, that means treating portfolio engines and
profile-to-portfolio mapping as mission-critical services with defined RTO/RPO,
running chaos tests on market data/API dependencies, and gating deployments
on model-risk approvals. Canary releases and shadow-mode comparisonsbetween
challenger and champion models can catch regressions before they affect clients,
withrollbackproceduresdrilledlikefiredrills(EU,2022).
Vendor and cloud strategies should be framed as investor-protection controls,
not only cost or speed choices. DORA requires oversight of critical third parties,
whileMASOutsourcingguidanceexpectsduediligence,performanceSLAs,audit

rights, exit plans, and data-portability arrangements that survivestress(EU,2022).
Practically, robo platforms need dual data feeds where feasible, circuit-breakers for
stale or anomalous inputs, and read-only fallbacks that pause rebalancing rather than
propagate bad data. Contracts should encode supervisory accessandexittimelines,
andarchitectureshouldminimizesinglepointsoffailure—decisionsthatmaterially
improveclientoutcomesduringdisruptions(EU,2022).
Measurement closes the loop and turns “we think this helps” into evidence. The
Consumer Duty asks boards to monitor whether products deliver good outcomes;
that invites me tricssuchassuitabilityexceptions,vulnerable-customerescalations,
rebalancing error rates, and behavioral outcomes linked to DEPs (FCA, 2022).
For firms that use sustainability preferences in Europe, tracking whether portfolio
construction honors stated preferences without unintended concentration risk is sim-
ilarly important. Publishing periodicoutcomedashboardstogovernancecommittees
andactingonsignalsdemonstratestheculturethatsupervisorsincreasinglyexpect.
Roadmaps should be aligned to regulatory timelines, so innovation does not
force late retrofits. The AI Act entered into force in 2024 with phased obliga-
tions through 2025–2026, including transparency and governance expectations for
general-purpose AI that many firms will rely on. DORA has been applied since

live for EU financial entities (EU, 2022). A “strictest-standard-first” philosophy—

5 Case Studies
5.1 Charles Schwab Intelligent Portfolios CashFloors&
Conflicts
Schwab’s automated portfolios brought the industry’s attention to how apparently
“neutral” portfolio rules can encode meaningful economic choices that must be
explained with the same care as security selection. A mandated cash floor that is
systematically higher than peers or than a purely mean–variance specification will
tend to depress expected returns in many market states, yet clients can easily miss
that trade-off if disclosures emphasize the elegance of the algorithmic process while
relegating sweep mechanics or opportunity cost to footnotes. Properly engineered
robo-advice treats cashlikeanyotherallocation:ithasathesis(liquidity,volatility
dampening, rebalancing fuel), a measurable cost in forgone expected return, and
observable dynamics when interest rates or spreads move. Compliance becomes
the forcing function that aligns elegant math with plain-English truth-telling: if
the engine’s rules predictably change the client’s long-run risk/return, what, why,

190 N.Nahidi
how much, and for whom must appear prominently in onboardingscreens,portfolio
summaries,andongoingcommunications(SEC,2022a).
The U.S. fiduciary lens, the UK’s Consumer Duty, and ESMA’s MiFID II suit-
ability all converge on the same outcome question: would a reasonable retail client
understand the economic implicationsofthisdesign,andistherecommendationstill
suitable and fair value for that client segment (ESMA, 2022)? That pushes teams
to move beyond boilerplate risk factors toward concrete, decision-useful figures
such as “in a 60/40 model, a 6–8% cash corridor would have reduced annualized
returns by 0.5–1% bps over the past three rate cycles” alongside an explanation
of why the platform nonetheless believes the corridor improves client outcomes
(liquidity, smoother drawdowns, behavioral benefits). It also reframes “conflicts” as
a quantitative discipline: if affiliated sweep revenue exists, quantify it, disclose it
incontext,andevidencegovernancethatpreventsrevenuefromsilentlyoverriding
suitability.Theobjectiveisnottoeliminatecashoraffiliationperse,buttoensure
clients and supervisors can see cause, effect, and control plainly (ESMA, 2022;
SEC, 2024).
Turning that policy intent into daily practice starts with a conflict inventory
wired directly into model governance. Each rule that can be advantageous to the
firm (cash, affiliate ETFs, order routing) needs an owner, a metric, and board-
level visibility. For cash, firms should backtest expected drag across rate regimes,
track realized drag versus a benchmark model, and surface exceptions when the
engine drifts beyond corridor bounds. Under the Consumer Duty, those data feed
theproduct’spriceandvalueassessment;underMiFIDII,theysitinthesuitability
file and periodic reviews; under the Advisers Act, they support “full and fair
disclosure” and supervision evidence (ESMA, 2022). Importantly, this is not a
one-time paper exercise: corridor changes, fee changes, or market conditions that
materially alter th e economics must trigger synchronized updates to disclosures,
help-centercontent,adviserscripts,andclientnotifications.
Model governance must document who can change the cash logic, what evidence
is required, how changes are rolled out, and how clients are told. Release trains
should block any code/config change that affects cash unless the disclosure package
has been refreshed and archived, with exact client-facing wording versioned
alongside the code commit. Where sustainability preferences are collected (EU),
thefileshouldshowhowhighercashinteractswiththosepreferencesifitindirectly
crowdsoutexposuresnecessarytohonorthembecausesuitabilityunderMiFIDII
nowincludessustainability-preferencefit,notjustrisk/returnfit(ESMA,2022). In
UK contexts, product and distribution assessments under the Consumer Duty should
make explicit whether higher cash aligns with the target market and whether any
segment is likely to experience foreseeable harm from persistent cash drag (FCA,
2022).
A final layer is client comprehension and ongoing outcome testing. Disclosing
that “cash may reduce returns” is not the same as demonstrating that retail clients
grasp the magnitude and conditions. Short, tested explanations (“Holding 8% cash
in this model would have reduced average returns by about 0.8% per year in the
last decade, but helped cushion 12% of drawdowns and reduced trading costs by

RegulatoryandComplianceIssuesinAI-DrivenFinancialServices 191
15 bps per trade”) make the trade-off tangible. Periodic outcome reviews tracking
realized performance deltas, complaint themes, opt-outs, and the incidence of “cash
exceptions” give boards evidence that the design is delivering what it promises.
The regulatory message across jurisdictions is consistent: automation i s welcome,
but if the algorithm bakes in a non-obvious economic effect that also touches a
potentialconflict,transparency,governance,andmeasurableoutcomesmustbethe
safeguards.
5.2 Wealthfront and Hedgeable Automation Claims andTLH
Reality
The early robo cases established a durable principle: when a platform claims an
automated feature will monitor, prevent, or optimize something on a client’s behalf,
that claim is an objective statement of fact, not brand rhetoric, and it must be
consistently true across the messy edges of real accounts (SEC, 2018). Tax-loss
harvesting (TLH) is a perfect stress test for this principle because it sits at the
intersection of market timing, brokerage operations, lot selection, wash-sale rules,
and client heterogeneity. A promise like “we monitor for wash sales” collapses
into many fragile sub-promises once fractional shares, multiple custodians, external
accounts, and settlement timing a reinplay.Thelessonfromenforcementissimple:
if any of those sub-promises routinely fail for a material subset of users, the
disclosuremustreflectthatrealitybefore,notafter,clientsrelyonit(SEC,2018).
Re-engineering TLH for compliance means defining feature service-level objec-
tives: what harvesting frequency and loss thresholds the system targets; when
harvesting pauses (e.g., after buys that risk a wash sale); which account linkages
are required for cross-account visibility; and how the system behaves when data are
stale or incomplete. Each constraint must be surfaced in the UIthemomentitapplies
(“WedetectedactivityinyourexternalIRAthatcouldtriggerawashsale;harvesting
ispausedfor30days”),pairedwithaccessiblehelptextandahumanescalationpath
(ESMA,2022). From a U.S. perspective, that is both anti-fraud (truthful statements)
and supervision under the Compliance Rule; from a UK/EU perspective, it supports
“fair, clear, not misleading” communications and suitability because tax outcomes
dependonclientcircumstances(ESMA,2022).
Suitability extends deeper than many product teams assume. Aggressive TLH
can be unsuitable for thinly funded accounts with high transaction costs, for clients
with limited current or future tax liability, or for those whose behavioral preferences
favor simplicity over frequent trades. Under MiFID II, suitability documentation
should explain why TLHison,off,orconstrainedforagivenprofile,andunderthe
Consumer Duty, firms should test whether clients understand the feature’s caveats
andpotentialsideeffects(ESMA,2022). That nudges platforms to build a decision
explainer that goes beyond marketing (“we add after-tax returns”) to show theclient
theirlikelybenefitdistributionandtheconditionsunderwhichbenefitdropstonear
zero.

192 N.Nahidi
Marketing governance is the other half of the equation. Every sentence in a
landing page, blog, email, or app-store listing that implies detection, prevention,
or optimization must trace back to an internal evidence file: test cases, failure-mode
analyses, incidence rates, and change-control history. Growth teams should adopt
a content circuit-breaker that blocks campaigns if telemetry shows the feature is
under-delivering for a segment (“<60% of eligible accounts harvested in the past 90
days” triggers a pause and a disclosure review). For U.S. advisers, this discipline
aligns with the spirit of the Marketing Rule even if the content is not hypothetical
performance; for UK/EU firms, it aligns with financial promotions rules and the
ConsumerDuty’scustomerunderstandingoutcome(ESMA,2022).
Books and records turn good intentions into demonstrable compliance. Keep
exact versions of client-facing copy, in-app prompts, A/B variants, and help-center
articles; tie them to code releases and feature flags so the firm can reconstruct
what any client saw on any date. Archive internal validations and model/feature
change logs and maintain a“knownlimitations”registerthatproduct,compliance,
and support teams can reference. When regulators ask “How did you know this
wasworkingasclaimed?”theanswershouldbeproduced,notreconstructed(SEC,
2023).
The thorniest operational risks arise at the edges: fractional-share rounding that
trips wash-sale windows, delayed brokerage data that hides purchase activity, exter-
nal accounts that break visibility, and seasonal crowding of harvest requests that
push trades into less favorable liquidity. None of these absolves the firm of accurate
claims; they simply demand robust fallbacks (graceful pausing, clientalerts,human
review) and transparent messaging about when the feature is constrained. Across
jurisdictions, the regulatory expectation is that platforms either deliver what they
promiseorchangethepromisebeforeclientsareharmed(ESMA,2022).
5.3 Titan Hypothetical Performance and th eMarketingRule
The Titan order crystallized how the amended U.S. Marketing Rule treats hypo-
thetical and back-tested numbers in retail-facing materials: they are hazardous
content that demands tight eligibility, careful presentation, and durable records
(SEC, 2023). Hypothetical results are not inherently misleading, but they become
so when broadcast to mass audiences that cannot reasonably contextualize assump-
tions, when the numbers are cherry-picked, or when a firm cannot reproduce the
charts months later. For digital-first advisers whose growth relies on performance
storytelling, the operational stakes are high: either build a publication factory that
meets the rule’s engineering standard, or minimize the use of hypotheticals in public
channels. Eligibility is step one. The rule expects firms to limit the distribution
of hypothetical performance to investors for whom it is relevant and likely to be
understood, typically in controlled portals, after profiling, with acknowledgment
flows, not on social feeds or open landing pages (SEC, 2023). That expectation
must be implemented in code, not justpolicy:SSO-gatedpages,role-limitedCMS

RegulatoryandComplianceIssuesinAI-DrivenFinancialServices 193
publishing, disable-by-default settings for affiliates and influencers, and automated
checks that block upload of images containing performance figures to public
channels. The more di stributed your marketing operation, the more you need
technicalcontrolsthatmakethecompliantpaththeonlypath.
Presentation discipline is step two. Where applicable, show net-of-fees out-
comes; disclose the central assumptions succinctly (rebalancing cadence, cash han-
dling, trading costs, tax treatment, data v intage,benchmarkconstruction);articulate
limitations (model risk, survivorship bias); and avoid time-window cherry-picking
(SEC, 2023). The communication should be written at a reading level appropriate
for retail an explicit link to the UK Consumer Duty’s “customer understanding”
outcome and tested periodically with real users. In EU settings, similar ex pectations
flow from MiFID II’s requirements on fair, clear, and not misleading communica-
tions and from ESMA’s stance on suitability and appropriateness (ESMA, 2022).
Multi-channel governance is step three. It is not enough to police the corporate
blog while ignoring app-store screenshots, PDFs, investor decks, or partner posts.
Firms need a single source of truth for performance assets, route all variants through
compliance, and hash/version each artifact so the archive proves exactly what was
published, where, and when. Influencer or affiliateprogramsrequirespecificrules:
pre-approvedscripts,noad-libbingperformance,andplatform-levelmonitoringthat
flagsuploadscontainingnumbersthatlooklikereturns.Ifanychannelcannotmeet
thosestandardsreliably,itshouldnotbeusedforperformancecontent(SEC,2023).
Data lineage and reproducibility are step four. Hypothetical charts must be re-
creatable: the firm should retain the data inputs, back-test code, parameter files,
and rendering scripts needed to generate the exact figure clients saw. That package
sits alongside the approval memo and the campaign brief in the archive. Six months
later, a revi ewershouldbeabletopressabuttonandregeneratethechart,including
footnotesanddisclaimers.Thisiswheremarketingoperationsintersectswithmodel
risk:ifyoucannotreproduceit,youprobablyshouldnotpublishit(SEC,2023).
Cross-border platforms should design to the strictest common denominator. Even
where the U.S. rule does not directly apply, UK financial promotions rules and the
Consumer Duty’s emphasis on comprehension, as well as EU MiFID II’s fairness
and suitability expectations, point in the same direction. It is cheaper to treat all
hypothetical numbers as hazardous everywhere than to vary controls by region
and hope distribution teams never mix assets (ESMA, 2022). Firms that sell into
professional channels can build a parallel pipeline with different entitlements, but
they must be confident that those materials never leak into retail spaces. Commercial
pressures are the persistent friction. Performance sells, speed matters, and creators
move fast. The operational antidote is to slow down the riskiest content by design:
fewer users with publishing rights, longer SLAs for reviews, automatic expiry of
approvals when numbers change, and telemetry that records views and audiencesso
youcanshow,notjustassert,thatdistributionstayedwithintheintendedperimeter.
Regularretrospectives—howmanyassetswereblockedbythegate,howmanywere
corrected, how many comprehension tests failed—turn governance into a learning
loopthatgrowthleaderscanrespect(SEC,2023).

194 N.Nahidi
Finally, remember that hypothetical performance often travels with AI claims in
modern marketing. A chart that implies predictive power plus a caption that says
“our AI finds the winners” is a two-fer: Marketing Rule exposure and potential “AI-
washing” risk if the claim outpaces the evidence. The safest pattern is to build an AI
claims register and subject any AI-plus-performancepackagetobothreviewtracks
beforepublication.Theregulator’sperspectiveisstraightforward:ifyouaregoing
to persuade retail investors with numbers and algorithms, build the controls that
retailinvestorsdeserve(SEC,2023).
5.4 Betterment Code, Disclosures, and Tr ustLoopsinTLH
The Betterment matter highlights a deceptively simple truth: in automated advice,
softwarereleasemanagementisinvestorprotection(SEC,2023). When a change in
code, configuration, or vendor behavior alters how a touted feature like TLH (Tax-
Loss Harvesting) performs, the disclosure ecosystem must update in lockstep, or
clients will continue making decisions on outdated assumptions. That means prod-
uct teams need to treat compliance artifacts, client-facing explanations, eligibility
criteria, risk factors, and limitations as dependencies of the release, not optional
post-hocedits.Ifthereleasetogglesaconstraintorchangesexpectedbenefitsfora
segment,thepipelineshouldfailsafeuntilthewording,FAQs,andsupportscripts
arerefreshedandarchived.
A robust telemetry layer is the practical heart of this posture. Measure realized
harvests against model-expected opportunity; flag accounts or cohorts whose
realized benefit persistently trails expectations; and monitor leading indicators (e.g.,
increased pause rates, spikes in wash-sale blocks, vendor latency). Tie those signals
to content circuit-breakers that pause new campaigns or trigger in-app banners
when the feature is under-delivering for meaningful segments. From a regulatory
standpoint, this issimplygoodsupervisionand“booksandrecords,”butintheUK
andEUsettings,italsoservestheConsumerDuty’sgoodoutcomesrequirementand
MiFID II’s suitability reviews by showing that the firm is watching client benefit,
notjustcodemetrics(FCA,2022).
Change control must also extend to explainability. If TLH is constrained for a
client, the UI should say why in terms a layperson understands, and the suitability
file should reflect the decision. Some clients may prefer to switch the feature
off temporarily when constraints dominate; others may accept reduced benefit for
continuity.Eitherway,aplain-languageexplainercoupledwithahumanescalation
route preserves customer understanding and trust—the core currency under the
ConsumerDuty—andapracticaldefenseinanysupervisorydialogue(FCA,2022).
Client remediation planning deserves the same engineering rigor as detection.
Where constraints or bugs reduced expected benefits, quantify the tax impact by
cohort, consider fee credits or other remediation, and communicate proactively with
personalized letters that translate thetechnicalissueintoinvestorreality(“Because
ofWashsales,youraccountharvestedfewerlossesthanexpected;hereiswhatwe

RegulatoryandComplianceIssuesinAI-DrivenFinancialServices 195
did and what changes going forward”). The tone and timing of this communication
are compliance choices: fast, transparent remediation aligns with fiduciary duties
and fair-value expectations and prevents a technical problem from becoming a
conductproblem(SEC,2023).
The enduring constraint set is non-trivial: cross-custodian wash-sale interactions
that the platform cannot see directly; brokerage API timing that hides same-day
activity; tax-lot fragmentation that complicates lot selection; and jurisdictional
differences in tax treatment. None of these absolves firms of accurate claims; they
simply necessitate graceful fallbacks (pausing, alerts, human checks), humble copy
that acknowledges limits up front, and gov ernance that ties product ambition to
evidence.AcrosstheSEC,FCA,andESMAregimes,thethrough-lineisthesame:
promise carefully, instrument deeply, explain clearly, and fix quickly when reality
divergesfromthebrochure(SEC,2023).

Robo-Advisory and Auditing: Internal
and Ex ternal Controls
Ahmad Hatamabadi Farahani and NarminNahidi
Abstract This study examines how artificial intelligence (AI) reshapes auditing
practices in robo-advisory systems through the integration of internal and external
control frameworks. It explains how internal audits ensure algorithmic reliability,
data integrity, cybersecurity, and regulatory compliance, while external audits
provide independent verification of financial reporting under IFRS, GAAP, Basel
III, and MiFID II. The chapter highlights how AI technologies—machine learning,
natural language processing, robotic process automation, and explainable AI—
transform auditing into a continuous, data-driven, and predictive function. Ethical
dimensions such as bias, transparency, accountability, and data privacy are also
analyzed, emphasizing the importance of gov ernance frameworks and regulatory
oversight. Drawing on real-world examples from leading financial institutions and
auditfirms,thechapterproposesadual-layerauditmodelcombiningtechnological
and ethical assurance to enhance trust, transparency, and resilience in AI-driven
financialecosystems.
Keywords Auditing · FinTechgovernance · Internalcontrol · External
assurance · ExplainableAI · Ethicalaccountability · Continuousauditing ·
Financialtransparency

1 Introd uction
The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into financial advisory systems, known
as robo-advisors, has profoundly transformed investment management and financial
planning. Robo-advisors automate portfolio management, risk assessment, and
client interaction, providing scalable, cost-efficient services previously accessible
only to high-net-worth individuals (Baker and Dellaert 2018; Hossnofsky and
Junge 2019). These platforms leverage complex algorithms and vast datasets to
deliver tailored investmentsolutionsrapidlyandefficiently(PhoonandKoh2018).
Despite their widespread adoption, the increased reliance on automated systems
introduces new risks, necessitating sophisticated auditing p ractices to maintain
accuracy,regulatorycompliance,andconsumertrust(HossnofskyandJunge2019).
Internal auditing serves as a critical safeguard in AI-driven financial systems by
providing independent assurance over the efficiency and reliability of operations,
particularly as robo-advisors automate complex financial decisions (Alles et al.
2008). Effective internal audits scrutinize the underlying algorithms for performance
accuracy, data integrity, and security, ensuring continuous compliancewithinternal
policies and external regulatory standards (Mittelstadt et al. 2016). Historically,
internal audits focused primarily on financial statement accuracy and compliance;
however, modern approaches have evolved significantly to address emerging risks
associated with AI, such as algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, and cyberse-
curitythreats(Appelbaumetal.2017). Contemporary internal auditing frameworks
emphasize algorithm transparency, rigorous model governance, and proactive risk
management to address thedynamiccomplexitiesofAIsystems(Rajietal.2020).
Concurrently, external auditing frameworks tailored for robo-advisory platforms
have emerged as essential components for validating financial disclosures and
regulatory compliance. External audits are mandated to attest to the accuracy and
reliability of financial statements, compliance with accounting standards such as
the International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and Generally Accepted
AccountingPrinciples(GAAP),andadherencetoregulatoryframeworkslikeBasel
IIIandtheMarketsinFinancialInstrumentsDirectiveII(MiFIDII)(Zetzscheetal.
2016). Traditional auditing methods have primarily been manual, time-consuming,
and prone to human error; however, modern external auditing practices increasingly
incorporate digital technologies, blockchain, and advanceddataanalyticstoenhance
efficiency,accuracy,andtransparency(DaiandVasarhelyi2017). This integration of
advanced technology supports auditors in effectively navigating complex regulatory
landscapes and ensuring ro bust compliance in rapidly evolving financial markets
(Issaetal.2016).
AI technologies themselves increasingly contribute to the auditing process by
automating routine audit tasks and detecting anomalies with heightened accuracy
and efficiency. Advanced data analytics, machine learning, and natural language
processing allow auditors to swiftly identify irregularities and potential fraud,
significantly reducing the likelihood of undetected errors in financial reporting
(Appelbaum et al. 2017). Classical audit methods relied heavily on sampling and

Robo-AdvisoryandAuditing:InternalandExternalControls 199
manual verification, which were often limited in scope and accuracy; however,
contemporary practices harness sophisticated algorithms capable of analyzing vast
datasets in real time, dramatically improving audit coverage and precision (Issa
et al. 2016). This evolution in audit practices enhances overall audit quality,
reduces operational costs, and enables auditors to proactively identify and mitigate
emerging financial risks, fundamentally reshaping the landscape of traditional
auditingmethodologies(ACCA2022).
Finally, ethical considerations remain paramount at the intersection of AI and
auditing, particularly regarding automated financial reports. Concerns about fair-
ness, accountability, and transparency inAI-generatedfinancialoutputsnecessitate
comprehensiveethicalframeworksandguidelines(Floridietal.2018). Historically,
ethical frameworks in financial auditing focused primarily on professional stan-
dards and compliance obligations; today, auditors must navigate complex ethical
issues surrounding automateddecision-makingprocesses,algorithmictransparency,
accountability, and data privacy (Mittelstadt et al. 2016). Contemporary ethical
standards increasingly emphasize transparency in algorithmic decision-making,
accountability in algorithmic governance, and safeguarding the privacy of sensitive
financial data, underscoring the importance of maintaining both technical and
ethicalrigorinauditingpractices(EuropeanCommission2021). Addressing these
ethical challenges is crucial not only for maintaining public trust but also for
fostering sustainable and ethically responsible growth within AI-driven financial
ecosystems(OECD2020b).
2 The Role of Internal Auditing in AI-DrivenFinancial
Systems
Internal auditing is essential in the governance of AI-driven financial systems, offer-
ing critical independent assurance over operational efficiency, algorithm reliability,
andcompliancewithevolvingregulatoryframeworks(InstituteofInternalAuditors
(IIA)2017). Internal auditors systematically evaluate the robustness of algorithms,
data management practices, and cybersecurity measures, ensuring that financial
institutions effective ly mitigate the inherent risks associated with automated advi-
sory processes (Appelbaum et al. 2017). A critical function of internal auditing
involves assessing the transparency and fairness of algorithms employed by robo-
advisors. Auditors verify that AI models produce consistent, unbiased outcomes
across di verse client portfolios, thus protecting against discriminatory financial
practicesandensuringfairnessinautomateddecision-makingprocesses(I.Leeand
Shin 2018). Internal auditors also confirm the integrity and completeness of input
data, recognizing that flawed or bi ased data can significantly impair algorithmic
accuracyandfinancialreliability(IBMResearch2020).
Internal auditors play a crucial role in safeguarding sensitive client data by eval-
uating cybersecurity frameworkswithinAI-drivenplatforms.Giventheheightened

200 A.H.FarahaniandN.Nahidi
cybersecurity risks associated with digital financial services, auditors assess security
protocols, encryption methods, and response strategies to potential breaches, ensur-
ing robust protection against cyber threats (Chui et al. 2020). This responsibility
extends to verifying adherence to data privacy regulations such as the General
Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), further emphasizing the auditor’s role in
complianceoversight(Altmanetal.2018). Additionally, internal auditors contribute
to regulatory compliance assurance by regularly evaluating adherence to standards
such as Basel III, IFRS, and MiFID II. Continuous monitoring of compliance
practices ensuresthatrobo-advisorsmaintainnecessaryregulatoryalignment,thus
mitigating potential financial penalties and reputational risks associated with non-
compliance(FinancialStabilityBoard2017).
For instance, JP Morgan’s use of internal auditing for its AI-driven platform
“Chase Digital Assistant” provides a clear demonstration of the critical role internal
auditing plays in practical contexts. Internal auditors at JP Morgan regularly perform
comprehensive assessments of the digital assistant’s decision-making algorithms,
ensuring their fairness and impartiality across diverse customer segments. They
meticulously audit cybersecurity protocols, examining layers of security from data
encryption to intrusion detection systems. Additionally, compliance with rigorous
financial reg ulationssuchasBaselIII,IFRS,andMiFIDIIiscontinuouslyvalidated
through scheduled audits. The rigorous auditing practices at JP Morgan have
notablyenhancedtheplatform’soperationalreliability,significantlyreducingboth
the frequency and severity of potential security breaches and ensuring regulatory
adherence,therebyincreasingclientsatisfactionandtrust(IOSCO2021).
Similarly, Wealthfront, a leading robo-advisory service provider, employs exten-
sive internal auditing practices to ensure platform robustness and reliability. Internal
audit teams at Wealthfront systematically review the accuracy of algorithms respon-
sible for investment decisions, stress-testing these algorithms under diverse market
scenarios to verify their stability and adaptability. Additionally, comprehensive data
integrity audits are regularly conducted to ensure the accuracy and completeness
of client data inputs, thus maintaining the reliability of automated advice pro-
vided to clients. Auditors at Wealthfront also emphasize verifying adherence to
evolving regulatory frameworks, thereby proactively mitigating legal and compli-
ance risks. These rigorous internal auditing measures have substantially improved
Wealthfront’s ability to detect and correct potential system weaknesses, maintain
stringentregulatorycompliance,andenhanceconsumertrustthroughdemonstrated
transparencyandaccountability(Jungetal.2018).

202 A.H.FarahaniandN.Nahidi
Bridging Internal and External Oversight
Internal auditing practices in robo-advisory platforms are not merely about com-
pliance but represent the foundation of operational trust in automated financial
services. These audits go beyond verifying financial statements; they examine the
heart of robo-advisory operations—the algorithms themselves. Internal auditors
scrutinize whether investment models are transparent, reliable, and free from
systemic bias. For example, Betterment, one of the earliest U.S. robo-advisors,
integrates internal auditing into its product development cycle by continuously
testing its asset allocation algorithms under different market scenarios. Such
practicesdemonstratehowauditingsafeguardsbothinstitutionalintegrityandclient
welfare,ensuringthatdigitalplatformsremainaccountabletothesamestandardsof
fairnessandprudenceexpectedoftraditionalhumanadvisors.
Yet, internal auditing on its own is insufficient in a financial environment defined
by rapid innovation and global regulation. External auditing provides an additional,
independent layer of oversight that ensures credibility for both regulators and
investors. Independent auditors assess the completeness of financial disclosures,
compliance with international standards such as IFRS and GAAP, and adherence to
regulatory frameworks like Basel III and MiFID II. Consider the case of Nutmeg, the
UK-based digital wealth manager, which has routinely s ubjected itself to external
evaluations to validate its compliance with EU investor protection rules. Such
independentverificationstrengthensmarkettrustbyassuringclientsthatalgorithm-
driven advice has been tested not only internally but also by third parties with no
vestedinterestintheplatform’ssuccess.
The interaction between internal and external auditing is particularly critical
given the complexity of algorithmic finance. Robo-advisors execute thousands
of client transactions daily, each influenced by real-time data and automated
rebalancing. Traditional audit techniques, which relied on periodic sampling, cannot
capture the full picture of such systems. As a result, firms like Vanguard Digital
Advisor have adopted hybrid approaches, embedded internal continuous monitoring
while cooperating with external auditors forannualandquarterlyreviews.Thisdual
modelallowsriskssuchasalgorithmicdrift,cybersecuritybreaches,orcompliance
lapsestobeaddressedswiftlywhilemaintainingexternalcredibility.Together,these
practicesformalayereddefensesystem,ensuringresilienceinenvironmentswhere
financialadviceisautomatedatscale.
Technology itself is reshaping how both internal and external audits are per-
formed. Internal audit teams are increasingly using explainable AI to evaluate
algorithm decisions and employing stress-testing to simulate extreme scenarios.
Externally, audit firms have begun to rely on blockchain for transparent record-
keeping and AI-driven anomaly detection for efficiency. A notable example is
StashAway, a Singapore-based robo-advisor that uses advanced analytics to con-
tinuouslyaudititsriskmanagementmodelsinternally,whileengagingindependent
auditors to verify cross-jurisdictional compliance. This dual adoption of cutting-
edge technology demonstrates how the auditing profession is evolving into a

Robo-AdvisoryandAuditing:InternalandExternalControls 203
real-time, proactive governance function rather than a backward-looking check on
pastperformance.
These developments underscore why internal and external control frameworks
are indispensable in AI-driven finance. Without clear frameworks, audits risk
becoming fragmented and reactive, failing to keep up with the speed of techno-
logical change. Effective frameworks provide structure: they embed accountability
at every organizational level, clarify responsibilities between internal auditors and
external examiners, and ensure that compliance, transparency, and ethical conduct
are integral to daily operations. As platforms such as Schwab Intelligent Portfolios
and others demonstrate, when robust framewo rks are in place, robo-advisors can
balanceinnovationwithaccountability,reassuringbothclientsandregulators.The
next section examines how these internal and external control frameworks are
formallystructuredandapplied,highlightingtheirroleinstrengtheningreliability,
transparency,andethicalresponsibilityinAI-drivenfinancialecosystems.
This conceptual framework illustrates how internal and external controls jointly
safeguard robo-advisory platforms. Internal controls focus on operational reliability,
including algorithm validation, data integrity, and cybersecurity. External controls
provide independent oversight, reinforcing compliance with IFRS/GAAP, Basel III,
andMiFIDII.Together,theselayerscreateacomprehensiveassuranceframework
thatintegratestechnologicaloversightwithregulatoryaccountability.
The framework in Fig. 1 is designed around two concentric circles, which
visually separate the scope of internal and external audit controls. The inner circle
represents those processes that are embedded within the robo-advisory platform
itself. These controls are the responsibility of the organization’s management and
auditteams,formingtheplatform’sfirstlineofdefense.Byplacingtheminsidethe
Fig. 1 Dual structureof audit
oversight inAI-driven
robo-advisorysystems

204 A.H.FarahaniandN.Nahidi
circle, the framework highlights their proximity to day-to-day operations and their
role in maintainingthereliabilityofthesystemfromwithin.
Three main internal controls are emphasized: algorithm validation, data integrity,
and cybersecurity. Algorithm validation ensures that decision models perform
as expected under different conditions, reducing the risk of biased or flawed
investment recommendations. Data integrity refers to the accuracy, consistency, and
completeness of the information feeding into the algorithms; without trustworthy
data, even the mo stadvancedmodelwillproduceunreliableresults.Cybersecurity
representsprotectionagainstbreaches,hacking,ordatatheft,whichisparticularly
importantindigitalfinance.Together,theseinternalelementsfocusonthetechnical
andoperationalsoundnessofrobo-advisorysystems.
Surrounding the inner circle is the outer layer, which represents external controls.
These are not managed by the organization itself but are imposed by independent
auditors, regulators, or global standard-setting bodies. Their separation into the
outer circle underlines their independence and their broader perspective, which
extends beyond the boundaries of the firm. External controls are concerned not
onlywithwhethertherobo-advisorisfunctioninginternallybutalsowithwhether
italignswiththeexpectationsofthewiderfinancialsystemandglobalregulation.
Four external controls are highlighted. Independent assurance involves third-
party auditors verifying financial reporting and governance. IFRS/GAAP com-
pliance ensures that financial statements follow recognized accounting standards,
promoting comparability and transparency. Basel III risk governance addresses
capital adequacy and systemic resilience, a critical safeguard when AI models could
amplify risks. Finally, MiFID II investor protection ensures that clients’ interests
are safeguarded, particularly in European markets. By surrounding the inner circle,
these external controls provideaprotectiveoutershellthatvalidatesandstrengthens
the work of internal controls. The separation between the circles symbolizes the
differentresponsibilitiesandperspectives,whiletheirconcentricdesignshowsthat
bothlayersmustworktogethertoachievecomprehensiveoversight.
3 Internal and External Control Frameworks for AI-Driv en
Robo-AdvisorySystems
An effective control framework is pivotal for managing the unique risks associ-
ated with AI-driven robo-advisory platforms, where r apid decision-making and
algorithmic complexity pose distinctive auditing challenges. IOSCO (2021) pro-
poses an integrated control framework, emphasizing essential activities specifically
designed for AI systems. This framework combines principles from traditional
financial auditing with novel elements required by emerging technologies. Central
to this framework are internal components such as the Control Environment, Risk
Assessment, Control Activities, Information and Communication, and Continuous
Monitoring,alongsideexternalauditingpractices,eachexplicitlytailoredtoaddress

Robo-AdvisoryandAuditing:InternalandExternalControls 205
the intricacies of robo-advisors and AI-driven financial services. The Control
Environment component within the framework provides the foundational ethos
and operational context, emphasizing management oversight,integrity,andethical
standardscrucialforAIapplicationsinfinance.TheEuropeanCommission(2021)
emphasizes the importance of fostering an organizational culture that prioritizes
transparency and accountability in automated decision-making processes, especially
within high-risk AI systems. Establishing clear governance structures, defining
explicit roles and responsibilities, and reinforcing e thicalguidelinesformthebasis
forrobustAIgovernance,creatinganenvironmentwhereAIrisksaresystematically
identifiedandmanaged.
The workflow in Fig. 2 outlines the sequence of steps involved in auditing
AI-driven robo-advisory platforms. It begins with data input, where information
from markets, clients, and risk assessments flows into the system. This stage is
critical because the quality of outputs depends entirely on the reliability of inputs;
inaccurate or biased data wi ll compromise every subsequent step of the process.
Oncethedataisprocessed,thesystemmovestointernalauditcheckpoints.Atthis
stage, automated and human auditors verify three elements: bias detection, model

and external audit processes
inAI-drivenrobo-advisory
systems

206 A.H.FarahaniandN.Nahidi
validation, and compliance monitoring. Bias detection ensures that algorithmic
recommendations are not systematically unfair to certain groups of investors.
Model validation checks whether algorithms perform as intended under various
market conditions. Compliance monitoring confirms that the system aligns with
internal policies and relevant financial regulations. The third component is the
audit feedback loop, which differentiates AI-driven auditing from traditional, static
methods. Instead of waiting for periodic reviews, the system provides continuous
oversightbyfeedingauditfindingsbackintotheplatform.Thisallowsforongoing
corrections, real-time learning, and the early identification of risks or anomalies.
It makes the audit function proactive, not just reactive, and ensures that errors are
addressedbeforetheyescalate.
This process culminates in external audit validation. Here, independent auditors
and regulators provide a third-party check on the system’s performance and
reporting. This stage verifies that financial statements comply with standards such
as IFRS and GAAP, that risk management aligns with Basel III, and that client
protections under MiFID II are being met. By placing this step at the end of the
workflow,theframeworkhighlightsthecomplementaryroleofexternaloversightin
confirmingtherobustnessofinternalauditprocessesandenhancingoveralltrustin
robo-advisoryplatforms.
Risk Assessment forms the second critical internal component, explicitly tailored
to address algorithm-specific risks, such as data bias, model drift, and cyberse-
curity vulnerabilities. This component necessitates continuous evaluation of both
external and internal risks, including regulatory compliance, technological threats,
and market vol atility. Regular and proactive risk assessments ensure the robo-
advisory platform’s algorithms remain reliable, unbiased, and resilient against
evolving threats, significantly reducing financial and reputational risks (Financial
Stability Board 2017). Control Activities represent the practical internal mecha-
nisms employed to mitigate identified risks. These include detailed procedures for
algorithm validation, rigorous data quality checks, cybersecurity safeguards, and
compliance verification routines. Appelbaum et al. (2017) highlight embedding
automated controls into routine operations to swiftly detect and address anomalies,
thus enhancing operational efficiency and accuracy. This component also stresses
integ rating redundancy measures and fallback mechanisms, enhancing resilience
againstalgorithmicfailuresandcyberincidents.
Information and Communication practices ensure the timely, accurate dis-
semination of critical data across all organizational levels, facilitating informed
decision-making and rapid response capabilities. Effective internal communica-
tion protocols within AI-driven systems involve continuous documentation and
reporting me chanisms transparently conveying algorithmic changes, compliance
issues, and identified risks to relevant stakeholders, thereby fostering a cohesive
risk management culture (IOSCO 2021). Continuous Monitoring is pivotal for the
real-time internal supervision of robo-advisory systems, enabling ongoing oversight
ofperformance,compliance,andriskmanagement.IOSCO(2021) advocate using
automated monitoring tools capable of real-time data analysis and predictive
analytics to swiftly identify emerging risks and operational irregularities. These

Robo-AdvisoryandAuditing:InternalandExternalControls 207
advanced monitoring practices significantly enhance the capacity to pre-emptively
identify and rectify issues, reinforcing platform reliability and regulatory adherence.
Externally, auditing frameworks play a critical role in verifying the effectiveness
and compliance of robo-advisory platforms with established financial and regulatory
standards. External auditors perform independent evaluations of algorithm accuracy,
data integrity, and adherence to financial reporting standards such as IFRS and
GAAP,alongsideregulatorycompliancewithframeworkslikeBaselIIIandMiFID
II.Theseexternalauditsprovidethird-partyassurance,enhancingthecredibilityand
transparencyofrobo-advisorsinfinancialmarkets(Deloitte2018).
As a practical illustration, BlackRock’s Aladdin platform exemplifies the suc-
cessful integration of both internal and external control frameworks. Internally,
Aladdin employs rigorous continuous monitoring mechanisms, leveraging advanced
analytics to assess algorithm performance, cybersecurity integrity, and compliance
adherence constantly. Externally, independent audits validate Aladdin’s adher-
ence to regulatory standards, algorithm reliability, and data integrity, significantly
improving risk management capabilities and enhancing market trust (BlackRock
Sustainability Disclosure 2024). Similarly, Charles Schwab Intelligent Portfolios
demonstrates effective implementation of comprehensive internal and external
control practices. Internally, Schwab rigorously focuses on algorithm validation,
data integrity checks, and proactive compliance monitoring. Externally, Schwab
undergoes regular independent audits assessing compliance with regulatory frame-
works and financial reporting standards. This dual internal and external approach
ensuresalgorithmicreliability,regulatorycompliance,andoperationaltransparency,
significantlyenhancingclientconfidenceandoperationalresilience(IOSCO2021).
To further enrich understanding of auditing AI-driven systems, the UK’s Digital
Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) emphasizes the necessity of arobustframe-
workforalgorithmicauditing.AccordingtotheDRCF(2023)’s findings, auditing
algorithms involves systematically examining algorithmic systems to assess com-
pliance with legal standards, ethical guidelines, and performance expectations.
The report highlights current regulatory challenges, including transparency issues,
data accessibility, and the need for clearly defined standards and competencies
among auditors. Furthermore, it underscores the importance of collaboration among
regulators, industry stakeholders, and auditors to establish comprehensive standards
for auditing algorithms effectively. These insights from the DRCF underline the
need for continuous evolution in auditing practices, reinforcing the critical role of
regulation and oversight in maintaining trust and reliability in AI-driven financial
advisoryservices(DRCF2023).

4 Ensuring Compliance with IFRS, GAAP, Ba selIII,
andMiFIDII
Ensuring compliance with global financial standards such as the International
Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
(GAAP), Basel III, and the Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID
II) is a cornerstone of sound governance for AI-driven robo-advisory platforms.
As these p latformsoperatewithincomplex,highlyregulatedfinancialecosystems,
maintaining compliance is essential for safeguarding market integrity, protecting
investors, and fostering public trust (Rozario and Vasarhelyi 2018). However, the
inherent opacity and complexity of AI-driven systems present significant chal-
lenges to traditional compliance methodologies, necessitating adva nced auditing
frameworksandadaptiveregulatoryapproaches(Arrietaetal.2019). Robo-advisors
must implement sophisticated internal controls, robust data management practices,
and advanced compliance monitoring tools to navigate this regulatory landscape
effectively.

Robo-AdvisoryandAuditing:InternalandExternalControls 209
The International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS), issued by the Interna-
tional Accounting Standards Board (IASB), provide a globally recognized frame-
workforpreparingandpresentingfinancialstatements(IASB2019). For AI-driven
robo-advisors, IFRS compliance involves ensuring the accuracy and transparency
of financial reporting, particularly in areas such as fair value me asurement,revenue
recognition,andfinancialinstrumentdisclosures(TheIFRSAccountingStandards
Navigator 2021). Given the reliance of robo-advisors on dynamic algorithmic
models and real-time data, it is crucial to establish clear methodologies for valuing
complex financial instruments and disclosing algorithm-driven financial outcomes.
Furthermore, IFRS requires transparent documentation of model assumptions,
risk exposures, and data sources, underscoring the importance of comprehensive
algorithmicaudittrailsandmodelgovernancepractices(PWC2020).
Similarly, compliance with the Generally Accepted Accounting Principles
(GAAP), particularly as applied in the United States, entails adhering to ri gorous
accounting standards concerning financial reporting, revenue recognition, and
disclosure requirements (FASB 2021). Robo-advisory firms operating in or
serving U.S. markets must align their financial reporting processes with GAAP
principles, ensuring that automated systems accurately capture and report financial
transactions. This includes establishing robust controls to verify the accuracy of
automatedbookkeepingprocesses,ensuringcompletenessandaccuracyoffinancial
data, and maintaining auditability of AI-driven financial operations (Kokina and
Davenport2017). The complexity of integrating AI-driven financial decisions with
traditional accounting frameworks necessitates ongoing collaboration between
auditors,datascientists,andcomplianceofficers(Appelbaumetal.2017).
Basel III, developed by the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, introduces
comprehensive risk management standards aimed at enhancing the resilience of
financialinstitutions(CommitteeonBankingSupervision2017). For robo-advisory
platforms affiliated with or integrated into banking structures, Basel III compliance
entails robust capital adequacy, liquidity risk management, and operational risk
controls(CommitteeonBankingSupervision2017). Given that AI-driven systems
can amplify systemic risks through interconnected algorithms and data dependen-
cies, ensuring compliance with Basel III requires continuous stress testing, scenario
analysis, and dynamic risk modeling. Furthermore, the integration o f AI into risk
management processes demands enhanced model risk governance frameworks to
mitigate potential unintended consequences of automated decision-making (EY
2020).
The Markets in Financial Instruments Directive II (MiFID II), a cornerstone of
EU financial regulation, seeks to enhanceinvestorprotection,markettransparency,
and financial stability (ESMA 2018). For robo-advisors operating within the
European market, MiFID II compliance is multifaceted, encompassing requirements
for suitability assessments, product gover nance,bestexecutionpractices,andtrans-
parencyinclientcommunications(RingeandRuof2018). AI-driven platforms must
ensure that their recommendation algorithms adhere to suitability standards, taking
into account individual client profiles, risk tolerances, and investment objectives.
Additionally,MiFIDIImandatesrigorousdisclosurerequirementsandtransaction

210 A.H.FarahaniandN.Nahidi
reporting, necessitating comprehensive data management and auditability of AI-
drivenadvice(Buczynskietal.2025).
A comparative analysis of these regulatory frameworks highlights both common-
alities and distinctive challenges for robo-advisory compliance. While IFRS and
GAAP primarily focus on financial reporting accuracy and transparency, Basel III
emphasizes risk management and capital adequacy, and MiFID II prioritizes investor
protection and market conduct. Together, these frameworks demand a holistic
compliance strategythatintegratesfinancial,operational,andconductriskcontrols.
Robo-advisors must adopt a unified compliance architecture, leveraging advanced
data analytics, automated monitoring, and cross-functional collaboration toensure
seamless alignment with these diverse regulatory mandates (Gurrea-Martinez and
Wan2021).
A practical example of comprehensive regulatory compliance in action is seen
in the operations of UBS Wealth Management’s AI-driven advisory services. UBS
employs a sophisticated compliance framework integrating IFRS-based financial
reporting, GAAP alignment for U.S. operations, Basel III-compliant risk manage-
mentpractices,andfulladherencetoMiFIDIIstandardsforEuropeanclients(UBS
2022). Through advanced AI auditing tools, automated compliance monitoring,
and proactive regulatory engagement, UBS successfully navigates the complex
global regulatory landscape, demonstrating best practices for the industry. Another
notable example is Revolut, which, as a fast-growing fintech, has developed agile
compliance mechanisms thatalignitsAI-drivenofferingswiththeaforementioned
regulatory frameworks, leveraging continuous auditing and real-time compliance
dashboardstomaintainregulatoryalignmentacrossjurisdictions.
