5 AI’s Role in Automating Audit Pro cessesand Detecting
Anomalies
The integration of AI technologies into auditing processes is transforming the land-
scape of financial oversight, particularly within AI-driven robo-advisory platforms.
Traditional audit methodologies, which relied on manual sampling and retrospec-
tive reviews, are being replaced by continuous auditing frameworks powered by
advancedAItools(Leeetal.2020). AI-driven audits enable real-time monitoring of
financial transactions, detection of anomalies, and verification of compliance with
regulatory requirements. This transformation not only enhances audit efficiency but
also improves the accuracy and timeliness of financial oversight, thereby reducing
operationalandcompliancerisks(ICAEW2019).
Machine learning (ML) plays a pivotal role in automating audit processes. By
training models on historical financial data and audit outcomes, ML algorithms
can learn to identify patternsassociatedwithnormaloperationsandflagdeviations
indicative of potential errors or fraud (Gallego Sánchez et al. 2021). For robo-
advisors, this capability is particularly valuable given the volume and complexity
of transactions processed by algorithmic systems. ML-driven audit tools can
continuously analyze large datasets, detecting subtle anomalies that might elude
traditional audit techniques (W S R 2025). Additionally, unsupervised learning
techniques, such as clustering and anomaly detection algorithms, allow auditors
to identify outliers without predefined rules, further enhancing audit coverage and
precision(ThiprungsriandVasarhelyi2011).
Natural Language Processing (NLP) extends AI’s auditing capabilities to
unstructured data sources, such as contracts, client communications, and regulatory
filings. NLP tools can automatically extract and analyze relevant information
from these documents, facilitating compliance verification and risk assessment.
For example, NLP algorithms can assess whether client communications adhere
to MiFID II disclosure r equirements or whether contract terms align with IFRS
revenue recognition principles. By automating the analysis of unstructured data,
NLP significantly broadens the scope of audit processes and enhances auditors’
abilitytoidentifycompliancegaps(FotohandMugwira2025; Onyenahazi2025).

212 A.H.FarahaniandN.Nahidi
AI-powered Robotic Process Automation (RPA) further streamlines audit work-
flows by automating routine, rule-based audit tasks. RPA tools can automatically
perform data extraction, reconciliation, and reporting tasks, freeing auditors to focus
on higher-value activities such as risk analysis and judgment-based evaluations.
Within robo-advisory platforms, RPA can automate t hereconciliationoftransaction
data with accounting records, the generation of audit reports, and the monitoring
ofkeyriskindicators,therebyenhancingauditefficiencyandreducingoperational
costs(CharlotteandJacob2024; Lacurezeanu et al.2020).
A key innovation in AI-driven auditing is the development of Continuous
Auditing and Continuous Monitoring (CA/CM) frameworks. CA/CM leverages AI
and real-time data analytics to provide ongoing assurance over financial processes,
rather than periodic retrospective assessments. For robo-advisors, CA/CM enables
real-time monitoring of algorithmic decisions, cl ient transactions, and compliance
metrics,allowingauditorstodetectandaddressissuesastheyarise.Thisproactive
approach enhances the resilience of financial systems and supports a culture of
continuousimprovementandregulatorycompliance.
Explainable AI (XAI) is increasingly critical for ensuring the transparency and
auditability of AI-drivenfinancialprocesses(BarredoArrietaetal.2020). As robo-
advisors rely on complex machine learning models, it is essential that auditors
can understand and explain the rationale behind algorithmic decisions. XAI tools
provide interpretable insights into model behavior, enabling auditors to verify
compliance with fairness, accountability, andtransparencystandards.Byenhancing
theexplainabilityofAIsystems,XAIsupportsmoreeffectiveauditsandstrengthens
stakeholdertrustinAI-drivenfinancialservices(Cheong2024; Kuiper et al.2021).
A practical example of advanced AI-driven auditing can be seen in the practices
of KPMG’s Clara platform. Clara integrates AI, ML, and NLP tools to automate
audit processes, perform advanced data analytics, and provide continuous mon-
itoring of client operations. By leveraging Clara, KPMG auditors can efficiently
analyze large volumes of financial data,detectanomaliesinrealtime,andgenerate
insightful audit reports. This advanced auditing approach has been successfully
appliedtoseveralfintechandrobo-advisoryclients,demonstratingitseffectiveness
inenhancingauditqualityandregulatorycompliance(KPMG2024, 2025).
Another leading example is Deloitte’s Cortex AI platform, which offers advanced
anomaly detection and risk assessment capabilities. Cortex AI employs ML algo-
rithms to continuously monitor transactional data, identify emerging risks, and pro-
vide real-time insights to auditors. In the context of robo-advisory platforms, Cortex
AI enables proactive detection of compliance breaches, operational anomalies, and
financial irregularities, thereby strengthening the platform’s control environment
and supportingrobustregulatorycompliance.Thesecasestudiesillustratethetrans-
formative potential of AI in automating audit processes and detecting anomalies,
setting new benchmarks for audit quality and effectiveness in the era of AI-driven
finance(Deloitte2025).

6 Ethical Considerations in AI-Au ditedFinancialReports
The adoption of AI in auditing processes introduces a range of ethical challenges
that demand critical attention from regulators, auditors, and financial institutions.
As robo-advisory platforms increasingly rely on AI-driven audits for compliance
andriskmanagement,concernsariseregardingalgorithmicbias,fairness,account-
ability,transparency,anddataprivacy(Deloitte2025). The complexity and opacity
of AI models, especially black-box machine learning systems, can obscure audit
outcomes, leading to questions about the trustworthiness and ethical integrity of AI-
audited financial reports. Addressing these concerns requires a multi-dimensional
ethicalframeworkthatintegratestechnical,legal,andsocialperspectives(Barham
etal.2024).
One of the most pressing ethical risks in AI auditing is algorithmic bias. AI
models used infinancialauditsareoftentrainedonhistoricaldatathatmayreflect

214 A.H.FarahaniandN.Nahidi
existing biases or structural inequalities. If unchecked, these biases can propagate
through audit outcomes, leading to unfair or discriminatory financial reporting. For
example, biased anomaly detection algorithms may disproportionately flag certain
types of transactions or clients, thereby undermining the fairness and objectivity
of the audit pr ocess. Ethical AI auditing requires rigorous bias detection and
mitigation strategies, including diverse training datasets, fairness-aware machine
learningtechniques,andcontinuousmonitoringforbias(Kamalarubanetal.2024).
Transparency is another foundational ethical principle in AI auditing. Stake-
holders including investors, regulators, and clients must beabletounderstandhow
AI-generatedauditfindingsareproduced(Mökander2023). Yet, many modern AI
models, especially deep learning algorithms, lack interpretability, posing a signif-
icant barrier to transparency (Doshi-Velez and Kim 2017). Explainable AI (XAI)
is emerging as a crucial tool for addressing this challenge, offering interpretable
insights intomodelbehavioranddecision-makingprocesses(RegulationandForum
2022). Integrating XAI into AI-audited financial reporting enables auditors to justify
their conclusionsandfosterstrustamongstakeholders(Guidottietal.2019).
Accountability is closely linked to transparency but extends to the assignment of
responsibility for AI-driven audit outcomes. In traditional auditing, human auditors
are held accountable for errors or misconduct. However, with AI-driv enprocesses,
responsibilitycanbecomediffusedacrossmultipleactors,includingdatascientists,
softwaredevelopers,andauditors(Cobbeetal.2023). Ethical AI auditing requires
clear accountability structures that define who is responsible for AI system design,
deployment, oversight, and outcomes (Raji et al. 2020). Auditors must remain
ultimately accountable for ensuring the integrity of financial reports, even when
AItoolsareusedtoautomateaudittasks(OECD2023).
Data privacy is another key ethical concern in AI-audited financial reports. Robo-
advisory platforms process vast amounts of sensitive personal and financial data,
whichareusedtotrainandoperateAIauditmodels(GoodmanandFlaxman2017).
Ethical auditing demands strict compliance with data protection regulations such as
the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), a swellasbestpracticesfordata
anonymization, encryption, and secure storage (OECD 2023). Moreover, auditors
must ensure that AI systems do not inadvertently expose or misuse personal data
duringauditprocesses(OECD2024).
The UK’s Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum (DRCF) highlights the evolv-
ing role of regulators in shaping ethical standards for algorithmic auditing. Their
2022 report emphasizes the need for collaboration between regulators, industry,
and academia to develop ethical frameworks for auditing AI systems. The DRCF
also underscores the importance of algorithmic transparency, regulator access to
AI systems, and the creation of sector-specific ethical guidelines. Their findings
offeravaluableroadmapforenhancingtheethicaloversightofAI-auditedfinancial
reports, aligning with broader calls for responsible AI governance (DRCF 2022;
PWC 2024).
A compelling real-world example of ethical AI auditing can be found in PwC’s
Halo for Blockchain platform. Halo is designed with embedded XAItoolsandstrict
dataprivacysafeguards,enablingtransparent,accountable,andprivacy-preserving

Robo-AdvisoryandAuditing:InternalandExternalControls 215
audits of blockchain-based financial systems. PwC’s approach demonstrates how
ethical considerations can be operationalized in AI auditing, balancing the benefits
of automation with the imperatives of fairness, accountability, transparency, and
privacy(PWC2024).
Similarly, EY’s use of XAI in AI-driven audits for financial services clients
highlights best practices in ethical auditing. EY integrates XAI methods to provide
interpretable audit outputs, while also employing comprehensive bias detection,
accountability frameworks, and GDPR-compliant data practices. This ethical-
by-design approach ensures that AI-audited financial reports uphold the highest
standardsofintegrityandtrustworthiness.AsAIauditingcontinuestoevolve,such
examplessetanimportantprecedentfortheindustry(EY2025).

7 Conclusion and P racticalImplications
The integration of AI into auditing processes within robo-advisory platforms
offers transformative potential, enabling continuous monitoring, enhanced anomaly
detection, and more efficient, accurate financial oversight. However, this evolution
also introduces complex regulatory, technical, and ethical challenges that must be
carefully navigated. As demonstrated throughout this chapter, ensuring compliance
with key g lobal standards such as IFRS, GAAP, Basel III, and MiFID II requires
robustinternalandexternalcontrolframeworks,supportedbyadvanced AI-driven
tools and transparent governance practices (Chang et al. 2018). AI’s role in
automating audit processes extends beyond efficiency gains; it enhances audit
quality by enabling real-time insights and proactive risk management (Chang et
al. 2018). Yet, the increasing reliance on complex algorithms necessitates the
adoption of Explainable AI, bias mitigation strategies, and rigorous accountability
mechanismstoensureethicalintegrityandstakeholdertrust(BarredoArrietaetal.
2020). These insights underscore the need for collaborative regulatory frameworks
and sector-specific ethical standardstoaddressemergingchallengesinAIauditing.
For practitioners, this evolving landscape demands a shift in audit method-
ologies and skillsets. Auditors must increasingly collaborate with data scientists,
AI engineers, and compliance officers to design, monitor, and interpret AI-driven
audit systems (Chang et al. 2018). Furthermore, organizations should prioritize
the development of ethical AI governance frameworks, embedding transparency,
fairness,andaccountabilityintothecoreoftheirauditpractices(OECD2020a).
For regulators, the rapid advancement of AI auditing technologies calls for adap-
tive and forward-looking policy development. This includes promoting transparency
in algorithmic systems, fo steringcross-sectorcollaboration,andenhancingregula-
tors’technicalcapacitytoauditAIsystemseffectively(DRCF2022). Collaborative
efforts between regulators, industry leaders, and academia will be essential to ensure
that AI auditing serve s the broader public interest, upholds market integrity, and
protectsconsumerrights.
For students and future professionals, the key takeaway is that AI-driven
auditing is not simply a technical enhancement; it is a paradigm shift that requires
rethinking traditional audit roles, ethical responsibilities, and regulatory approaches.
Developing interdisciplinary expertise in AI, finance, law, and ethics will be critical
for succeeding in this dynamic and increasingly complex field. As AI continues
to reshape the financial auditing landscape, a commitment to ethical, transparent,
andaccountable practiceswillremainthefoundationoftrustandresilienceinAI-
poweredfinancialecosystems.

Cybersecurity Risk an d Robo-Advisory
Nader Virk and MohammedAl-Khalidi
Abstract This chapter outlines the increasing cybersecurity risks in digital and
AI-driven finance while focusing on robo-advisors. This chapter contextualises
robo-advisory architecture, threat taxonomy and entry points, and how AI presence
adds to cybersecurity attack surface area. Then it moves into a deeper analysis of key
attack vectors like insecure APIs, misconfigured cloud infrastructure, and exposed
data pipelines as common entry points. Building on this, the chapter examines
advanced attack techniques, including adversarial machine learning methods such
as data poisoning, model evasion, and backdoor insertion, targeting AI decision-
making reliability. These techniques exploit AI model complexity,highlightingthe
need for explainable AI (xAI). Advanced Persistent Threats increasingly deploy
these for long-term unauthorised access. Furthermore, the chapter investigates
systemic vulnerabilities from interconnected digital ecosystems, including cloud
services and distributed computing. Decentralised finance (DeFi) asset risks like
smartcontractexploits,flashloanattacks,andoraclemanipulationaregivenspecial
attentionasnovelthreats.
The chapter also addresses the growing importance of data privacy in AI-powered
financial services, especially for robo-advisors handling sensitive client data. It
examines increasing regulatory scrutiny and emphasises the need for compliance,
transparency, and robust ethical standards. Ethical considerations like algorithmic
bias and trust are integrated throughout. Towards the end, thischapteralsoexplores
theroleplayedbyAIandxAIapplicationsinforensicaccountingandauditingfor
frauddetectionandinvestigations.Itconcludeswithstrategicrecommendationsfor
securingdigitalwealthmanagementplatforms,encompassingadvancedencryption,

1 Introd uction
Cybersecurity risk is scaling in financial services as they are mapped increasingly
into digital space. Global loss projections are expected to be approximately 10.5
trillion USD by the end of 2025. This underscores the macro relevance of cyber
resilience for investors and policymakers (Morgan 2024). International Monetary
Fund (2024) report highlights that for financial firms direct losses might appear
relatively small; however, the risk of extreme losses—at least 2.5 billion USD—is on
the rise and poses a threat to macro-financial stability. The emerging robo-advisory
financial landscape is no exception. The widespread use of AI in robo-advisory
platforms introduces significant systemic and cybersecurity risks. These challenges
stem from the inherent characteristics of AI systems and their growing reliance on
interconnected digital in frastructure.Thesemayincludetheamplificationofmarket
instabilityandcorrelatedtradesfortherelianceonasmallnumberofdatavendors,
and increased adoption of similar AI models. Consequently, herding in financial
markets—algorithmic synchronised trading—will amplify market volatility and
increasessystemicrisk(Kirilenkoetal.2017; Budish etal.2015). Automation and
Autonomy features in robo-advisory architecture further inflate these ri sksandhave
beenflaggedbysupervisors(FSB2017, 2024;ESMA2025).
This chapter outlines a typical robo-advisory architecture, attack surface area—
taxonomy and entry points, and convergence and systemic nature of the cyber-
security threats. A deeper analysis of several attack vectors, data contamination
in robo-advisory systems, and the convergence of attack vectors follows. Then
dimensions of deepfake concerns, identity theft, and vulnerabilities linked to human
inter-looping in robo-advisory are considered. This chapter allocates considerable
space to the impact of AI and xAI in forensic accounting and auditing to handle
typicalreportingandcorporatemisconductandevidentialscopeincomplianceand
legalsettings.
2 Cybersecurity Threat La ndscapein Robo-Advisory
Robo-advisory platforms aggregate private client information and operate over
application programming interface (API)-driven and cloud and AI-enabled infras-
tructures. They also connect, assimilate, and transform data from external news-
feeds, data supply lines, and market rails. This architecture creates multiple

DeFi platforms, particularly those powered by AI, and distributed ledger tech-
nologies (DLT), rely on a complex interplay of APIs, data flows, and chain
securitised and smart contract infrastructures. While these interconnections drive
efficiency and innovation, they simultaneously expand the scope of exposure to
cybersecurity risks, offering adversaries multiple entry points into robo-advisory
systems,Fig.2 highlights different attack points in a typicalrobo-advisoryplatform.
Table2 outlines common attack vectors for robo-advisory systems and users. Three
categories of attack vectors stand out as both prevalent and uniquely damaging:
insecure APIs, data contamination, and robo-advisory-specific exploits targeting
smart contracts, and oracle mechanisms—no cryptographic security, poor data
latency,amongothers.

3.2  Data Contamination and Model IntegrityAttacks
Robo-advisors and AI-driven financial platforms rely heavily on large, diverse
datasets to train and update models for portfolio allocation, risk assessment, and
fraud detection. This dependence makes them vulnerable to data contamination,
a form of adversarial manipulation where malicious actors inject misleading or
poisoneddataintotrainingoroperationalpipelines.
•  Data poisoning: Corrupting datasets with biased or fraudulent entries can skew
model outputs, leading to misallocation of funds or faulty risk assessments. In
2021, researchers demonstrated how adversarial data contamination could trick
arobo-advisorprototypeintosystematicallyunderweightingblue-chipequities,
producingsystematicallyunbalancedportfolios(Yussuf2025). Similar risks have

228 N.VirkandM.Al-Khalidi
been highlighted in credit scoring where manipulated datasets can causebiased
orfraudulentlendingdecisions.
• Model evasion: Carefully crafted adversarial inputs exploit model blind spots,
bypassing fraud detection systems or misclassifying risk profiles. A notable
case occurred when fraudsters exploited machine learning-driven anti-money-
laundering (AML) systems by structuring transactions just below reporting
thresholds, evading detection algorithms. These “ structuring” attacks resemble
adversarial examples in vision models, but in interconnected systems, they
allow criminals to launder money without raising alarms (Borrajo et al. 2020).
Conceptually, this threat is also applicable to robo-advisory systems: users might
ex ploitthesethresholdswiththeserviceproviders.
• Backdoor insertion: Attackers embed triggers within training data that allow
them to manipulate outputs later without raising suspicion. Academic studies
have shown how backdoored financial prediction models can be induced to
make specific trades when encountering hidden triggers such as acoustic data
positioning (Mengara 2024). While not yet publicly tied to a real-world heist,
the threat is emerg ing as financial institutions increasingly outsource AI model
development.
These threats highlight the dual role of data: as a driver of financial intelligence
and a potential attack vector. Contaminated data undermine not only technical
reliabilitybutalsoregulatorycomplianceandclienttrust.
3.3 DeFi-Specific Exploits Applicable toRobo-Advisory
Systems
DeFi introduces unique systemic risks due to its reliance on immutable code and
external data feeds. Unlike traditional financial systems, robo-advisors within the
DeFi family of systems often lack intermediaries capable of halting malicious
activitiesoncetheyareinmotion.Twoexploitclassesareparticularlycritical:
• Smart contract vulnerabilities: Errors in contract logic, such as re-entrancy
flaws or unchecked arithmetic operations, can allow attackers to drain liquidity
pools, mint unauthorised tokens, or trigger cascading failures across intercon-
nected protocols. The DAO hack of 2016 remains the most famous example:
attackers exploited a re-entrancy bug in the DAO’s Ethereum smart contract to
siphon $60 million in Ether (Li 2024). In 2022, a bug in the Wormhole bridge
smart contract allowed hackers to mint 120,000 ETH (then worth over $320
million) without proper collateralisation, highlighting how contract logic flaws
canbecatastrophic(Azadetal.2025).
• Oracle manipulation: Oracles bridge on-chain and off-chain environments,
supplying asset prices and market data. Attackers can manipulate oracle inputs
through flash loan-driven market swings or by compromising the oracle infras-

CybersecurityRiskandRobo-Advisory 229
tructure itself. Distorted price feeds can lead to under-collateralised loans, forced
liquidations, or arbitrage exploitation at systemic scale. In 2020, the bZx protocol
suffered a series of oracle manipulation attacks, where flash l oans were used
to distort price feeds. Attackers extracted around $8 million by borrowing and
selling assets at artificially inflated valuations (Deng 2024). More recently, in
2022, Mango Markets on Solana was drained of $114 million when an attacker
manipulatedoracle-basedcollateralvaluationstoborrowfarbeyondtheiractual
holdings(Scharfman2024).
These exploits illustrate how digital systems introduce not only technological
vulnerabilities but also economic attack surfa ces, where adversaries weaponise
marketdynamicsinadditiontocode.
3.4 The Convergence of Attack Vectors Into Sophisticated
Pathways
Attack vectors can be integrated into modular cyberattacks. A sophisticated adver-
sary may chain them together—for example, by leveraging an insecure API to
access training pipelines, contaminating models to influence trading strategies,
and finally exploiting system protocols th rough manipulated oracles to maximise
financial gain. This convergence of technical, economic, and data-driven attack
vectorsunderscoresthenecessityformulti-layereddefencestrategies.
Robo-advisory platforms, which are API-first and cloud-hosted, have multiple
exposure points. Authorisation flaws, excessive data exposure, and weak rate-
limiting in API-first architectures can enable th e enumeration of client data or
tampering with configurations that influence model inputs (Florackis et al. 2023).
Similarly, misconfigured cloud resources and leaked credentials increase lateral-
movement risk into data lakes and feature stores, concentrating thedamagefroma
singlekeycompromise(Aldasoroetal.2022). The model supply chain introduces
additional attack surfaces: poisoning of historical market or behavioural data can
bias training, while adversarial perturbations or manipulated feeds can cause real-
timemisallocation.
The use of blockchains: oracles bridging off-chain data to on-chain environments
are a critical point of failure. Experimental systemisations show thatdesignchoices
can affect truthfulness, latency, and manipulation resistance (Eskandari et al.
2021). DeFi exposures complicate matters when robo-advisors integrate tokenised
products or yield strategies. Foundational analyses of decentralised exchanges
show that transaction reordering and miner/maximal extractable value (MEV) can
distort prices and create consensus instability, enabling adversaries to profit from
frontrunningandsandwiching(Daianetal.2019). Flash loans lower capital barriers
for complex exploit chains; empirical and constructive work demonstrates how
attackers can compose protocolvulnerabilitiestomanipulatepriceswithinasingle
block(Qinetal.2021). Recent program analysis advances can evensynthesiseprof-

230 N.VirkandM.Al-Khalidi
itable flash loan exploit transactions automatically, raising the baseline capabilityof
adversaries(Chenetal.2024).
For robo-advisory connectors, this implies a need for independent pricing, circuit
breakers, and strict segregation between core advisory logic and experimental
DeFi interfaces. Data governance should include source authentication, lineage
tracking, canary datasets, and continuous monitoring to detect distribution shifts
andanomalouscorrelationsconsistentwithpoisoningorfeedtampering(Eskandari
etal.2021; Florackis et al.2023).
4 Deepfake Concerns inRobo-Advisory
The rise of deepfakes has introduced a critical new dimension of cyber risk
to the DeFi ecosystem. Within robo-advisory systems, deepfakes compromise
identity verification, client authentication,dataintegrity,andtheoveralltrustupon
which automated financial advice depends (Chesney and Citron 2019; Maras and
Alexandrou2019).
4.1 Deepfakes and the Erosion of DigitalTrust
Deepfakes exploit neural networks to produce highly realistic yet fabricated images,
voices, and videos that convincingly impersonate real individuals. This techno-
logical capability poses a direct threat to digital trust, the foundation of online
financial engagement. As robo-advisors rely on AI-mediated interactions, often
without human oversight, synthetic identities can manipulate clients or staff to
executefraudulenttransactions(AithalandAithal2021).
Remote onboarding processes, particularly video-based Know Your Customer
(KYC) protocols, are vulnerable to deepfake spoofing. A falsified video identity
can subv ertbiometricverificationandleadtounauthorisedaccountcreationorfund
access(Europol2022). Such attacks not only compromise individual clients but can
also erode publicconfidenceinthereliabilityofautomatedfinancialsystems.
4.2 Threat Vectors and A ttackScenarios
Deepfakes intersect with and amplify existing attack vectors in AI-driven finance,
transforming theoretical vulnerabilities into practical, high-impact risks. Several
real-world incidents and credible demonstrations have illustrated how synthetic
mediacanbeweaponisedtounderminefinancialintegrityandclienttrust.

CybersecurityRiskandRobo-Advisory 231
4.2.1 Synthetic Identity Fraud
Fraudsters increasingly use deepfake-generated images and videos to bypass bio-
metric verification systems. A prominent example emerged in 2023, when the
Hong Kong police reported a case in which criminals used AI-generated deepfake
video calls toimpersonatecompanyexecutivesanddefraudamultinationalfirmof
approximately HK$200 million (around USD 25 million) (South China Morning
Post 2023). Attackers convincingly mimicked the facial and vocal features of
legitimate employees during an online meeting, successfully authorising large-scale
fund transfers. This incident demonstrates how deepfakes can be combined with
synthetic identity creation and social engineering to exploit remote onboarding and
transaction authorisation processes in fintech and robo-advisory platforms. Given
the reliance of these systems on automated KYC and digital identity verification,
thepotentialforsimilarexploitationissubstantial.
4.2.2 Voice Phishing and AI-Drive nSocialEngineering
Deepfake voice technologies have already been deployed in financial fraud with
significant success. In 2019, criminals used an AI-generated replica of a CEO’s
voice to convince an employ ee at a UK energy firm’s German subsidiary to
transfer AC220,000 to a fraudulent account (The Wall Street Journal 2019). The
attackers replicated the executive’s accent and speech patterns so accurately that
the employee believed the instructions were authentic. Such incidents exemplify the
evolution of “vishing” (voice phishing) into AI-driven deception. As robo-advisors
increasingly integrate voice-based user interfa ces and hybrid human AI advisory
models, the potential for adversaries to impersonate trusted individuals, including
clients,advisors,orcomplianceofficers,posesamajoroperationalandreputational
risk(Europol2022).
4.2.3 Market Manipulation Via FabricatedMedia
Deepfakes can also be leveraged for strategic disinformation and market manipula-
tion. In 2020, a falsified video purporting to show a US CEO making a controversial
statement briefly circulated online, leading to a measurable dip in the company’s
stock before the video was debunked (Nguyen et al. 2022). Similarly, in 2023,
analysts at Reuters identified an emerging trend of AI-generated fake news anchors
used in state-linked disinformation campaigns promoting false economic data and
stockcommentary(Reuters2023). Such incidents demonstrate how deepfakes can
indirectly influence robo-advisory algorithms that rely on sentiment analysis or
news feeds for portfolio recommendations. A targeted synthetic video or voice
clip could distort data inputs used for automated investment decisions, amplifying
volatility and creating systemic information risks in digital wealth management
systems.

4.3 Model and Data Vulnerabilities
Deepfakes also present indirect systemic risks by contaminating datasets or AI
models used in robo-advisory. Synthetic data introduced into client communication
logs or sentiment analysis systems can degrade model accuracy, bias financial
recommendations, or trigger compliance violations (Goodfellow et al. 2020).
As robo-advisors increasingly integrate natural language processing (NLP) and
video interfaces, deepfake-generated inputs could be misclassified as legitimate.
This contamination introduces feedback risks, whereby AI models inadvertently
learn from manipulated data, reinforcing misinformation or unethical decision
patterns(Brundageetal.2018). In 2024, the UK’s National Cyber Security Centre
(NCSC) warned of model extraction attacks targeting financial sector chatbots,
where attackers attempted to reconstruct proprietary algorithms through iterative
querying (NCSC 2024). Accordingly, an attacker could probe a robo-advisor’s
Large Language Model (LLM) to infer risk models, investment strategies, or
compliancethresholds,compromisingintellectualpropertyandenablingadversarial
marketbehaviour.

CybersecurityRiskandRobo-Advisory 233
4.4 Detection and M itigationStrategies
Mitigating deepfake and AI-driven threats in robo-advisory systems requires a
multi-layered approach that combines technological, operational, and regulatory
measures. In addition to AI-based detection algorithms, several complementary
strategiesarecriticalforsafeguardingdigitalwealthmanagementplatforms.
4.4.1 Liveness De tection
Liveness detection during video authentication ensures that clients are physically
present and not represented by synthetic media such as deepfake videos or recorded
clips. Modern systems confirm real-time interaction through motion and gesture
verification, depth analysis, and behavioural cues, providing a robust defence
against impersonation and identity fraud. Banks including HSBC and Standard
Chartered have successfully deployed such systems to mitigate fraudulent remote
accountopenings(Europol2022).
4.4.2 Blockchain-Enabled Digital Id entityVerification
This provides immutable and tamper-proof records of client identity. Decentralised
identity frameworks and smart contracts allow institutions to verify credentials
cryptographically while maintaining transparent, auditable trails. Pilot initiatives
by the Sovrin Fo undation and fintech projects in Singapore and Switzerland
demonstrate improved security and regulatory compliance for KYC and AML
processes(Mungai2024).
4.4.3 Inter-institutional Intelligence Sharing
Intelligence sharing enhances early detection of synthetic identity threats, deep-
fake campaigns, and adversarial AI attacks. Financial institutions can contribute
anonymised indicators of compromise to centralised repositories, enabling pattern
recognition across organisations. Regulatory technology tools facilitate secure,
compliant data exchange, while initiatives such as Financial Services Information
Sharing and Analysis Center (FS-ISAC) provide global alerts on AI-driven scams
affectingrobo-advisoryplatforms.
Together, these measures form a layered defence that strengthens security,
supports regulatory compliance, and protects client trust in AI-powered financial
services.

234 N.VirkandM.Al-Khalidi
4.5 Regulatory and E thicalConsiderations
Regulatory frameworks are evolving to address synthetic media threats. The EU
Artificial Intelligence Act (2024) mandates transparency and disclosure for AI-
generated content, while GDPR provisions on data accuracy and consent apply
directly to deepfake identity misuse. In the United S tates, the Federal Trade
Commission (FTC) and Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) have
both issued warnings regarding synthetic identity fraud in digital finance (FTC
2023).
Ethically, deepfake manipulation challenges principles of fairness, authenticity,
and accountabilityinAIdeployment(FloridiandCowls2019). For robo-advisory,
maintaining transparency in client interactions and ensuring data authenticity are
essentialtosustainingconsumertrustandupholdingfiduciaryduties.
4.6 Strategic Implications fo rRobo-AdvisorySecurity
A holistic security approach must integrate deepfake detection and prevention
withinbroadercybersecurityarchitectures.Recommendedpracticesinclude:
• Continuous AI-based monitoring for sy ntheticmediaanomalies
• Behavioural analytics to identify inconsistencies withclientinteractionbaselines
• Staff awareness training to recognise deepfa ke-enabledfraudtactics
• Collaborative partnerships with regulators, cybersecurity firms, and fintech
associations to devel opstandardisedresponseframeworks
Ultimately, shielding robo-advisory platforms from deepfake threats transcends a
purely technical challenge; it becomes a fundamental test of infrastructural integrity,
ethical resilience, and institutional trustworthiness within the age of synthetic
reality.

and intermediaries interact with increasingly autonomous advisory platforms, cog-
nitive biases, behavioural lapses, and weak security practices can undermine even
themostadvancedtechnicalsafeguards.

5.1  Phishing and SocialEngineering
Phishing remains one of the most prevalent enablers of id entity theft in financial
technology (Zhou et al. 2023). Attackers exploit clients’ trust in branded commu-
nication to harvest login credentials, personal data, or multi-factor authentication
tokens. In 2024, the FS-ISAC reported a marked increase in AI-generated phishing
emails targeting investment clients. These campaigns often combine traditional
phishing with “vishing” and “smishing” techniques, as well as deepfake voice or
videoimpersonationsofsupportstaff(FS-ISAC2024c).
Robo-advisory clients are particularly vulnerable because of limited direct
human interaction—an environment that encourages implicit trust in automated
digital communication. Mitigation strategies include adaptive phishing detection
filters driven by natural language processing, client aw  areness campaigns, and
transaction-levelverificationprocessesthatrequiresecondaryconfirmationthrough
securechannels(e.g.,in-appbiometricsortime-lockedapprovals).
5.2  Credential Theft and We akAuthenticationPractices
Credential theft is frequently facilitated by password reuse, inadequate multi-
factor authentication, or insecure data storage. Compromised credentials can grant
attackers full access to client portfolios, enabling unauthorised trades or fund
withdrawals. According to Verizon’s Data Breach Investigations Report (2024),
over 60 per cent of financial sector breaches still originate from stolen or weak
credentials.

236 N.VirkandM.Al-Khalidi
In robo-advisory contexts, credential theft can occur through both client-side
and back-office vulnerabilities. Cloud-based authentication services and third-
party API integrations magnify the exposure. Advanced mitigation approaches
include hardware-bound multi-factor authentication, behavioural biometrics that
analyse keystrokeordeviceusagepatterns,andzero-trustidentityframeworksthat
continuouslyverifybothuseranddeviceintegrity.
5.3 Insider Threats and BehaviouralRisks
Even in highly automated systems, human operators—developers, analysts, and
compliance officers—retain privileged access that can be exploited deliberately
or inadvertently. Insider threats range from data exfiltration and model tampering
to negligence leading to unauthorised exposure of client information. A notable
example occurred in 2022 when a European wealth-management firm discovered
that a contractor had exported anonymised but reconstructable client data from its
robo-advisoryanalyticsenvironment,breachingGDPRconfidentialityrequirements
(ENISA2025).
Mitigation requires a combination of least-privilege access control, continuous
monitoring of priv ilegedaccounts,andorganisationalcultureinterventions.
Behavioural analytics can detect anomalous employee activity, while periodic
ethics and cybersecurity training reinforce accountability. From a governance per-
spective, integrating insider-risk management into the firm’s overall AI assurance
frameworkalignssecuritywithfiduciaryresponsibility.
5.4 Jurisdictional and Regulatory Human Factors
Identity management in global robo-advisory platforms often crosses multiple
legal jurisdictions, each with distinct standards for privacy, authentication, and
liability. Discrepancies between GDPR (EU), GLBA (US), and PDPA (Asia-Pacific)
can result in regulatory blind spots that criminals exploit by routing identity
theft operations through less stringent regions. Moreover, differences in reporting
obligationsmaydelaycross-bordercoordinationandincidentresponse.
To mitigate such jurisdictional vulnerabilities, firms are increasingly adopting
unified identity governance frameworks anchored in international standards such as
ISO 27701 and NIST 800-63. Participation incross-jurisdictionalregulatorysand-
boxes also promotes harmonisation of best practices for digital identity assurance
andbreachnotification.

CybersecurityRiskandRobo-Advisory 237
5.5 Strategic Implications
Human-centred vulnerabilities illustrate that even the most sophisticated AI infras-
tructures remain only as secure as the individuals who design, operate, and use
them. For robo-advisory firms, embedding human-factor resilience into cyberse-
curity architectures—through continuous education, behavioural analytics, ethical
governance, and cross-border policy alignment—is essential to preserving both
operationalintegrityandpublictrust.
6 AI and xAI in Forensic AccountingandAuditing
Another area in financial services and DeFI solutions where AI and ML are
increasingly reshaping is forensic accounting and auditing. Traditional methods in
financial reporting and auditing work rely heavily on manual inspection, sampling,
and rule-based analytics. Whereas AI systems enable detection of subtle and large-
scale patterns that humans would miss. However, the adoption of black-box models
introduces risks ofopacity,due-diligenceandlegalliability,regulatoryuncertainty,
and ethical concerns. This is where xAI becomes indispensable. Explainable
AI bridges the gap between predictive accuracy and interpretability, ensuring
accountability and transparency in financial forensics (Zhang et al. 2022), which
becomes essential evidence to track cybersecurity vulnerabilities that exploit the
use of AI approaches—from data normalisation to portfolio choice/construction
models—in the post-attack scenarios. That is xAI providesevidence(digital)—just
notexplanations—inadversescenariosinrespondingtocompliance,fiduciary,and
legalchallenges.
6.1 The Role of AI in ForensicAccounting
AI-enabled tools can process structured and unstructured financial data at scale,
including general ledgers, invoices, contracts, and communications. ML models
detect anomalies in transaction flows, classify potentially fraudulent entries, and flag
irregularities that merit investigation. For in stance, ensemble learning techniques
have demonstrated significant effectiveness in identifying accounting fraud across
large datasets, outperforming traditional regression and ratio analysis (Bao et
al. 2020). Neural networks, decision trees, and support vector machines allow
forensic auditors to capture nonlinear dependencies, and complex fraud schemes
thatconventionalmethodsfailtoidentify.
Beyond fraud detection, AI is increasingly applied to compliance monitoring,
AML surveillance, and detection of financial misstatements. By embedding AI
in auditing workflows, firms can improve efficiency while reducing human error,

238 N.VirkandM.Al-Khalidi
thereby reallocating auditors’ attention to higher-judgement tasks. Yet, these effi-
ciency gains are tempered by thechallengeofdefendingalgorithmicconclusionsin
regulatoryorcourtroomsettings.
6.2 Why Explainability Matters
The black-box nature of advanced ML models conflicts with the evidentiary
requirements of forensic accounting. Courts, regulators, and professional standards
require that decisions be justifiable, auditable, and replicable. xAI tools such as
SHAP (Shapley Additive Explanations) and LIME (Local Interpretable Model-
agnostic Explanations) clarify how input features contribute to model outputs,
therebyprovidinganaudittrailofalgorithmicreasoning(Zhangetal.2022). Zhou
et al. (2023) emphasise that user-centred xAI can align investigative needs with
model design, producing explanations that regulators and auditors can understand
without diluting predictive accuracy. Table 6 lists the application of different xAI
approaches inforensicaccountingandauditing.
Virk (2025) stresses that trustworthy AI adoption in financial services depends on
embedding explainability, ethical safeguards, and governance frameworks. Without
these, AI risks amplifying systemic vulnerabilities, bias, and public mistrust. For
forensic accounting, explainability thus transforms from a technical add-on to a
legalandethicalnecessity.

6.5 Challenges and Po licyImplications
While AI and xAI provide powerful capabilities, several challenges remain. First,
forensic datasets are often imbalanced, with relatively few fraud cases compared
to legitimate transactions. This complicates training and may yield biased models.
Second, data privacy regulations constrain access to sensitive records, creating
tension between investigative scope and compliance. Third, adversarial manipula-
tion of inputs such as falsified invoices or doctored communications can mislead
both humans and machines, requiring robust data validation. Addressing these
limitations, the training datasets should therefore capitalise on audit logs, model
interpretability, and mechanisms to correct for bias. These elements should be
integratedintodesignprocessesfromtheoutset.
Policy recommendations from the UK Parliament inquiry highlight the need
for governance frameworks, auditability requirements, andprofessionaltrainingto
ensure responsible AI deployment (Virk 2025). Crucially, achieving auditability
requires that these deployed systems must develop tools that offer justifications for
their actions; this need for fundamental AI/xAI utilisation is especially pronounced
in forensic accounting and auditing where results have to be utilised in legal
proceedings or compliance documentation. To support this shift, regulators ma y
need to establish minimum standards for explainability in audit tools, alongside
ethicalguidelinestomitigatealgorithmicbias.FirmsadoptingAIforensicsolutions
must, therefore, balance innovation with compliance, transparency, and societal
trust.
7 Summary
Robo-advisors move beyond simple rule-based allocation to perform dynamic,
multi-factor analysis, aligning a client’s specific risk tolerance and financial goals
with a diversified portfolio. This algorithmic approach ensures consistency and
mitigates potential human biases in security or fund selection, providing a more
transparent and auditable investment process. The convergence of automated tech-
nology and core financial services is set to accelerate, fundamentally reshaping
capital allocation towards optimised efficiency, accessibility, and robust risk man-
agement.TheemergenceofagenticAIintegrationwillfurtherenableautonomous
tradingandhyper-personalisation.
Beyond robo-advisory, AI and xAI are also reshaping another critical area
of financial services—forensic accounting and auditing. Traditional auditing and
compliancefunctions,oncereliantonmanualsamplingandrules-basedchecks,are

CybersecurityRiskandRobo-Advisory 241
being transformed through AI-driven anomaly detection and explainable modelling.
xAI bridges predictive accuracy and interpretability, ensuring accountability and
transparency in financial forensics. These tools allow auditors to trace how algo-
rithms flag irregularities, detect information content in misstatements, or detect
potential fraud, which becomes vital evidence in post-incident investigations involv-
ingcybersecuritybreaches ordatamanipulation. Inthisway,AIandxAInotonly
enhance operational efficiency but also strengthen the evidentiary and compliance
foundationsofdigitalfinance—complementingtheautomationandpersonalisation
advancesseeninrobo-advisorysystems.
Unfortunately, at the same time, this technological sophistication will heighten
systemic exposures and risks. As highly interconnected, data-driven, and cloud-
hosted systems, robo-advisory platforms face concentrated exposure to cybersecu-
rity threats. Their inherent interconnectedness makes them susceptible to various
cyber dangers, while their reliance on external data sources, NLP, Gen-AI textual
analysis, and cloud infrastructure significantly expands the attack surface area.
Moreover, the dependency on similar AI models and concentrated data vendors
raises concerns of herding, procyclicality, and amplified volatility in stressed
markets(FSB2024;ESMA2 025).
The financial impact of cybersecurity threats is tangible and is expected to
intensify as robo-advisory platforms become increasingly interconnected within
digital financial ecosystems. The highly networked nature of these systems means
that cyber incidents are rarely isolated; rather, they can propagate rapidly through
supply chains, third-party vendors, data pipelines, correlated model errors, and
opaque technological dependencies. Empirical evidence shows that cyber risk is
already priced in equity markets, predicts stock performance, and spreads swiftly
across financial networks, thereby elevating the likelihood of extreme event risk
(Aldasoro et al. 2022; Florackis et al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2024; Crosignani et al.
2023).
To ensure robust protection, mitigation strategies should include the adoption
of zero-trust architectures, which operate on the principle of “never trust, always
verify”, alongside th e deployment of adversarial robustness techniques to defend
against data poisoning (Biggio et al. 2012; Rose et al. 2 020; Zhao et al. 2024).
Adversarial attacks—where malicious data are intentionally introduced to corrupt
an AI model—pose a direct threat to the integrity and reliability of automated
investmentadvice.
Beyond cybersecurity, algorithmic bias represents an equally critical and inter-
connected risk. Adversarial attacks can intentionally exploit or amplify existing
model biases by injecting data that reinforce discriminatory patterns, thereby
undermining both the fairness and accuracy of automated investment decisions.
Such biased algorithms can generate unfair or exclusionary outcomes, manifesting
as disparate impact, where ostensibly neutral models disproportionately disadvan-
tage protected groupsofinvestors.Tomitigatethesevulnerabilities,robo-advisory
platforms should adopt structured AI risk management frameworks, such as the
NISTAIRiskManagementFramework(RMF)andguidancefromregulatorybodies
like ENISA. Regular bias testing, adversarial stress testing, model auditing, and

242 N.VirkandM.Al-Khalidi
robust governance are essential to ensure algorithmic fa irness, transparency, and
accountability.
In parallel, the integration of AI and xAI into forensic accounting and auditing
introduces a complementary governance dimension. While AI-driven analytics
enhance fraud detection, compliance monitoring, and anomaly identification, xAI
ensurestransparencyandaccountabilityintheseprocesses(Zhangetal.2022;Bao
et al.2020; Zhou et al.2023). By generating interpretable audit trails and clarifying
model reasoning, xAI supports the evidentiary and regulatory defensibility of AI-
based financial systems—particularly vital when addressing cybersecurity incidents
or disputed algorithmic decisions. Embedding explainability within robo-advisory
and auditing frameworks therefore strengthens both technical assurance and legal
resilience, bridging compliance, forensic oversight, and trust in digital financial
ecosystems.
The measurable market consequences of cybersecurity vulnerabilities and threats
reinforce cyber risk management as afirst-orderconcernforDeFi(Florackisetal.
2023; Jiang et al. 2024). Consequently, effective mitigations must move beyond
perimeter defence, incorporating authenticated data sources, lineage tracking, hard-
ened APIs, ri gorous cloud security, and continuous monitoring to detect data
anomalies(Eskandarietal.2021; Aldasoro et al.2022). Furthermore, strengthening
user-oriented security controls—such as multi-factor authentication and targeted
employee training—can complement these systemic measures by reducing human-
relatedvulnerabilitiesandoverallsusceptibilitytocyberthreats(Franzetal.2021;
Zhuo et al.2023).
Cybersecurity threats, data poisoning, and algorithmic bias collectively demand
proactive and adaptive governance frameworks to maintain both resilience and
fairness. These intertwined risks underscore the urgent need for responsive regu-
lation and robust supervisory engagement, ensuring that technological innovation
strengthens—rather than undermines—financial stability. These threats ha vesignif-
icantgovernanceimplications.Marketsincreasinglypenalisefirmswithhighcyber
exposure,creatingincentivesformeasurableriskreductionandtransparentcontrols
(Jiang et al. 2024). Within firms, broad oversight should cover secure software
development, dependency risk, and model lifecycle management. Across firms, het-
erogeneity in digitalisation and supervisory regimes—regulatory maturity—implies
uneven baseline resilience, so cross-vendor testing and data lineage validation are
criticalforgloballyoperatingplatforms(Aldasoroetal.2022).
For robo-advisory platforms, these considerations apply not only to safeguard-
ing their own operations but also to evaluating and pricing the cybersecurity
vulnerabilities of investee firms during portfolio construction at both micro and
macro levels. Ultimately, effective defence for robo-advisors blends identity-centric
security, zero-trustarchitecture,andend-to-endMLoperations(MLOps)assurance
fordataprovenanceandmonitoring,aligningtechnicalcontrolswiththeempirically
observedpricingandpropagationofcyberrisk(Crosignanietal.2023; Florackis et
al. 2023; Jiang et al. 2024). Embedding MLOps into robo-advisory and forensic
accounting frameworks will enhance documentation of model development and
deployment, traceability, verifiability, and consequently, audit readiness and regu-

CybersecurityRiskandRobo-Advisory 243
latory compliance. This will ensure not only transparency and model auditability
but also the integrity of the underlying data and model logic. Integration of
MLOps could pave the way for Regtech, transforming operational oversight into
technical governance, bridging automated decision-making with accountability,
and fortifying trust in digital financial infrastructures. T his chapter concludes that
tailored controls and governance for automated, autonomous, and personalised
wealthmanagementservicesareurgentlyneeded:cybersecurityriskscanpropagate
through financial markets, disrupt investment processes, and exacerbate systemic
instability(Table8).

Progress in Contemporary Fraud
Detection Through the Fintech
Application of Artificial Intelligence
Aymen Tu rki
Abstract The Global Financial Crisis (GFC) served as a catalyst for the emergence
of financial technology (Fintech), driven by a decline in trust towards traditional
financial and a rise in financial irregularities. The COVID-19 pandemic later
accelerated its adoption, leading to a notable surge in digital fraud threats and an
arms race with fraudsters. This chapter concentrates on the application of Fintech
innovations following the recent global crises, particularly those associated with the
automation of fraud detection driven by artificial intelligence (AI). Fraud incidents
and their associated losses are still troubling, creating a dual challenge that involves
the effective deployment of innovative AI-based Fintech solutions together with the
vital necessity for ethical transparency. The objective of this chapter is to identify
advanced AI technologiesthatcanofferacontemporaryoutlookonfrauddetection
within the modern finance sphere. AI-driven Fintech solutions tailored for various
categories of fraud detection will enhance ethical transparency and aids in the
promptdetectionoffraudulentpracticesbeforetheycausesubstantialdamage.The
chapterreachestheconclusionthatthefutureoffrauddetectiondependsnotsolely
onadvancementsinAItechnologybutalsoonhumanaccountabilityandacollective
commitmenttopreservingethicalintegrityandpromotingresponsibleinnovation.
Keywords Frauddetection · Fintech · Artificialintelligence
1 Introd uction
In recent decades, Fintech, defined as the integration of digital technologies such
as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, data and graph analytics, and cloud
computing, has emerged as a potentially transformative game changer within
the global financial markets (Schueffel 2016; Philippon 2016; Puschmann 2017;

ContributionstoFinanceandAccounting,
https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-18109-1_11

250 A.Turki
Goldstein et a l. 2019; Thako r 2020). As a leading technology, AI and Machine
Learning (ML) facilitated fraud detection (Bao et al. 2020; Zhong and Goel
2024) and helped to automate risk management (Gu et al. 2020). Additionally,
Regulatory Technology (RegTech), which automates compliance procedures such
as KYC (Know Your Customer) and AML (Anti-Money Laundering), employed AI
to help effectively adhere to regulatory requirements (Charoenwong et al. 2024).
Also, Insurance Technology (InsurTech) integrates AI and data analytics to provide
tailored in surancesolutions,automatedclaims,andadaptivepricing(Debeneretal.
2023). Other financial technologies used AI to automate, predict, and personalize
customer consulting se rvices through robo-advisory and chatbots (Tiberius et al.
2022). In our current economic landscape facing a dual challenge of the proper
application of this emerging AI-based Fintech along with the imperative of ensuring
ethical transparency, the r oleofAItechnologyinidentifyingfinancialirregularities
toachievetransparencygoalsremainsambiguousandstilluncleartoimplement.
To address this question, it is essential to explore in greater detail two concepts
that are significantly involved in this debate, namely AI and fraud detection,
and also to define the various forms that AI technology takes in the finance
industry, particularly around fraud detection. From a technical standpoint, AI in
finance integrates several components which are mainly based on data-driven
learning algorithms with intelligent automation to enhance efficiency, decision-
makingquality,compliance,andcustomerexperience(Ahmedetal.2022). Given its
widespread use, the key aspect of AI in the financial sector is ML, which translates
to algorithms that learn from historical financial data to make predictions or
decisions.Theirapplicationsinvolvecreditscoring,frauddetection,andstockprice
forecasting, among others (Berdiyeva et al. 2021). Another principal component
is the Natural Language Processing (NLP) which allows systems to understand
and process human language. Their functionalities are generally associated with
chatbots, customer support, and sentiment analysis of market news (Chen et al.
2023a). Predictive analytics is another segment of AI applied to finance which
uses statistical and ML models to forecast future events or trends and is practically
invol ved in predicting loan defaults, market movements, and customer behavior
(Chhikara et al. 2025). Another technique of AI applied to finance involves Deep
Learning which simulates complex patterns and connections within large datasets,
and it eff ectively renders in algorithmic trading image recognition for financial
document verification (Ng 2020). Lastly, AI that allows computers to process and
interpret visual data translates into another component of AI in finance which is
computer vision. It is used for KYC verification based onfacialrecognition,reading
andvalidatingdocuments(e.g.,invoices),andbiometricauthenticationoffinancial
institutions’customers(Guptaetal.2023;Entrust2 025).
Despite the algorithmic bias and explainability issues, these main technologies
of AI applied in the different financial domains (i.e., banking, wealth management,
risk management, fraud detection and security, RegTech, InsurTech) improved
accuracy by reducing human error in analysis and decision-making and detected
abnormal patterns faster than manual systems (AFME 2023). Undoubtedly, irreg-
ularities in finance constitute the cornerstoneofregulatorycomplianceandethical

ProgressinContemporaryFraudDetectionThroughtheFintechApplication... 251
transparency’s challenges (Puplampu 2024). In this regard, fraud detection, being
among key aspects, refers to the process of detecting and preventing fraudulent
or illegal financial activ ities before they inflict damage on individuals or organi-
zations (Wells 2017). Within finance and Fintech, it predominantly involves the
utilization of AI, ML, and data analytics t o detect irregular or suspicious patterns
in transactions, accounts, or customer behavior (EY 2024b; PwC 2 023). More
specifically, fraud categories can be sorted into payments and card-not-present
(CNP)1 fraud (Bodker etal.2022), detecting account takeover (ATO), fraud in the
process ofonboardingandverifyingidentity(McKinsey2019; Vanini etal.2023),
document forgery (Sukhija et al. 2025), AML transaction monitoring (Singh and
Best2019), procurement fraud problem(RendonandRendon2016), and financial
statement manipulation (Albrecht et al. 2015). In this chapter and based on these
dimensions of fraud detection in conjunction with the assigned AI technologies,
we will first explore the occurrences of fraud detection in the wake of the recent
global crises. In the second section, we will outline the dimensions and categories
of contemporary fraud detection within modern finance and accounting. The third
section of the chapter presents examples of innovative and emerging solutions to
addressthedifferenttypesoffraud,andfinally,thelastpartconcludesanddiscusses
thechallengesandethicalimperatives.
2 Occurrences of Fraud Detection in the Af termath
oftheLastGlobalCrises
The Global Financial Crisis (GFC) of 2008 and the COVID-19 pandemic crisis were
two major shocks that accelerated the emergence of Fintech and AI by rev ealing
vulnerabilitiesinconventionalfinanceandtransformingregulatoryandtechnolog-
ical frameworks (Bartlett et al. 2022). More precisely, the GFC highlighted the
breakdown of trust due to a lack of transparency, risky lending practices, and
a deficiency in accountability. Consumers and businesses lost trust in incumbent
banksandbecamemoreopentoalternativeandAI-drivenfinancialservices(Babina
etal.2025). Moreover, post-crisis reforms, such as Basel III and Dodd-Frank, have
enhanced the safety of banking; however, they have also led to a higher need of
deve lopedcompliancetechniques,whichhavecompelledincumbentstoreducetheir
small-scalecomplianceactivities(GozmanandCurrie2014). Fintech startups filled
this gap by offering faster, cheaper, and more transparent financial services, and also
by implementing innovative compliance mechanisms that facilitate fraud detection
andcreditscoringthroughtheutilizationofadvancedtechnologiessuchasAI(Vives
andYe2025).
1 Card-not-present fraud refers to the unauthorized utilization of credit or debit card information
to acquire goods and se rvices in a non-face-to-face environment such as through e-commerce
platforms.

252 A.Turki
On the other hand, the COVID-19 pandemic accelerated digital adoption through
spurring AI innovation in RegTech such as complianceautomation,andInsurTech,
as seen in pandemic coverage (Ceron and Monge 2023; Erel and Liebersohn
2020). Traditional banks accelerated partnerships with Fintech ventures to digitize
operations quickly and bridge resilience gaps amid the pandemic (Fu and Mishra
2022). Consequently, in conjunction with GFC, the pandemic created a disruptive
legitimacy making financial technology not just an alternative, but a mainstream
partoftheglobalfinancialecosystem(Kwanetal.2024). In this regard, corporate
surveys indicate an increased incidence of fraud throughout the 2010s. PwC’s
worldwide surveys conducted around 2011 revealed that approximately one-third
of companies had encountered fraud in the preceding year; by 2018, the re ported
prevalence had risen to about 49% (based on a global sample). This represents a
significantincreasefromthebaselineobservedintheearly2010s(PwC2011).
The convergence of disruption and digitization has led to an increase in external,
cyber-enabled fraud, with numerous organizations documenting new incidents
associated with the disruptions caused by COVID-19. AI, in the hand of fraudsters,
can create significant vulnerabilities. The increase in AI adoption has been made
possible by the reduction of technical barriers to AI utilization, as demonstrated
by accessible platforms such as ChatGPT and Copilot, which democratize access
to advanced AI functionalities. Fraudsters are exploiting these same technologies
to create more intricate schemes, thereby presenting challenges to current fraud
detection systems (Deloitte 2024). According to PwC’s 2022 Global Economic
Crime and Fraud Survey (GECS), almost 70% of organizations that encountered
fraud indicated that their most significant disruptive incident originated from an
external attack or a combination of ex ternalandinternalcollusion;thereportclearly
associates the emergence of new fraud incidents with the disruptions related to
the pandemic (PwC 2022). Levels of fraud incidents continue to be high during
the last seventeen years, and the mix (according to fraud category and third-
party exposure) is constantly changing. EY reports a rise in integrity incidents
and observes that approximately 68% of significant incidents involve third parties
(EY 2024a). KPMG’s fraud barometer (2025b) reveals high volumes and values
of fraud. Conversely, the report indicates a decrease in the total amount of losses
due to payment transfer fraud from £83.7 million in 2023 to £11.2 million in 2024.
The observed ongoing evolution of payment fraud has seen remote purchase fraud
emerge as a key concern in addition to other fraud threats including phishing attacks
and the utilization of automated bots for credential stuffing and the creation of
fraudulent accounts. This same report attributes the downturn trend in payment
fraud losses to the combined effect of regulatory enforcement and technological
innovation, especially the advancements in AI and ML technologies such as
generative AI and deepfakes. From another perspective, the most reliable global
estimatebyNasdaqVerafin(2024) indicates that fraud losses for 2023 are projected
to be around US$486 billion, highlighting a substantial and ongoing issue, even
as certain categories show signs of stabilization. In the UK, the value of alleged
fraud cases in the courts has bounced back to pre-pandemic levels by 2022 and
has continued to exhibit significant case-driven volatility throughout 2023–2024

ProgressinContemporaryFraudDetectionThroughtheFintechApplication... 253
(KPMG 2021). Ultimately, there is no universally accepted global total in dollars
from the major consulting firms such as PwC, EY, Deloitte, and KPMG, and ev en
current empirical literature about the progression of the trend throughout time
generatesmixedinferences(Karpoff2021), but one thing is certain: fraud incidents
and their resulting losses are still alarming, and takingactiontoadequatelyaddress
thisissuehasbecomeapressingnecessity.
3 Dimensions of Contemporary Fraud Detection Across
ModernFinanceand Accounting
Contemporary fraud detection in modern finance and accounting has evolved into a
multidimensional field where traditional scrutiny and control have to deal with new
fraudulent practices’ emergence,digitalization,advancementofAItechnology,and
thetransitiontoproactivefraudmanagement(Moody’s2023). In this regard, it can
be comprehended through various complementary dimensions that together define
thescopeofcontemporaryfrauddetection(Okuretal.2021; Van Belleetal.2023;
Papadakis et al.2020).
The first dimension is functional. It differentiates between fraudulent practices in
finance and those in accounting. In the accounting field, when a manager commits
fraud, they deliberately alter accountingrecordstopresentthecompany’sfinancial
situation as more favorable than it truly is (Punch 1996; Zimmer 1998; Clike man
2010; Cooper et al. 2013). This includes financial reporting, which generally
manifests as manipulated statements, earnings distortion, fictitious revenues, or
understated liabilities (Adelberg 1979; LoPucki 1996; Beneish 1999). It also
concerns procurement and payables through false in voicing, duplicate payments,
or supplier collusion (Piper 2017). Payroll and expenses (e.g., ghost employees,
inflated reimbursements) (Kelly 2023) and receivables and treasury (e.g., lapping,
unauthorized transfers, diverted collections) illustrate additional forms of fraud
withinaccountingpractices(KPMG2025a). In the finance area, fraud management
extends to payments, lending, trading, and asset management, where fr audcantake
theformofpaymentscams(Toh2024), insider trading (Esen etal.2019; Liu et al.
2020; James et al. 2023), or misappropriation of client funds, among others. AI-
enabled systems are becoming an integral part of t hese workflows, continuously
auditingtransactions,andidentifyinganomaliesinrealtime.
Alongside this functional distinction (finance vs. accounting) in fraud detection,
a second dimension classifies fraud by the type or nature of misconduct with
the emergence of new types due to the advent of digitalization. The conventional
practices such as asset misappropriation, along with financial statement fraud, still
constitute the core of fraudulent activities. However, digitalization has introduced
new typologies such as cyber-assisted payment fraud, illegal appropriation of
personal information and the creation of artificial identities, account takeovers,
and AML violations. Each type requires different data and different analytical

254 A.Turki
techniques. For instance, AI applications in payment fraud depend on recognizing
behavioral patterns and detecting anomalies, whereas AML analytics prioritize
graph analysis and transaction network modeling to uncover hidden connections
among entities. PwC’s Global economic crime and Fraud survey (2022) shows that
44% of fraud experienced by the financial services industry are customer fraud,
38%refertocybercrime,and29%relatetoknow-your-customerfailure.According
toVisaAcceptance(2025)’s report, fraud in payment continues to be a global issue,
with 98% of merchants encountering one or more forms of payment fraud over the
last 12 months. The surveyed data indicate a steady decrease in the occurrence of
fraud in digital payment to merchants, alongside notable reductions in fraud types
likefirst-partymisuse,phishing,andcardtesting,andasignificantriseinreal-time
paymentfraudaffecting45%ofmerchantsworldwidein2024.
A third and increasingly crucial dimension is the advancement of AI technology.
AI-driven systems may greatly enhance accuracy in fraud detection and diminish the
number of false positives that have overwhelmed fraud reports (Moody’s 2025c).
Traditional rule-based and statistical techniques, which are previously employed
by auditors and controllers, are being replaced by ML-driven systems which utilize
supervised mo delstocategorizetransactionsaseitherfraudulentorlegitimatebased
on historical data (Bao et al. 2020; Hunt et al. 2022; Bertomeu et al. 2021; Zhang
Parker et al. 2025) and unsupervised models to identify new patterns without
prior labels (Gomes et al. 2021; Debener et al. 2023). Additionally, techniques
such as natural language processing (NLP) facilitate the automated examination
of text-based evidence, including emails and invoices (Qatawneh 2025), whereas
graph analytics uncover collusive networks among suppliers, customers, and bank
accounts (Motie and Raahemi 2024). Within Fintech ecosystems, companies like
Feedzai, Featurespace, and Forter have developed real-time AI engines that apply
adaptive behavioral analytics to millions of transactions per second, consistently
learningasnewfraudtypologiesemerge(Omdia2025).
Ultimately, a maturity dimension defines the transition from reactive fraud
management to proactive strategies (Moody’s July 2025a). Earlier systems were
retrospective, focusing on the post-occurrence detection of fraud. In contrast,
contemporary organizations leverage AI and a continuous flow of data to establish
prev entivestrategiesandimplementpredictiveandprescriptivesystems(Brownet
al.2020). Predictive models anticipate potential fraud scenarios, while prescriptive
analytics trigger autonomous responses, such as blocking transactions, amplifying
alerts,ordynamicallyadjustingthresholds(ZhangParkeretal.2025). In the Fintech
sector, this evolution occurs in the framework of the emergence of autonomous and
self-learning risk management platforms that prioritize real-time prevention over
retrospectivedetection(Moody’s2025b).
In summary, these dimensions form a comprehensive framework for understand-
ing fraud detection in finance, accounting, auditing, and Fintech. Contemporary AI-
drive nsolutionsforfrauddetectionincreasinglyeliminatetheboundariesbetween
these domains (Vasarhelyi et al. 2018), which illustrates that the future of fraud
detection is not merely dependent on improved controls, but rather on dynamic

ProgressinContemporaryFraudDetectionThroughtheFintechApplication... 255
data-driven ecosystems where AI-based Fintech solutions continuously enhance
compliance andethicaltransparency(FinancialCrimeAcademy2025; Th reatMark
2025).

5 Conclusions and Discussions of Challenges and Ethical
Imperatives
The future of fraud detection is shaped by a complex interplay of AI-driven Fintech
innovation, regulatory compliance, and ethical responsibility. The ongoing rise of
AI solutions, driven by generative AI, deep learning, and NLP, heralds a significant
transformation in fraud investigations. The reverse side of the coin is that in the
possession of fraudsters, AI has the potential to create substantial vulnerabilities.
Indeed, the progress in large language models (LLM) has enabled the creation of
AI-generated text that closely resembles human-written material, thereby enhancing
the effectiveness of scams. The rising use of deepfake technology and the creation
of synthetic identities introduce new risks, as scammers can now mimic reputable
figures, such as CEOs, using convincingly cr afted audio and video. The central
questioniswhetherthetwocontradictoryphenomenacontinuetoevolveinthesame
manner and at the same pace; if they do, we will be trapped in a vicious cycle of
being unable to outpace fraudsters, thereby compromising our goal of achieving
enhanced ethical transparency. In this scenario, the impact of AI technology is
trivial,andweinevitablyreverttothesolutionthatshouldserveastheengine,which
istheethicalresponsibilityoffinancialactors.
Another primary challenge lies in maintaining data privacy while adopting new
AI technologies and complying with changing regulatory frameworks, such as
the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the upcoming EU AI Act.
Financial institutions must navigate the tension between effective fraudprevention
and the preservation of individual privacy, ensuring that AI-driven models do not
violateuserrights(Naimetal.2023; Zhou et al.2024).
Equally significant to note is the challenge regarding algorithmic bias and
fairness. When AI systems are trained on historical data, they can accidentally
reproduce systemic biases,whichmayleadtoinequitableoutcomessuchasbiased
fraudclassificationsormisleadinginvestmentrecommendations (Baoetal.2022).
To alleviate this issue, organizations need to carry out regular algorithmic audits,
engage in bias testing, and implement explainable AI interfaces that enhance trans-
parency and trust. This will lead to additional sources of costs and time-consuming
tasks that are similar in volume to those existing without AI,thuscreatingavicious
cycleofalengthyandexpensivefrauddetectionprocess.Consequently,theroleof
humaninvolvementisundeniable,andhumanaccountabilityremainsavitalethical
requirement.
As emphasized by Bianchi and Briére (2023) and PwC (2023), the frame-
works that incorporate human oversight are crucial to ensure that the ultimate
responsibility for decision-making lies with professionals instead of autonomous
algorithms.PwC(2023) stresses the importance of integrating AI risk management
into the overall enterprise strategy, which includes compliance, cybersecurity,
and ethical governance across all AI-related activities. Overall, these challenges
togetherindicatethatthefutureoffrauddetectionreliesnotonlyontechnological

ProgressinContemporaryFraudDetectionThroughtheFintechApplication... 261
progress but also on the collective commitment to maintaining e thicalintegrityand
responsibleinnovation.

Part I V
Technological Innovations and Financial
Integration

Enhanced Cryptocurrency Volatility
Forecasting via Local Linear Forests
Joep Noot and ImtiazSifat
Abstract We examine the effectiveness of Local Linear Forests (LLF) for forecast-
ing cryptocurrency volatility, comparing their performance against traditional mod-
els Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH), Glosten–
Jagannathan–Runkle GARCH (GJR-GARCH), realized volatility approaches
Heterogeneous Autoregressive model of Realized Volatility (HAR-RV), and
machine learning methods (Random Forests). Using data from eight cryptocur-
rencies (2021–2024), we find that LLFs consistently outperform benchmark
models in out-of-sample forecasting, particularly during market transitions and
high-volatility periods. Through extensive simulation studies and empirical
analyses, we demonstrate that LLFs exhibit superior adaptability to cryptocurrency
markets’ nonlinear dynamics and regime shifts. The economic significance of
these improvements is validated through a utility-based framework for risk-
targeting investors. Notably, we find that volatility forecasting accuracy is
systematically higher for mid-cap versus larg e-cap cryptocurrencies, suggesting
importantimplicationsformarketefficiencyandportfoliomanagement.Ourfeature
importance analysis reveals that simple market metrics are sufficient for effective
volatility prediction, challenging the conventional wisdom that cryptocurrency
forecastingrequirescomplexhigh-frequencydatainputs.Thesefindingscontribute
tothegrowingliteratureonmachinelearningapplicationsinfinancialmarketsand
offerpracticalinsightsforcryptocurrencyriskmanagement.
Keywords Cryptocurrency · Volatilityforecasting · LocalLinearForests ·
Operationalresearch · Machinelearning
