3.2 Growth in Sustainable Investing, Regulatory
Devel opments,andESG ReportingStandards
Retail and institutional demand, combined with regulatory developments such
as the EU’s SFDR, have fuelled growth in thematic funds targeting issues like
clean energy, water, and gender equity. Impact investing has risen alongside
ESG integration, explicitly seeking measurable positive environmental and social
outcomesinadditiontofinancialreturns(GlobalImpactInvestingNetwork2020).
Active ownership and engagement remain central to ESG investing, with selective
divestment used toaddresssystemicriskssuchasfossilfueldependence(UNFCCC
2015;PRI2 020).
However, academic research has long pointed to multiplicity of guiding prin-
ciples and their conflicting nature that had hampered standardisation in ESG
products and instruments as well as what is meant by ESG. For a detailed review
of guidelines, initiatives, and frameworks that have shaped today’s sustainability
reportinganddisclosureframeworks,seeTable3. It maps key developments starting
from Kyoto Protocol adopted at Third Conference of the Parties (COP) 3 organised
by United Nations Framework Convention o nClimateChange(UNFCCC)in1997
toCSRDin2022todevelopsustainablycompetitivemarkets.
Table 6 outlines recent regulatory standards introduced between 2023 and
2024 that strengthen sustainability and climate disclosure, aiming to improve
transparency,comparability,andinvestoraccountability.
The multiplicity of guidelines and reporting initiatives, compounded by
widespread greenwashing and corporate misconduct (Noori and Athota 2024),
is a leading factor in the divergent methodologies adopted by data providers.
This, in turn, has created significant confusion and disagreement across ESG data
provided by sev eral data providers. These ESD data divergences are well reported
(Avramov et al. 2022; Berg et al. 2 022). This undermines their reliability and,
in result, usability by asset managers and investors. This has led to the issues of
comparabilityandenabled‘greenwashing’(Ilhanetal.2023;Starks2 023).
This is changing with the emergence of robust global frameworks such as
the International Sustainability Standards Board (ISSB) and its IFRS S1 and S2
standards, which establish a baseline for reporting sustainability-related financial
risks and opportunities. In parallel, the EU’s SFDR and the United Kingdom’s
Sustainability Disclosure Requirements (SDR) aim to improve fund labelling,
transparency, and investor comparability. Importantly, all these frameworks are

It is important to mention that the EU has been pushing the envelope in
leading the way to develop comprehensive sustainable finance disclosure and
complianceframeworks,asshowninTable3. Key regulatory drivers include the EU
Taxonomy Regulation, which defines environmentally sustainable activities, and the
SFDR, which standardises ESG disclosure for financial products. CSRD expands
mandatory reporting across companies using European Sustainability Reporting
Standards, while the Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CS3D)
moves towards full value-chain accountability when firms generate a significant
portion of their turnover in the EU. These regulatory initiatives have set the gold
standardinsustainablefinancereporting,disclosures,andcompliancemechanism.
In the USA, the SEC has finalised their own climate-related disclosure rules.
The SEC rule has faced significant political and legal opposition. A key feature
is the tiered approach to reporting, with mandatory disclosures for some climate
data but a less stringent requirement for supply chain carbon emissions—indirect
emissions from a company’s value chain. The rule’s compliance is staggered across
time, with a few of the largest companies expected to report in the year 2025.
However, the most significant regulatory development in the USA has taken place in
the State of California, i.e., California Climate Laws—mandating advanced climate
disclosures. It embeds CDP and TCFD disclosure requirements. The c limate law
willbephasedinfrom2026to2027butisinfluencinginvestorexpectationsbecause
SECrulesonlyrequirestringent-formdisclosuresiftheyhavefinancialmateriality,
whereas California Climate Laws require a full disclosure of all activities falling
under Scope 3. It shows that the US regulatory environment is yet not settled, as
state-levelrequirementsaddcomplexity—notcomplementarity—forfirmspursuing
federalrequirements.
In parallel, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) in the UK has developed
an explicit labelling regime with clear, voluntary labels for financial products while
adopting a gradual rollout. Once a fund has adopted a voluntary labelling regime, the
naming and marketing rules are mandatory from2024to2025.SDRtightlyaligns

asset managers to make prudent, suitable sustainability claims and adopt suitable

4 Robo-Advisory
Traditional investment management relies on human advisers who evaluate clients’
objectives, constraints, and risk tolerance to build and overseediversifiedportfolios
withtheirprofessionaljudgement(Jungetal.2018). AI-powered robo-advisers, on
the other hand, perform these tasks using online questionnaires, algorithmic asset
allocation, constant monitoring, and consistent, rules-based execution (Abraham
et al. 2019; Alsabah et al. 2021). Table 7 provides a list of leading robo-advisory
systems currently av ailableinthemarket.
Another key advancement is the use of hybrid models through robo-advisory
systems, which combine automation with human oversight for complex cases.
While traditional advisers benefit from personalised relationships, robo-advisers
improve scalability, accessibility, and cost efficiency. Despite these advantages,
opportunities for further innovation remain. These opportunities include inte-
gratinglow-latencyarchitecturestoenabledynamicandpersonalisedrecommenda-
tions(Jungetal.2018). The capability of these architecture designs enables inges-
tion and processing of vast amounts of real-time market data—from incorporation
of client-level transaction h istoriestoharmonisingdatamodels,decision-making,
andtradeexecutionasclosetoreal-timeaspossible.
Table 8 categorises key data supply lines used in robo-advisory for sustainable
investing, ranging from financial markets and analyst forecasts to geospatial and
IoT data, while alsonotingtheirrespectiverolesandlimitations,suchasbias,data
reliability,andintegrationchallenges.
4.1 Efficiency, Accessibility, and Democratisation
of Inv estmentAdvice
Robo-advisers offer significantly lower fees than traditional advisers, typically
0.25–0.50% of assets under management (AUM), while providing diversified and
continuously monitored portfolios (Abraham et al. 2019; Alsabah et al. 2021).
Automated rebalancing helps enforce discipline and counters behavioural biases like
inertia and overreaction, while digital onboarding makes inv estingmoreaccessible
to clients who may not meet traditional account minimums (Aristei and Gallo
2025; Jung etal.2018). For investors with complex needs, hybrid models combine
automated portfolio management with human consultations to address unique
circumstanceswhilemaintainingscalability(BianchiandBrière2023).

Despite these advantages, key challenges to widespread adoption remain, includ-

professional advice at scale, democratising access to strategies once reserved for
high-net-worthindividuals(Abbas2024; Aristei andGallo2025).
To achieve this robust governance, robo-advisory systems are built on a mod-
ular architecture. The robo-advisory architecture can seamlessly chain specialised
modules, e.g., Natural Language Processing (NLP) engines to extract sentiment
from financial new s, ML predictive approaches model to forecast returns, and
reinforcementlearningagentstooptimiserebalancingfrequencyundertransaction
cost constraints (Zhang et al. 2020). Guardrails such as position limits, sector
caps, and risk budget constraints help contain agent autonomy and mitigate
unintended strategies (Bianchi and Brière 2023; Alsabah et al. 2021). When
properly constrained and monitored, robo-advisors can improve responsiveness
to market changes, reduce implementation shortfall, and sustain target risk-return
characteristicswithhumansupervision.

4.1.1 Data Sources and Architecture
A robo-advisory platform depends on robust, continuous data feeds covering market
prices, returns, volumes, corporate actions, index me mberships, macroeconomic
indicators,andanalystforecasts.Robo-advisorsuseseveraltypesofdata:
• Structured Financial Data: This includes prices, volumes, returns, and corpo-
rate fundamentals, which are used as inputs for portfolio optimisation, factor
models,andriskestimations.
• Alternate Datasets: This encompasses non-traditional sources, often available
in unstructured formats. These include financial news, earnings call t ranscripts,
andintradaytradingpatterns,whichcanbeusedtorefinetacticalallocationand
riskdetection.
Robo-advisory platforms are highly integrated digitalplatforms.Table8 outlines
several data sources that are aligned in a robo-advisory platform from ingestion to a
structured database.
Typically, data sources are channelled via application programming interfaces
(APIs) or direct exchange connections and areprocessedthroughingestionpipelines
thatvalidateaccuracy,removeduplicates,andapplytimestampingforpoint-in-time
integrity(Samueletal.2020). Storage in cross-sectional, time series, or longitudinal
structures ensures both real-time and historical retrieval fo r back and forward
testing, as well as dynamic decision-making (Alsabah et al. 2021). Establishing
the architecture for robo-advisory systems therefore involves configuring reliable
data pipelines, applying rigorous data cleaning and stratification, and building
processable database structures—a foundational stage in platform development
(Samueletal.2020; Adusupalli2025).
In designing and developing robo-advisory architecture, several technical, opera-
tional, and layout-related data issues arise. For instance, latency-accuracy trade-offs
arise when systems must balance rapid data delivery with precision; studies in
inference serving highlight how adaptive frameworks can navigate such trade-offs
to maintain accuracy under tight latency constraints (Salmani et al. 2023; Nigade
et al. 2024). Survivorship bias skews performance analysis by excluding failed or
delisted firms, resulting i noverlyoptimisticbacktestresults(CarpenterandLynch
1999; Daniel et al. 2008; Fung and Hsieh 1997; Brian 2 020). Inconsistent data
formats and semantic heterogeneity hinder seamless integration—schemas, units,
naming conventions, and encoding vary across data vendors, complicating data
fusionandinterpretation(Abbas2023;ShethandLarsen1990). Finally, erroneous
data propagation through optimisation pipelines amplifies errors if cleansing and
validation are inadequate. Addressing these issues through harmonised schemas,
validation checks, and latency-aware architectures can markedly improve data
quality and model reliability.
The application of AI modules starts even before the availabilityofthefinaltime-
synchronised,processing-ready,andmachine-readabledatabase.Forexample,NLP
techniquestransformunstructuredtextintoquantitativefeatures.Alternatedatasets
are crucial for making early-stage predictions on market states, sentiment, and

4.1.2 Robo-Advisory, Data Processing, and AnalyticalFrameworks
The functionality of a robo-advisor is built on a sophisticated, synchronised, and
multi-stage architecture. To visualise a conceptual framework of a typical AI-
poweredrobo-advisortomakeinvestmentrecommendations,pleaserefertoFig.1.
This conceptual framework can be broken down into a five-stage loop, starting from
investor’s preference exploration to reinforcement learning from inv estor choices
made from different scoring methods in the robo-advisory environment (Tables 9
and 10):
• Investor Profiling: capturing goals, constraints, horizon,andrisktolerance.
• Investor Policy Formulation: translating preferences into allocation ta rgets,risk
budgets,andconstraints.
• Portfolio Optimisation and Execution: generating cost-efficient trade lists
usingalgorithms.

For this multi-stage architecture to be effective, robust robo-advisory perfor-
mance depends on rigorous backtesting protocols that guard aga inst overfitting,
look-ahead bias in predictions, and data leakage (Abraham et al. 2019). Avoiding
these pitfalls requires timestamped and event-drive n validation systems (Smigel
2023). With the availability of a dynamically functional database, robo-advisory
platforms integrate analytical frameworks—AI modules—for data processing and
decision-making. Table 11 lists several AI capabilities in robo-advisory systems.
These analytical frameworks often operate in three layers: feature engineering
(returns, volatility, sentiment, factor exposures), estimation (Bayesian shrinkage,
regularised regressions, ensemble models), and decision policies such as mean-
variance optimisation, Black Litterman induced portfolio allocation choices, or
reinforcement learning allocation (Shen et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2020). These
layers enable a dynamic and adaptive refinement of investorpoliciesanddecision-
making.

ESG investing brings additional data handling and processing needs due to
its unique materialities. Robo-advisors are particularly well-suited for sustain-
able investing because they can manage the complex and voluminous ESG data
efficiently. They are key enablers in scaling sustainable investing, as they can
organise, modulate, and process diverse data types including structure d financial
metrics,unstructuredtextualdisclosures,andmixed-formatESGdatasets.This
capabilityallowsthemtotranslatelargevolumesofheterogeneousESGinformation
intotransparent,rules-basedportfoliodecisions—deliveredatalowcost.
However, the integration of ESG considerations introduces a host of complexi-
ties. These include divergent ESG ratings, risks of greenwashing and green-hushing,
inconsistent regulatory frameworks, and potential legal liabilities. Suchchallenges
canreadilydeterinvestorsandassetmanagers,renderingESGintegrationproneto
misjudgementandoperationalerror.
On the technical side, as ESG data volumes and taxonomies proliferate, ML
becomes critical. It supports screening, controversy detection, and climate-tilt
optimisation, which bridges investor preferences with measurable outcomes and
clear audit trails (Feng et al. 2024; Xu 2025). Furthermore, other factors, such
as automated profiling, continuous data ingestion, and explainable rebalancing, also
help scale sustainable investing. These features reduce the friction points in portfolio
policymaking and optimisation that often discourage retail participation, whereas
for institutional investors robo-advisors offer configurable pipelines that align to
their specific policy and fiduciary constraints (Mohapatra et al. 2025; Singh and
Kumar 2025). Collectively, these features offer efficiency and scalability, broad-
ening access and personalisation while also improving tractability and supporting

5.1 Robo-Advisory for ESG Data StandardisationandBaseline
Heterogeneity in ESG data is a bottleneck for scalable ESG investing. Fortunately,
robo-advisors are a great solution to manage heterogeneous ESG datasets and to
achieve standardisation and scalability in sustainable investing. ESG datasets often
contain a mix of qualitative narratives and quantitative key performance indicators
(KPIs). The data also suffer from i ssueslikeunevencoverageacrossdifferentsectors
andgeographies,time-lags,andsurvivorshipbias.Furthermore,discrepanciesarise
fromvendor-specificchoicesonmetricssuchasScope3emissions,controversies,
orboardquality.
A central ESG data challenge is rating divergence: providers disagree on what to
measure, how to weight it, and how to handle controversies,generatinglowcorrela-
tionsacrossscoresandclassifications(Bergetal.2022). That ‘aggregate confusion’
weakens naive screening and invites bias if not challenged. The use of divergent
methodologies (industry-relative vs. absolute risk) also complicates comparabil-
ity and portfolio construction. For example, MSCI assigns industry-normalised,
issue-weighted ratings (AAA–CCC) and a separate controversies overlay, while
Sustainalytics’ ESG RiskRatingsemphasise‘unmanagedrisk’onanabsolutescale
(negligible–severe),producingdifferentinvestabilitylistsforthesameissuer.Please
refertoTable10 for different ESG rating providers andtheirmethodologies.
AI-enabled robo-advisory can mitigate rating divergence in three ways. First, it
could be set to automate cross-provider ingestion and mapping, harmonising issuers
across identifiers and taxonomies, and learning stable signals across noisy vendor
inputs. This requires robo-advisors to explicitly model data quality (coverage,
timeliness, methodological drift) and rating divergence to avoid spurious precision.
That is, robo-advisors can seamlessly integrate procedures including cross-rating
consensus measures. Second, it can encode user-level materiality (e.g., climate
vs. labour metrics) and dynamically re-weight factors as disclosures improve. For
example, dynamic data feeds—new s, excessive supply chain carbon emissions, or
environmentaldamagelawsuits—canbesetascontroversyoverrides,anddynamic
guardrails (e.g., removing issuers when controversies breach severity thresholds
regardlessofcompositescore).Third,xAIpipelinescandocumentandauditevery
decision, aiding in client reporting and alignment with regulatory frameworks
(BianchiandBrière2023).

Robo-advisory plays a pivotal role in creating ESG baselines by automating the
ingestion and harmonisation of heterogeneous datasets across multiple providers,
denoising gaps in coverage. They provide consistent, standardised signals for sus-
tainable investing while reducing manual burdens, and governance risks. Through
AI-driven consensus measures, dynamic controversy overrides, and explainable
pipelines, robo-advisors create scalable ESG baselines that reduce bias, enhance
comparability, and support compliance with regulatory and client-specific mate-
riality requirements. The implementation of this multi-layered ESG data baseline
deliverswhatwouldotherwisebeexcessivelytime-consuming,costly,andproneto
human errors, if not misconduct. Robo-advisors will impute and denoise missing
KPIs and forecast emissions pathways to reduce gaps in small-cap/EM coverage
(Zhang et al. 2020) and streamline decision rules for efficiency , performance,
compliance,andaudit.
The robo-advisory can achieve a myriad of constraints to maintain ESG criteria,
as well as jurisdictional requirements, and all of this while standardising ESGdata—
safeguarding data quality. Robust ESG standardisation and baseline stacks will be
shapedby:
(i) Data layer: multi-vendor ingestion (MSCI, Sustainalytics, index-level
screens), issuer mapping, NLP over reports,andcontroversy/newsfeeds.
(ii) Policy and feature layer: harmonised metrics (emissions intensities, target
credibility, violations); learned cross-rating embeddings to exploit signal amid
rating divergence; inve stor-specificexclusions(e.g.,thermalcoal),stewardship
flags,andregulatoryconstraints(SFDR/SDRlabels).
(iii) Modelling layer: multi-objective optimisation for return–risk–ESG,
scenario/transition-path testing,andexplainability;and.
(iv) Governance layer: model management, fairness/bias tests, data-lineage log-

5.2 Portfolio Construction for SustainabilityGoals
AI-powered robo-advisor functionalities significantly enhance ESG integration in
investment portfolios. Once standardised ESG data baselines are available, robo-
advisory platforms can ensure a deeper alignment of investments with sustainability
goals. These platforms offer a scalable solution for implementing complex sus-
tainabilitypreferencesandprovidereal-time,explainableinsightsintoaportfolio’s
socialandenvironmentalimpact.
The portfolio construction process through ML approaches and advanced opti-
misation routines can be deployed to align investor intent with an implementable
strategy. For a detailed reviewofseveralAIapproachesintheportfolioconstruction
process,pleaserefertoTable11. ESG investing workflow in robo-advisorycanbe
streamlined:

370 N.Virk
1. Investor profiling: determine investor type, horizon, and liquidity (e.g., retail
vs. institutional), elicit sustainability priorities (e.g., decarbonisation pace, social
screens), and capture regulatory constraints (e.g., SDR label eligibility in the
UK).
2. ESG goals: translate preferences into quantifiable targets such as emissions-
intensity reductions, minimum ESG risk thresholds, exclusions,andstewardship
outcomes(voting/engagementcoverage).
3. Risk tolerance: establish volatility thresholds, drawdown , and tracking-error
budgets.
4. Risk management: incorporate climate transition and physical risk scenarios,
controversycaps,andconcentrationlimits.
5. Optimisation & review: execute multi-objective models with human monitor-
ing, re-estimation—via deep reinforcement learning, and provide explainable
changelogs.
After setting the necessary constraints, portfolio construction proceeds through
multi-objective optimisation, where return, risk, and sustainability preferences
are simultaneously traded off. For example, a system might minimise carbon
intensitysubjecttotracking-errorlimitsandsectorneutrality(NundlallandVanZyl
2023; Feng et al. 2024). The integration of penalisation constraints for emissions,
controversies, or ESG risk, while limiting factor drift to maintain market-like
exposures, defines the coremechanismthroughwhichESGobjectivesareembedded
into quantitative portfolio construction. MSCI (2024) ESG Leaders and Universal
index methodologies, for instance, illustrate the distinction between tilt-based and
optimisation-based variants of this integration.
This process can be further extended by applying advanced optimisation tech-
niques such as stochastic optimisation and deep reinforcement learning, which
allow for dynamic adaptation to evolving market conditions and provide more
nuanced incorporation of ESG objectives into the efficient frontier. In cases where
preferences conflict—for instance, excluding all fossil-adjacent rev enues versus
maintaining a tracking-error cap—the system quantifies the cost of purity,
offers diversified substitutes, and records the decision for audit. The system
can also use factor-based ESG integration, which considers explicit sustainability
factors alongside classic Fama-French risk premia (Vo et al. 2019). In addition,
to meet jurisdictional requirements, model selection should be conditioned on
label eligibility (e.g. FCA SDR investment labels impose criteria f orsustainability
‘Focus/Improvers/Impact’ strategies) and traceability, documenting the data, con-
straints,andrationale.
5.3 Active Stewardship: Impact andRobo-Advisory
Robo-advisory platforms can operationalise stewardship by systematically target-
ing engagements where they can have thegreatestimpact.Theycanbetunedtouse

selection mechanisms that consider both the materiality of issues and the momentum
of a company’s actions. To implement this, they can use several mechanisms:
goal-based reporting (like tracking progress on emissions or voting records),
commitment devices (such as automatically increasing stewardship intensity unless
an investor opts out), and communication strategies that reduce friction (for
example, framing market volatility as a ‘budget’ for long-term impact). Continuous
monitoring then adjusts portfolios as ratings, controversies, or regulatory thresholds
change, ensuring that stewardship ‘intent’isevidencedinvotesandengagements.
Thesetechnologicalandbehaviouralmechanismsdemonstrateafundamentalshift
in portfolio design. Designing ESG portfolios is transforming from setting static
constraints to a more dynamic, participatory optimisation problem. Here, ML and
digitaltoolsareworkingtogethertoredefinewhatisvaluabletoinvestors.
This approach extends the concept of the ESG frontier proposed by Pedersen
et al. (2021): maximising investor utility across financial returns, sustainability
outcomes, and participatory stewardship engagement. By combining AI-powered
robo-advisory with ESG-constrained optimisation, it is making the augmented
frontier achievable while making advisory services more accessible to ever yone.
ThisviewissupportedbyrecentresearchonML—optimisedsustainableportfolios
andstudiesonhowretailinvestorsareadoptingrobo-advisoryservices(Fengetal.
2024; Vo et al. 2 019). This evidence highlights how robo-advisory platforms are
embedding stewardship functions directly into the investment optimisation and
clientengagementprocesses.
5.4 ESG Personalisation and Behavioural Frictions
in SustainableInvesting
Customised portfolio development is the first step in unlocking the transformative
potential of AI in sustainable investing. It begins with a deep understanding
of investor sustainability priorities and objectives, setting clear rules to manage
potential conflicts, and leveraging deep reinforcement learning to adapt to their
evolving choices. Throughout the portfolio construction process, AI capabilities
facilitate hyper-personalisation. This ranges from detailed granular screens (e.g.,
animal welfare, water stress) to creating differential decarbonisation pathways
without the need for manual oversight. The use of these advanced technologies
makes sophisticated, ethically aligned investment strategies accessible to a wider
audience(Shenetal.2025).
Robo-advisors are particularly effective, as they can develop highly customised
portfolios that align with client ESG preferences while adhering to label criteria
and sector neutrality (Feng et al. 2024). Consequently, these platforms automate
the creation of resilient portfolios that not only aim for financial returns but also
dynamically manage and report on their tangible impact at a lower cost (Barile et
al. 2025; Shen et al. 2025). Robo-advisors typically charge much lower fees than

372 N.Virk
traditional advisors, often between 0.25% and 0.50% of assets under management.
Their use of digital onboarding and lower costs makes professional investment
management accessible to a broader client base (Aristei and Gallo 2025; Jung et
al. 2018): democratises advisory services. Robo-advisors increase transparency
and enable preference-driven customisation with an interactive selection process,
and automated rebalancing & reporting—addressing behavioural barriers to entry
(Mohapatraetal.2025; Singh and Kumar2025). In this vein, the embedding of ESG
rules, such as UK SDR labels, may further helpretailinvestors’comprehensionand
abilitytocompareESGportfolios.
To this effect, these platforms also tackle behavioural frictions like present bias,
confusion from conflicting ratings, and ambiguity aversion through effective choice
architecture. This includes offering pre-verified templates, transparent trade-offs,
and clear impact dashboards. Explainability features, such as highlighting the
drivers of inclusion or ex clusion and attributing emissions reductions, counter
informationoverload.Defaultescalationnudges,like‘improver’fundsthattighten
targets annually, help maintain client engagement. Mohapatra et al. (2019, 2025)
provide evidence that AI-enabled robo-advisors, through features like recommen-
dation engines and a focus on clarifying utility and ease of use, can strengthen
behaviouralintentiontowardssustainableinvesting.

In response to jurisdictional rules and guidelines, robo-advisors can opera-

monitoring of sustainability thresholds while reducing the manual burden on
compliance teams. They can ensure that transparent disclosures are not treated
as optional: the UK’s SDR package (PS23/16) and the anti-greenwashing rule
(FG24/3) mandate that sustainability-related claims be fair, clear, and not mis-
leading. Likewise, at the ecosystem level, the EU’s ESG Ratings Regulation
(2024/3005) mandates methodology transparency, governance, and conflict-of-
interest controls for rating providers operating in the Union. Stipulation of these
requirementsimprovesthecomparabilityandauditabilityofinputstorobo-advisors.

poration of xAI ensures transparency in decision pathways, which regulators

and accountability—helping investors na vigateevolvingESGruleswithconfidence

comprehensive audit trails for sustainability claims and ensuring that disclosures
remain consistent with regulatory expectations. Platforms can also be coded to
automatically detect and flag potential greenwashing by cross-checking sustain-

6 Summary
Robo-advisors are profoundly impacting ESG investing by democratising access
and enhancing analytical capabilities beyond traditional methods. These platforms
leverage algorithms to scale personalised investment advice, making ESG investing
accessible to a broader range of investors, including those with smaller portfolios
who previously could not afford bespoke financial planning (Fisch et al. 2019).
This democratisation is key to mobilising capital towards sustainable outcomes—
personalised portfolios at low cost, scaling ESG investing, and enhancing trans-
parency and regulatory alignment (Bianchi and Brière 2023; Feng et al. 2024).
The convergence of sustainable investing and robo-advisory is set to accelerate,
fundamentally reshaping capital allocation to wardsclimateresilience,socialequity,
andresponsiblegovernance.
The use of AI capabilities in robo-advisory enables continuous monitoring
of portfolio holdings against evolving ESG standards, allowing for real-time
rebalancing in response to new data or regulatory changes. This capability helps
address the risk of greenwashing and ensures that investment portfolios remain
aligned with stated sustainability goals (ACCA & CA ANZ 2021). These are
substantive development in an investment segment in which litigation risks are
intensifying. Greenwashing and ‘green-hushing’ have already prompted stricter
anti-misrepresentation rules, such as the FCA’s anti-greenwashing guidance, which
requires sustainability claims to be ‘fair, clear and not misleading’. Courts are
increasingly receptive to climate-related litigation, illustrated by high-profile cases
such as DWS facing investigation for overstating ESG credentials and lawsuits in
the USA against BlackRock and other asset managers over alleged greenwashing
of investment funds. These cases demonstrate that fiduciary duty is emerging
as a significant legal liability risk, where advisors may face claims not only

SustainableInvestingandtheRoleofAI-DrivenRobo-Advisors 375
for financial negligence but also for failing to integrate ESG considerations in
line with client mandates and regulatory standards (FCA 2023; Bronzini et al.
2024). Thus, future developments will likely see robo-advisors acting as engines
of ESG standardisation, bridging persistent rating divergences (Berg et al. 2022),
allowing dynamic portfolio rebalancing and embedding fast-tracked compliance
with revisions in regulatory frameworks such as the EU SFDR, UK SDR, and
ISSB’s IFRS S1/S2 standards. Advances in explainable AI will be critical, ensuring
thatclientsandregulatorsalikecantraceinvestmentdecisionswithclarity,thereby
mitigatingrisksofgreenwashingandmisrepresentation(FCA2023).
From a policy perspective, the coming years will be defined by how effectively
supervisory frameworks integrate technological innovation. Initiatives such as the
EU’s SFDR, the UK’s SDR, and ISSB’s IFRS S1/S2 standards already provide
an institutional backbone for global ESG disclosure (Busch 2023; ISSB 2023).
However, future regulation will need to go further—ensuring explainability of AI-
driven recommendations, setting guardrails against sy stemic risks from correlated
algorithms, and embedding robust cyber resilience (FSB 2024; ESMA 2 025).
Importantly, regulatory harmonisation will need to be dynamic, with machine-
readable formats to keep pace with rapidly evolving AI models and datasets (Virk
2025).
Looking ahead, the challenge for policy and industry alike is to ensure that the
democratisation of sustainable investing does not come at the expense of systemic
stability or investor protection. By embedding ethical AI, adaptive regulatory
integration,androbustcompliance,robo-advisorscantransformsustainabilityfrom
aspirational rhetoric into enforceable, auditable, and growth-oriented investing
space.

Robo-Advisory Under Review: The
Marke t’s Verdict
Yan H uang
Abstract This chapter examines the evolving landscape of robo-advisory services
through the lens of market responses from various players across both emerging and
developed economies. While robo-advisors entered the financial services scene with
the promise of revolutionising investment management through offering automa-
tion, scalability, and greater accessibility to everyday investors, recent developments
suggest a more complex reality. In the past few years, several major global banks,
including Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan Chase, and UBS, have notably scaled back
or exited their robo-advisory adventures. The primary driver behind this retreat
is profitability. Although robo-advisory platforms are efficient and low cost, they
charge minimal advisory fees and often require low account minimums to attract
mass retail clients. This business model also struggles to cover the substantial costs
involved in client acquisition, compliance with regulatory frameworks, and ongoing
technology maintenance. As a result, maintaining financial sustainability at scale
becomes increasingly difficult for firms. Despite these setbacks among legacy banks,
there are successful and inspiring players. Firms such as Vanguard and Better-
ment showcase how digital platforms can succeed when they deliver a clear and
compelling value proposition to a well-defined market segment. Looking beyond
maturemarkets,emergingeconomiesalsopresentsignificantopportunitiesforrobo-
advisoryexpansion.CountriessuchasIndia,SouthAfrica,China,andthoseinthe
Middle East are showing increasing interest in digital wealth management. These
regionsbenefitfromarisingmiddleclass,highmobilepenetration,andagrowing
appetitefortech-enabledfinancialsolutions.
Keywords Robo-advisors · Fintechinnovation · Automatedfinancialadvice ·
Digitalplatformcompetition · Hybridhuman–AIadvisory · Robo-advisor
businessmodels

Business School, University of Exeter, Exeter,UK
e-mail:y.huang8@exeter.ac.uk

382 Y.Huang
Financial decisions are complex at different life stages. Uncertainties further com-
plicate the management of individuals’ assets. With their professional knowledge
and expertise, financial advisors provide support to help people make informed
decisions. When a financial advisor offers financial advice to an investor, the
process normally involves evaluating her financial position, identifying her financial
objectives in different states of life, and assessing her risk appetite. Based on the
evaluation, the advisor proposes an investment portfolio that is suitable for the client
to meet her goals. Once the investment advice is taken, the advisor will monitor
the portfolio performance and periodically rebalance it to reflect market conditions
or any changes in the client’s circumstances. This service comes at a high cost.
Advisory service charges for advice are normally either on an hourly basis or as a
percentage of assets under management (AUM). Take the U.K. as an example. The
Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) reports that average charges are 2.4% of the
amount invested for the initial advice as a one-off charge and 0.8% of AUM annually
for ongoing advice (PDR/FAMR evaluation 2010). These high charges, plus a high
level of minimum asset requirements, create barriers for smaller inve storswhoneed
financial advice. However, the need for financial guidance extends beyond high-
net-worth individuals to include those with modest savings who also benefit from
structuredadvice.Withthetechnologicaladvancement,robo-advisorscameintothe
pictureasapotentialsolutiontoofferaccessibleandaffordableservicestoinvestors
with smaller assets. According to Morningstar’s 2025 Robo-Advisor report, the
median advisory fee is 0.25% of AUM annually, which is significantly lower than
traditionaladvisorycharges.Sincethelaunchofthefirstrobo-advisorservingretail
investors by Betterment in 2010, the growth of robo-advisory services has been
rapid, with the potential of scaling leveraging by technology. The early success
offintechinnovatorsgeneratedaherdingeffectacrossthefinancialsector.Statista
(2024) predicts that by 2029, the global robo-advisory market will grow to $2.38
trillion in AUM and serve around 35 million c lients. The U.S. market dominates
withanestimated$1.46trillioninAUMin2024(KPMG2024). The early success
of the fintech firms in providing the robo-advisory services sparked interest among
financial institutions, including asset managers and universal banks. However, the
strategies of firms involved in the robo-advisory wave led to different outcomes.
Some firms have been able to scale their services and take up the market shares.
Others withdrew when they could not achieve their goals. Both the successful
and failed cases are reviewed from the beginning of the firms’ journey in robo-
advisory services to the most recent development in this chapter to investigate the
opportunitiesandchallengesinthisevolvingservice.
1 The Robo-Advisor Fev er
The first robo-advisor platform was launched by Betterment, a financial savings
startup, at the TechCrunch Disrupt conference in 2010. At launch, it offered
portfolios composed of stock and bond index ETFs. Users could choose their

Robo-AdvisoryUnderReview:TheMarket’sVerdict 383
preferred asset allocation, receive an analysis of their portfolio, and compare their
choices with those of people in different age and income groups. The platform
initially charged a fee of 0.9% regardless of the number of trades an investor
made and had no minimum capital requirement. Betterment’s aim was to enter the
financial savings industry by giving retail clients easy access to diversified portfolios
of stocks and bonds that were automatically rebalanced against the market indices.
Based on modern portfolio theory, which advocates the benefit of diversification in
investment, a committee of academics and fund managers decided the portfolio mix
on a quarterly basis. This initiative, with zero-capital requirements, vastly reduced
the barriers for small investors who wanted to invest in a div ersifiedportfolio.Before
Betterment, index funds were not accessible to smaller investors as the cost for
them to serve smaller investors was high, and ETFs charged trading fees for each
purchaseandsale.Althoughtheservicefeewasnotmuchdifferentfromthehuman
robo-advisoryservices,thezero-capitalentryrequirementallowedsmalleraccounts
to combine automated risk profiling with low-cost portfolio diversification. This
innovationattractedmarketrecognition,withitsAUMincreasingfrom$10million
to$50millionafter2years.
Wealthfront followed with the launch of its robo-advisor in December 2011.
The firm had begun its Series A funding in 2007 under the name kaChing, during
which it tested virtual portfolios. Its products were built on modern portfolio theory,
giving smaller investors access to diversified portfolios without the high capital
requirements as for traditional financial advisors. The firm was able to use Goldman
Sach’s investment model as it was open sourced. At launch, clients were required
to complete a short questionnaire of 10 simple questions to establish their risk
profile, which the system used to recommend customised portfolios drawn from
a selection of low-cost exchange-traded funds (ETFs) across six asset classes. To
gain market share rapidly, Wealthfront charged no advisory fee on the first $25,000
and applied a fee of 0.25% on assets above that threshold. The minimum capital
was $5000. Within just two and a half years, its AUM had climbed to $800 million,
making it the largest robo-advisor at the time. Apart from providing advice to invest
in diversified portfolios, the firm also introduced the tax-loss harvesting feature
embedded in robo-advising. This feature offered small investors the premium
product which had been only available for high-net-worth investors. The process
of identifying assets that have declined in value, selling them, and reinvesting the
proceeds into assets with similar risk characteristics was automated to reduce the
costsignificantly.Smallinvestorscouldhavethebenefitofreductionoftaxliability
throughtherobo-advisoryservices.Thescalingpossibilityonadailybasisthrough
robo-advisoryservicesbyBettermentandWealthfrontreceivedmassivepopularity
among the investor community. It also gave confidence to other market players
to enter the field. SigFig, originally a financial information platform, tried out
its robo-advisory services, which allowed investors to track their portfolios while
receiving tailored recommendations. The advisory service itself was free, but the
firm generated revenue through commissions on new investments made via the
platform’srecommendations.ThismodeldifferentiateditselffromBettermentand
Wealthfront.

384 Y.Huang
The wave of new entrants gave inspiration to other market players to provide
robo-advisory services which target specific investor needs. In 2016, Ellevest was
launched for women only to address the gender gaps in investment by tailoring
financial decisions more closely to their needs. This demonstrated how technology
could be adapted to serve different market segments. While its portfolios were
broadly in line with the competitors, Ellevest charged a higher fee of 0.5%, com-
pared with competitor rates ranging from 0.15% to 0.35%. Its model incorporated
factors specific to women, such as salary progression patterns and longer life
expectancy. In the same year, OpenInvest introduced its robo-advisor focusing
on socially responsible investing through diversification of value-based services.
Investors could align investments with their personal beliefs, particularly on social
impact, i.e., excluding weapon manufacturers or tobacco firms, o r choosing firms
whichpromotegenderequality.Automaticrebalancingensuredportfolioscontinued
totrackmarketindicesclosely.Theannualfeerangedbetween0.20%and0.30%,
which was higher than typical index funds that charged around 0.05% to 0.16%.
Similarly,anothernicheemergedwithWahedInvestlaunchedintheUnitedStates
in2015astheworld’sfirstrobo-advisorofferingShariah-compliantportfoliosand
expandedtotheUnitedKingdomin2018.Portfoliosincludeglobalandemerging-
market equities, sukuk (Islamic bonds), and gold. Fees were tiered at 0.79% per
annum on asset value below $100,000 and 0.49% on asset value of $100,000 or
more.
The adventurous spirit of the pioneers and the bold initiatives taken by them
were evidenced by rapid growth in AUM and the number of investors choosing the
robo-advisory services. The disruption and early success of robo-advisors in wealth
management made financial institutions, such as asset managers or universal banks,
compelled toexplorethemarket’spotentialtoavoidbeingleftbehind.Somefirms
were cautious about participating by partnering with the established firms, while
othersstartedin-housepilotstobuildproprietarysolutions.
Before committing to its own branded robo-advisor, Fidelity formed a short-
term strategic alliance with Betterment in 2014, and the collaboration lasted a year.
During this partnership, Betterment designed a tool for Fidelity’s financial advisors
to allow them to manage clients and their assets on Betterment’s platform. This
tool effectively reduced the paperwork for advisors when accepting new clients.
Furthermore, it offers human advisor services to Betterment’s clients who would
like to opt for the services. This partnership worked well initially, as Fidelity
could focus on its strength in high-value services while Betterment provided the
technology and undertook cumbersome tasks, such as onboarding clients and
collecting fees from clients. But the model started to show its flaws. The financial
products offered in the platform remained limited to Vanguard ETFs, excluding
Fidelity’s own offerings. This exclusion led to the termination of the partnership.
In 2016, Fidelity Investments decided to build its own robo-advisor infrastructure
and embedded its own financial products. Fidelity Go had a similar portal design
as Betterment’s, serving both retail investors and financial advisors. Its primary
focuswasonattractingmillennialinvestors.Theminimumcapitalwas$5000,and

Robo-AdvisoryUnderReview:TheMarket’sVerdict 385
the advisory fee was between 0.35% and 0.40%. Betterment charged a 0.25% fee
withoutminimumcapitalrequirement.
Charles Schwab, another asset manager, joined the game ambitiously by launch-
ing its own robo-advisor. Schwab Intelligent Portfolios (SIP) offered automated
online investment advice to retail investors. At launch, the platform offered 54 ETFs
drawn not only from Schwab’s own range but also from providers such as Vanguard.
For premium clients, they also offered a hybrid model with human advisory services.
To stay competitive, the service charged no commissions, advisory fees, or account
service fees. The only cost to clients was the operating expense ratio of the ETFs.
However, a minimum investment of $5000 was required, similar to Wealthfront’s
threshold. The no-advisory-fee approach attracted significant market attention as
a successful marketing strategy. But the model was too good to be true. Many
critics questioned the fee structure and investigated the hidden fees. Clients seemed
to pay indirectly through reduced returns on their cash holdings, which was not
revealed to them. This lack of transparency fell onto the radar of regulators. The
SEC investigated the firm between March 2015 and November 2018, and more
details came to the surface. The investigation showed that the SIP account held
6% to 29.4% of clients’ assets in cash based on their risk tolerance. Then this
pre-set cash would be swept into the affiliate bank to earn interest rate spread.
This resulted in lowering the client’s total portfolio return, particularly during the
time when other assets outperformed cash. In 2021, a class-action complaint was
filed by three investors alleging undisclosed fees from the “cash d rag”, which has
negative impacts on clients’ portfolio returns. In 2022, the SEC charged the firm
for “misleading robo-advisor clients about absence of hidden fees”, and the firm
settled for $187 million. This was the first time a robo-advisory business model
was publicly scrutinised in depth. It raised questions about the sustainability of
the robo-advisory model. Was its main source of profit coming from fees or from
cash products? A majority of independent robo-advisors remain privately held
firms.Evenwhenrobo-advisoryservicesarepartoflargerpubliclylistedfinancial
institutions,theirindividualperformanceisrarelyreportedasaseparatelineitem.
However, with Wealthfront’s decision to file for an IPO on 29 September 2025, it
hasbecomepossibletoexamineindetailthefinancialaccountsofoneofthesector’s
largestmarketplayers.Wealthfront’srevenue isconcentrated incashmanagement
products, which accounted for 75% of total revenue in 2025, while investment
advisoryservicescontributedaround24%.Wealthfront’srevenuecompositionshed
lightonSchwabIntelligentPortfolios’model.
In the similar timeline, Vanguard also introduced its in-house robot advisor,
following a two-year pilot program that had been available to investors with
$100,000 or more. The full launch of Vanguard Personal Advisor Services lowered
the entry point to $50,000, and by March 2015 had already attracted over $7
billion in advisory assets. The services were in line with what was offered by
Schwab Intelligent Portfolios. The hybrid model and automated system were the
mainsellingpoints.Theadvisoryfeewaskeptlowat0.3%ofAUM.Theclientele
weremainlyBabyBoomers,bornbetween1946and1964.Thiswasdifferentfrom
theclientfocusofindependentrobo-advisors,suchasBettermentandWealthfront,

386 Y.Huang
who targeted Millennial investors. By 2019, its AUM reached $140 billion. The
firm did not want to miss out on the younger generation who are tech-savvy. So,
in 2019, it introduced a fully automated platform—Vanguard Digital Advisor. To
take in the younger investors with small assets to start with, this service reduced the
minimum investment requirement to $100. Together, the two m odelshavegrownto
becomethelargestrobotadvisorintermsofAUM($365bnbyJune2025).Itslow
fees, which are about half the industry average, and low capital requirement play
importantrolesinitssuccess.
BlackRock, among the asset managers, took the shortcut by acquiring FutureAd-
visor in 2015, a fintech firm focusing on robo-advisors since 2010. The deal
was worth $150 million. FutureAdvisor’s AUM was $600 million at the time of
acquisition. The robo-advisory services were mainly B2B. It offered the digital
solutions to its partner firms, including banks, insurers, and 401(k) platforms. One
major source of income from the robo-advisor is through licensing fees to partner
firms. The firm recognised the growing financial advisory needs from mass-affluent
investors, or those with less than $1 million in investable assets, and tried to leverage
the automation technology to build an ecosystem with more institutional players.
The management team of BlackRock was clearonthegoalofthefirmintherobo-
advisorrace.Thefirmwasaimingtoenhance itsowntechnology infrastructureto
better manage risk and construct portfolios. This innovative model provided new
perspectives to the market. Although the firm allowed organic growth of the retail
businessoftherobo-advisor,thegrowthofAUMwasconsiderablyslowerthanother
assetmanagers.
Universal banks followed suit, investing heavily in technology to capitalise on
their brand strength, sizeable client bases, and broad distribution channels. Bank
of America (BofA) introduced Merrill Edge Guided Investing (MEGI) in 2017 as
a hybrid robo-advisory platform. Its fees were broadly in line with competitors,
charging 0.45% with a minimum investment of $1000. For clients with deposits of
$20,000 or more, the service also offered access to a financial planner, at a higher
advisory fee of 0.85%. Like most robo-advisors, it uses algorithms to evaluate an
investor’s risk profile and construct portfolios built primarily from low-cost ETFs,
with Vanguard and iShares as the main providers. Its distinguishing feature is that
these portfolios are actively managed by the investment team. Asset allocations
are not fixed but are regularly reviewed and adjusted by the management team in
response to shifting market conditions. This service became “the biggest growth
area” for BofA and grew “faster than most of the FinTechs in the same pace” over
the following years. By leveraging its large existing client base, BofA was able to
reachthescaleofBettermentandWealthfrontinnearlyhalfthetime.Tomakethe
platformmorefriendlytousers,MerrillEdgeaccountswereintegratedwithBofA’s
Preferred Rewards programme and its banking services. Clients can manage their
savings and investment accounts in one app. This one-stop-shop business model
was well received by young investors, who accounted for 52% of MEGI accounts
in 2024. It enables cross-selling opportunities to this group of investors and also
gradually moves them from pure robo-advisory solutions with the lowest fees to
hybridmodels,eventuallygraduatesthemtohigher-net-worthservices.

Robo-AdvisoryUnderReview:TheMarket’sVerdict 387
To tackle the same group of investors, Morgan Stanley in 2017 also released
Access Investing with a $5000 minimum capital requirement and a 0.35% fee.
To capture the interests of the millennial generation, the firm targeted thematic
portfolios and socially responsible investment options. It also labelled its robo as a
premium offering, as retail investors can have access to the same research resources
as other elite clients. Its model is similar to BofA’s, which is to facilitate a smooth
transition of young investors to full-service clients once their wealth grows and
needs become complex. Morgan Stanley was clear that its robo-advisor would serve
as a complementary tool for clients and would not cannibalise the firm’s existing
business. However, the firm reconsidered its strategy after a few years into its own
robo-advisory journey. It acquired E*TRADE for $13 billion in 2020, marking
the biggest takeover by an American lender since the 2008 financial crisis up to
that point. CEO James Gorman’s comment (“it was always buy versus build”)
suggested that the bank may have realised that internal technology inve stmentalone
wouldnotjustifythecosts,andthatitwasbettertofocusonitscorestrengthsand
specialisation. The acquisition added to Morgan Stanley a substantial client base
ofmorethan5millionclientaccountswithover$360billionofretailclientassets

UBS, which focuses on high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth clients, recog-
nised the industry disruption and entered the robo-advisory arena in the 2010s.
It had an adventurous journey. It began with a partnership with SigFig, followed
by testing the waters with its own program, considered acquiring a robo-advisory
competitor but eventually abandoned the plan, and finally decided to withdraw from
the field. In 2016, UBS formed a strategic partnership with SigFig to leverage its
technology to build tools and services for UBS’s 7000 advisors in the United States.
The bank worked closely with SigFig through the Advisor Technology Research
and Innovation lab to explore new wealth management tools. UBS was also among
the investors in SigFig’s $40 million fundraising round. After 1 year, UBS launched
its own Smart Wealth in the U.K. to reach “a new audience” with the feature of
“no people at the back offering advice”. The minimum investment is £15,000, and
the bank was targeting “mass affluent”, defined as investors having £100,000 to
$2,000,000 in assets.Bytheendoftheyear,thisrobo-advisorwonthe“BestUseof
ITinPrivate/WealthManagementAward”attheBankingTechnologyAwards.But
surprisingly, after about 18 months, UBS decided to discontinue the program and
claimedthat“thenear-termpotentialislimited”.TheplatformwassoldtoSigFig.
UBS did not stop its exploration. It rolled out UBS Advice Advantage in 2018 in
the United States. This hybrid robo-advisory platform, designed with SigFig, was
aiming at “emerging affluent clients”. The capital threshold was $10,000, and the
advisory fee was 0.75%. Beyond its traditional client base, the bank recognised
the growing population of millennial and Gen Z affluent investors, like other

388 Y.Huang
competitors. The quickest way for the bank to penetrate the market for a specific
group was through acquisitions. In 2022, it announced plans to acquire Wealthfront
for $1.4 billion. At the time, Wealthfront had $27 billion in AUM and had nearly half
a million clients in the United States. The potential synergies offered by Wealthfront
were substantial. However, 8 months later, UBS decided to walk away from the
deal,whichwouldhavebeenthelargestacquisitionbyUBSsincethe2008global
financial crisis. The firm re-evaluated its robo-advisory ambitions and concluded
thatthismovecouldnot“bringalphainmass-affluent”.
Goldman Sachs had traditionally focused on corporate clients and ultra-high-
net-worth individuals. But it decided to diversify its business model, which had
been focusing on trading and investment banking revenues, by reaching out to
retail clients. Through the acquisition of GE Capital Bank’s US online deposit
platform in 2016, the firm opened its doors to retail clients. Marcus, a consumer
bank, was launched in 2017 to offer personal loans. The retail bank expanded
its business rapidly through a series of acquisitions and partnerships. By 2019,
Marcus had attracted $50 billion in deposits, $5 billion in consumer loans and 4
million customers in the USA. and the U.K. When competitors were exploring the
technological innovations to scale up retail banking, Goldman Sachs also joined the
race. It launched Marcus Invest, an automated investing platform, in 2021. The robo-
advisor allocated client assets to in-house-designed ETFs with a low entry capital of
$1000 and a fee of 0.35%. Within the first few months, ov er10,000accountswere
opened, and themajoritywereheldby existingclients.Although thebeginning of
therobo-advisoryjourneyappeared smoothandstrategicallyconsistent,thefirm’s
move to consumer banking became controversial as losses reached $1.2 billion
in 2022, making cumulative losses of more than $4 billion. The $100 billion in
deposits and more than 14 million clients did not appear sufficient to reverse the
situation.Asaresult,thescalingbackofconsumerbusinessbroughtinuncertainties
on the development of its robo-advisory business, even though it appeared to be a
promisingstrategytoscaleoperationsandreducetheexpensesperclient.
J.P. Morgan Chase launched its robo-advisor, You Invest Portfolios, in 2019 to
allow “digitally engaged customers” in the USA to invest in J.P. Morgan ETFs.
The firm built an online financial supermarket where “customers can now bank,
save, borrow, and invest”. The minimum investment was $2500, and the fee is
0.35%, or less than $1 a month. To pave the way for the robo-advisor launch, the
firm introduced the You Invest platform a year earlier, which offered customers
100 commission-free trades. The platform also included portfolio tools to assess
investors’ risk tolerance and design the portfolios to onboard investors before
introducing the robo-advisor. Within 2 years, the firm made a move to acquire
Nutmeg, a U.K.-based robo-advisor with around 140,000 retail investors and £3.5
billion of AUM. It aimed to build its digital wealth management services in
the U.K. by “using the very latest technology” Nutmeg had, while adding J.P.
Morgan’sproducts.Thisapproachsavedtimeandcostsinbuildingtherobo-advisor
infrastructure,helpedthefirmgaincustomersrapidly,andenabledthecross-selling

The growth of robo-advisors is a story of trial and adaptation to identify
which model best serves each firm. Betterment’s starting point with two simple
portfolios has turned into a broader portfolio mix. The fully automated model
has evolved into a hybrid model with a personal touch to further strengthen
customer relationships. Each stage has demonstrated an adaptive and adventurous
financial culture. Fintech firms took the initiative to welcome small investors, while
established financial institutions either collaborated with fintech firms or invested
in their own infrastructure to capture the growing population of “digital natives”.
Fintech firms increased the awareness of financial institutions of the generational
shift,especiallywithmillennialsandGenZinvestorswhodemandopenness,value,
andconvenience.
2 Survival of t he Fittest
The competition in robo-advisory services is fierce. The benefits of leveraging
technology in wealth management offer the potential to make scaling possible
and profitable when targeting markets with investors who have smaller assets.
By reviewing the different initial approaches adopted by different institutions
ranging from fintech startups to financial institutions, the initial mix of caution
and enthusiasm has evolved into more sophisticated and focused strategies. These
strategies now tend to align robo-advisors more closely with each firm’s long-
term goals, customer base, and areas of specialisation after more than a decade
of exploration and experimentation. This evolution leads to the next question: are
robo-advisorssurviving,andisthemodelsustainable?
Betterment has grown to become one of the largest independent robo-advisors,
with AUM of $46.96 billion by June 2025. The first decade of its growth was largely
organic. It experienced impressive expansion in the first 5 years. But growth began
to slow across several indicators thereafter. For instance, in the first 5 years, the
number of users increased by more than double annually. But this number dropped
significantly to 22% in 2020. Its AUM also recorded triple-digit growth in the initial
years but slowed to about 10% in 2020. The average account size has stabilised
at nearly $30,000. Since 2020, Betterment has undertaken a wave of acquisitions
to retain its market position. It began with the purchase of Wealthsimple Inc.’s
U.S. business in 2021, which had $197 million of AUM and 17,400 clients. It
later acquired Goldman Sachs’ Marcus Invest in 2024, followed by Ellevest’s robo
accounts and assets in 2025. The main synergies from these acquisitions were
the increased amount in AUM and the number of client accounts. As the firm
remains private, there was no publicly available data on its financial information
toevaluateitsprofitability.ItisworthnotingthatBetterment’sfundraisingrounds
endedin2021,withatotalof$435millionraised.TherecentmovesbyBetterment
showed it relied heavily on expansion, acquisition, and scaling to sustain growth.
Wealthfront had a similar early growth pattern to Betterment, driven primarily by
organic expansion. Its last round of fundraising ended in 2022, raising a total of

was $27 billion. After the deal failed through, the firm reported its first profit ($77

cash management business. In 2023, its cash account increased from $9 billion to
$27 billion as it attracted investors with competitive high-yield cash returns. Cash

reassessment of thisstrategy.Advisoryproductscontributeaboutaquarteroftotal

Bank of America is one of the few surviving robo-advisory service providers.
It provides both fully automated and hybrid solutions. With its broad retail client
base and a wide range of financial products and services, the bank has successfully
scaled the service and generated fee-based revenue growth. The platform is fully
integrated into the Merrill and Bank of America digital ecosystem, allowing clients
to manage banking, lending, and investing activities under a single login. Vanguard
and Fidelity also have found a way to make digital advice pay. Both manage
to combine scale, credibility, and accessible pricing. Vanguard’s hybrid Personal
Advisor Services and Fidelity’s Fidelity Go continue to attract a broad client base.
Unfortunately, many financial institutions’ robo-advisors did not survive in the
stand-alone mode. J.P. Morgan discontinued its operation of the fully automated
You Invest Portfolio service in 2023 and attributed the closure to weak demand.
It also retired Nutmeg, a U.K.-based robo-advisor. To maintain its presence in the

3 Robo-Advisory at a Crossroads
Robo-advisory services emerged in the aftermath of the global financial crisis
as a cost-efficient response to the inaccessibility of traditional financial advice.
With advisory fees as low as 0.25% of assets under management, compared with
traditional average rates of 1% annually, fintech firms such as Betterment and
Wealthfront democratised investing for clients with modest savings. The model
promised accessibility, scalability, and efficiency. It has become a race over the past
decade among financial institutions, as the growing momentum in robo-advisory
has led to a surge of entrants into the market. Partnerships, self-built solutions, or
acquisitions were popular approaches among financial institutions to join the race.
This robo-advisor wave pushed the global AUM prediction to exceed$2.38trillion
by 2025. However, as the industry matures, the market’s verdict remains mixed.
Someplatforms,suchasVanguardandFidelity,havesuccessfullyinstitutionalised
digitaladvice,whileothers,includingGoldmanSachs,UBS,andJ.P.Morgan,have
scaled back or exited the fully automated model. Fintech firms have managed to
survive by pursuing aggressive acquisitions to expand their AUM and client base,
orbymaximisingtheprofitabilityofcashaccounts.
The foundation of robo-advisory lies in a trade-off between automation and
personalisation. The automation process starts with “one-size-fits-all” question-
naires to identify the risk categories of investors. The questionnaires are based
on the assumptions of similar risk investors sharing identical financial goals and
behavioural responses. The simplification ignored the complexity of an individual’s
financial circumstances. For example, children’s education, job redundancy, and
family obligations. Furthermore, human advisors bond better with clients than
robo-advisors. Especially when clients experience market volatility or a change of
financial position, access to human advisors provides more reassurance than the
app or the website. Therefore, is a robo-advisor a substitute for a human advisor
or a complement? A hybrid model, which keeps human advisors as an option for
investors, appears to be a more popular approach adopted by firms. For example,
Vanguard Personal Advisor Services and Bank of America’s MerrillEdge Guided
Investingofferthisoptionatapremiumtoattracthigh-net-worthclients.Onemore
factortoconsiderwhenshiftingtorobo-advisoryservicesistheshortageoffinancial
advisors, which can reach 110,000 in the USA by 2033 based on McKinsey’s
2025 report. The U.K. market also echoed the concern. Based on FCA’s data,
more than 50% of advisors are aged above 50, and the number of young advisors
declined by 18% between 2022 and 2024. This demographic imbalance opens the
question of the advice gap. The growing demand for financial advisory services
outpacestheindustry’scapacity.Onesolutionisrobo-advisors,whichcantakeup
thecumbersometasksandfreeupthetimeforhumanadvisorstofocusoncomplex,
high-valuerelationships.
Ultimately, the sustainability of robo-advisory depends on its ability to evolve
beyond algorithmic standardisation. What works for one organisation does not
necessarily translate into success for another. Even firms with similar business

392 Y.Huang
models and clientele have experienced vastly different outcomes. Although there are
market survivors such as Betterment, Wealthfront, and Vanguard, a large proportion
of providers still do not disclose detailed robo-advisory results. Figures on AUM,
user numbers, and average account sizes provide only a partial picture of success.
The lack of transparency of the robo-advisory model makes it difficult for observers
or players t obeabletoanalysethesustainabilityofthemodel.Onlytimewilltell.A
fullerunderstandingwillrequiregreatertransparencyfrominstitutionsandamore
